Automakers keep shoving more tech into their cars, despite evidence that consumers are increasingly fed up with huge screens and glitchy software. In fact, the features that car owners appreciate the most happen to be the ones they barely notice, according to the latest tech survey from JD Power.
Car owners want tech they can ignore
You can keep your passenger screens.
You can keep your passenger screens.
The consumer research firm surveyed 68,084 owners of new 2026 model-year vehicles after 90 days of ownership. The survey touched on 40 automotive technologies covering comfort and convenience; connected vehicles; driver assist; electric vehicles; and smart vehicles.
The features that scored the highest were the ones that were the most inconspicuous, like smart ignition, in which the vehicle automatically starts and turns off based on driver actions, or smart HVAC systems, which use AI to automatically adjust the cabin environment for maximum comfort and efficiency. These were the big winners in JD’s survey — mostly because they require the least attention from the driver. Smart ignition, in particular, delivered the highest overall satisfaction, with only 2.4 problems per 100 vehicles.
“For automakers, the opportunity is to prioritize technology that makes driving simpler, not more complicated,” Doron Hikry, director of customer success at JD Power, said in a press release. “The features that solve real problems without adding effort or stress for the driver are the ones resonating most with customers.”
Superfluous tech features like passenger screens, in which an extra screen is embedded in the dash in front of passengers, rated the lowest in satisfaction. These screens first began cropping up in premium brands, like Mercedes, BMW, and Porsche, but have yet to bleed over to more mass-market vehicles. Apparently, they’re just wasted space on the dash, with more than one-third of owners who have a passenger screen reporting they’ve never tried to use it. Only 6 percent admitted to using their passenger screens every time they drive. Yikes.
Another tech feature that has more work to do in winning over customers is hands-free driving, also known as Level 2 Plus automation. These are features like Tesla’s Full Self-Driving, Ford’s BlueCruise, GM’s Super Cruise, and Mercedes’ Drive Pilot.
Unlike Level 2 systems, which require drivers to keep their hands on the steering wheel, these L2 Plus systems allow for completely hands-free driving on certain roads. Car owners told JD Power they preferred L2 systems in terms of design and quality of experience, suggesting that more automation does not necessarily mean more customer satisfaction. Interestingly, Level 2 systems were recording slightly higher problems per 100 vehicles (14.3) as L2 Plus ones (13.8).
“The results indicate that owners may currently be more comfortable with systems that clearly assist the driver rather than those that introduce a greater degree of automation,” said Hikry.
What these results suggest is that car owners don’t necessarily mind more technology in their vehicles, just as long as they don’t make the task of driving more complicated. The individual awards underscore this point: The Cadillac Escalade and Toyota Tundra both won for camera mirrors, while other automakers notched wins for blind-spot cameras, digital keys, one-pedal driving, and EV charging schedulers.

An upcoming election could produce modern Germany's 1st far-right state governor
An election in eastern Germany on Sunday could produce the first far-right state governor in the country’s post-World War II history
MOESER, Germany -- An election in eastern Germany on Sunday could produce the first far-right state governor in the country's post-World War II history as Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his unpopular national government struggle to dispel what he calls “widespread moroseness.”
Several polls show a large lead for the anti-migration Alternative for Germany, or AfD, ahead of the election to the state legislature in Saxony-Anhalt. Taking control of a state government would be the biggest prize in the party’s 13-year history, a political shock to Germany and at least a symbolic blow to Merz.
“If AfD wins the election and forms the government, that would be kind of breaking a taboo in Germany,” said Wolfgang Merkel, a political science professor with the WBZ Berlin Social Science Center. Modern Germany so far has been “an exception” in Europe in having no radical right-wing party governing at the national, state or big-city level, he added.
Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union has led Saxony-Anhalt, a region west of Berlin that's among the country’s less prosperous and is home to 2.1 million of Germany's 83.5 million people, since 2002. But it faces strong headwinds.
In last year’s national election, AfD achieved the best postwar showing by a far-right party, with 20.8% of the vote. It became Germany’s biggest opposition party.
It was stronger in the ex-communist east, including Saxony-Anhalt. And with Merz's government struggling to convince voters it can turn around a stubbornly slow economy, it has gained in national polls as it harnesses discontent with issues beyond its signature theme of curbing migration.
In Saxony-Anhalt, AfD is seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature. That would overcome the so-called “firewall” of mainstream parties’ refusal to work with AfD, whose regional branch is one of several classified by the domestic intelligence agency as a proven right-wing extremist group. AfD vehemently rejects accusations of extremism.
AfD’s campaign slogan is “Everything is possible.”
“This is a historic opportunity that we have here in Saxony-Anhalt,” its candidate for governor, Ulrich Siegmund, told The Associated Press at a campaign event in the small town of Moeser, where supporters lined up to meet the charismatic 35-year-old over beer and sausages. “We will write history here."
Among his top priorities, Siegmund lists “the deportation of people who are illegal, a deportation offensive and above all dropping the incentives for why people come here and exploit our social system.” He wants to initiate a long process to withdraw Saxony-Anhalt from the regional public broadcaster, citing concerns about “disinformation.”
AfD’s first and so far only head of a county administration was elected in 2023 in neighboring Thuringia state. A state administration would be a far bigger prize, fueling the party's ambitions of further gains and one day governing at the national level.
Germany’s 16 states have extensive powers, for example in overseeing security matters and running the education system.
In Saxony-Anhalt, AfD wants to allow home schooling, which so far isn't permitted in Germany. It pledges to ban schools from officially raising the rainbow flag and ensure they fly the national flag. It opposes taxpayers' money being “given away” to Ukraine and says it would push to lift sanctions against Russia, but that isn't a matter state governments can decide.
“No one here needs to be afraid, quite the contrary,” Siegmund said. “Every honest person in Saxony-Anhalt will benefit from an AfD-led government.”
Siegmund's main opponent, incumbent governor Sven Schulze from Merz’s CDU, told the AP at his party's offices in Magdeburg, the state capital, that AfD “wants the past back” and the state would face “isolation” with AfD in power.
He pointed to major progress made in strengthening Saxony-Anhalt's economy and bringing down unemployment since Germany was reunited in 1990. The far right, he said, effectively “doesn't want to have anyone here who was born abroad and lives and works here.” With many immigrants working in hospitals and companies, for example, that would be “a huge problem for Saxony-Anhalt,” he said.
“AfD does one thing — it describes problems,” said Schulze, who said that he won't work with the party and his own CDU is “100%” behind him. “But it never has a solution for a problem.”
AfD's chances of governing are uncertain even if it does become by far the strongest party. If it doesn't win an absolute majority, Merkel said he doesn't see it governing for lack of any potential coalition partner.
That likely would leave Schulze trying to cobble together some kind of alliance with multiple smaller parties to his left. That would leave many people saying that “they are clinging to power,” Merkel said.
It remains unclear how an AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt would affect the national government, particularly if Merz’s CDU and its coalition partners, the center-left Social Democrats, fare poorly in elections Sept. 20 in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, another eastern state.
Merkel said he believes Saxony-Anhalt is too small to have “any particular impact.” But a significant loss of votes would amplify a narrative that the traditional big parties are in decline.
Merz's government needs to prove its ability to reform Germany and so far lacks “visible successes,” Merkel added, noting that “when the economy isn't running, basically all areas of politics are infected.”
Merz sought to spread optimism after his Cabinet met last week to underline its determination to push through reforms.
“We must get out of this climate of glumness and anger,” he said. “Together, we must shake off this widespread moroseness that has long paralyzed our country.”

Protests against reservations were held at Jantar Mantar and Connaught Place in Delhi on 21 and 23 August 2026. The protests were part of an online campaign called the ‘Reservation Hatao Andolan’, which has over 5.6 million followers on Instagram. The protestors primarily demanded that government jobs and opportunities in educational institutions be provided based on financial status and merit, rather than caste. They also demanded the withdrawal of the 2026 Equity Regulations, which were brought in by the UGC to control discrimination in higher educational institutions.
In this context, a video of a huge crowd blocking a road is being shared on social media, claiming to show the protest at Jantar Mantar on 21 August 2026, demanding the withdrawal of the UGC Equity Regulations, 2026. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video of massive crowd at Jantar Mantar, Delhi, protesting against reservations and demanding a rollback of the UGC Equity Regulations on 21 August 2026.
Fact: The video actually depicts a July 2026 farmers’ protest in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, demanding minimum support price (MSP) for their Moong crop. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to an identical clip (archive), which was uploaded on the Facebook page of Ramakant Dwivedi on 29 July 2026. The description states that it shows a farmers’ protest in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. We found several other videos of this protest on social media, which can be seen here and here.
The protest site can also be identified on Google Maps as Narmadapuram Road in Bhopal. According to reports (here, here & here), the farmers were protesting to demand 100% procurement of their Moong (green gram) crop at the Minimum Support Price (MSP), among other issues. The farmers marched from Narmadapuram to Bhopal, demanding the abolition of the e-token system for procurement and fertiliser distribution. However, the protest ended after talks with the government.
To sum it up, the viral video depicts a July 2026 farmers’ protest in Bhopal and is falsely being shared as UGC roll back protests in Delhi.

Srinagar, Aug 31: On the death anniversary of former President of India Pranab Mukherjee, Chairman of the Kashmir Policy and Strategy Group Ashok Bhan paid tribute to the veteran statesman, describing him as a “towering statesman, an unwavering Constitutionalist and a political scholar” whose public life embodied the finest traditions of Indian democracy.
Bhan said Mukherjee’s journey from a modest beginning in a village in Bengal to the highest constitutional office of the country was marked by intellect, humility, experience and an abiding commitment to public service.
He said Mukherjee possessed a rare understanding of India’s political institutions and the complexities of its democratic journey, earning respect across political lines.
‘A man of culture and political scholarship’
Recalling Mukherjee’s multifaceted personality, Bhan said his journey included his early years as a teacher and journalist in a small village in Bengal before he emerged as an avid reader, prolific writer and standard-bearer of India’s intellectual heritage.
His vast knowledge of history, politics, economics and parliamentary practice made him an exceptional repository of institutional wisdom, Bhan said.
“His vast knowledge of history, politics, economics and parliamentary practice made him an exceptional repository of institutional wisdom,” he said.
Bhan added that Mukherjee believed deeply in dialogue, accommodation and the strength of democratic institutions.
“His interventions were informed not merely by political expediency but by scholarship and a profound understanding of India’s civilisational and constitutional inheritance,” he said.
‘His legacy continues to inspire’
Bhan said Mukherjee remained, above all, an unwavering Constitutionalist whose commitment to the rule of law and good governance was central to his political and administrative philosophy.
He said Mukherjee consistently urged younger generations of leaders to uphold India’s constitutional values and demonstrate deep respect for democratic institutions.
“His passing left a void in public life, but his legacy continues to remind us that politics, at its finest, is an instrument of national service, constitutional responsibility and the pursuit of the common good,” Bhan said.
Pranab Mukherjee, who served as the 13th President of India from 2012 to 2017, passed away on August 31, 2020, aged 84. His death anniversary is observed on August 31.

For crores of Indian families, the financial shock of hospitalisation — especially in a private hospital — begins even before treatment is complete. The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare, in its 176th Report tabled in Parliament on August 7, 2026, noted that the average cost of hospitalisation is ₹50,508 in a private facility, compared with ₹6,631 in a government facility. For childbirth, the average out-of-pocket medical expenditure in private facilities is ₹37,630, against ₹2,299 in public facilities.
Some of the contradictions
The committee has made 368 recommendations, including standardised package rates and mandatory pre-treatment cost estimates. Among the widely reported proposals is that basic room tariffs in metropolitan private hospitals should not exceed the average tariff of three-star hotels that are nearby. It has also suggested that large corporate hospitals earning from medical tourism, foreign patients and high-net-worth individuals should cross-subsidise poorer Indians and reserve beds for Ayushman Bharat-Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) beneficiaries at regulated rates. Yet, there is a contradiction. India wants more private and foreign capital in health care, particularly in Tier-2, Tier-3 and rural areas, while simultaneously asking the government to review foreign direct investment rules related to the acquisition and management of existing hospitals.
There is a strong case for continued investment in Indian health care. Hospitals require substantial capital. Land, equipment, intensive care units, digital systems, laboratories and trained personnel are expensive. Public hospitals cannot currently meet all demand for secondary and tertiary care. Private hospitals therefore fill an important gap. Foreign investors and private-equity funds can bring capital, managerial capacity, technology and the capacity to expand hospital networks. India also needs investment in pharmaceutical and medical-device manufacturing. If regulation becomes excessively restrictive or unpredictable, some investment may move elsewhere. This could slow capacity expansion and delay the development of better health-care infrastructure in cities and districts where need is genuine.
However, in all sectors, capital comes with expectations of returns. In health care, it creates a special concern because patients are not ordinary consumers. A patient rarely decides independently whether an MRI is required, whether hospital admission should continue for two more days, or whether a procedure is necessary. Health care is shaped by what economists call information asymmetry: the provider knows more than the patient. Therefore, when financial incentives become too strong, they can influence not just the price of care but also how much care is delivered.
A closer look at private care
This is where the role of private equity and venture capital in health care deserves closer attention. Corporate hospital groups increasingly compete for well-known specialists, sophisticated technology and premium infrastructure. These can improve quality, but also create a high-cost ecosystem. Hospitals that pay very high salaries to senior specialists and super-specialists, acquire expensive equipment and operate under pressure to increase revenue must eventually recover these costs. Revenue targets, procedure-linked incentives, higher occupancy expectations and higher revenue per bed can gradually influence institutional behaviour. Most doctors act in patients’ interests. Yet, systems shape behaviour. If hospitals and doctors are rewarded for doing more, the direction becomes predictable.
The result is not only higher cost but also a worrying medicalisation. Lab investigations may detect abnormalities that would never have caused harm. More screening can lead to unnecessary follow-up tests. A patient who could be managed as an outpatient may be admitted. Caesarean sections, angioplasties, intensive-care admissions, diagnostic packages and long lists of medicines must therefore be seen not only as individual clinical decisions but also within the incentive structure of the health system. This does not mean these interventions are usually unnecessary. It means that a system rewarding interventions and procedures needs strong safeguards against unnecessary prescriptions, surgeries, investigations and medications.
That is why a review of FDI in the acquisition of existing hospitals is justified. Domestic investors can be equally profit-oriented, while foreign investment can create valuable capacity. The more useful question is about what an investment does to the health system. Does it create new beds or simply acquire existing ones? Does it improve competition or lead to market concentration? Does it enter an underserved district or add another high-end facility in a metro? If an investor receives concessional land, tax benefits or other public support, are there enforceable obligations related to affordable beds or participation in public insurance schemes? India should encourage greenfield investment and manufacturing, while scrutinising acquisitions that reduce competition or raise the risk of excessive pricing.
Price regulation also needs to be approached carefully. The proposal to link hospital room charges to nearby three-star hotels is easy to understand, but cannot by itself solve the affordability problem. A hospital room includes nursing, infection-control and emergency support that a hotel room does not. More importantly, if one component of the bill is capped, hospitals may increase charges elsewhere. India’s experience with coronary stent price regulation showed that government intervention can reduce excessive mark-ups. But hospital care is more complex; what matters is the total cost of an episode. Package rates, transparent estimates, billing standards and audit mechanisms are therefore more useful than isolated caps on individual components. There is also an established approach to such payments: Diagnosis-Related Groups (DRG). A DRG is a patient-classification system that standardised hospital reimbursement by paying a fixed, predetermined amount for an inpatient stay based on the diagnosis and procedures, rather than reimbursing each service separately.
Focus on public health
There is a larger policy question. India cannot regulate its way out of weak public health care. If government hospitals remain overcrowded, understaffed or difficult to access, citizens will continue to depend heavily on private providers. Experience from OECD countries has shown that one effective form of regulation is a strong public health system that provides a credible alternative.
Public hospitals must therefore become a genuine option, not merely the last resort for those who cannot afford private care. Primary health care needs strengthening so that disease is prevented, detected and treated early. Insurance systems, including AB-PMJAY, should reward appropriate care rather than simply higher volumes of procedures. Clinical audits, evidence-based treatment protocols and transparent billing can protect both patients and doctors from commercial pressures.
The Parliamentary Committee is right to focus attention on affordability and to question whether the current pattern of investment in private health care aligns with public interest. Price caps and an FDI review are reasonable starting points, but India needs a wider conversation about the kind of health-care system it is building. Private investment will remain essential, and profit by itself is not the problem.
The problem begins when the pursuit of returns starts a key influence. A health-care system should attract capital, but its clinical priorities must still be set by medical need. The true measure of India’s health-care progress will not be how much money flows into hospitals or what is the annual compounded growth rate in medical tourism, but whether Indian citizens can enter them with confidence that they will receive what they need. No more, no less.
Chandrakant Lahariya is a practising physician specialising in preventive and cardio-metabolic medicine, whose upcoming book, Pill-Free: You Don’t Need Everything You Have Been Prescribed, will be released in September 2026

Sony is adding free TV channels to PS5
Ad-supported streaming channels are hitting Sony's console in the US today.
PlayStation 5 owners in the US will be able to stream free, ad-supported TV (FAST) channels starting today. The console's media tab will offer more than 100 live channels from Sony Pictures Television along with on-demand options. There are channels for movies, TV shows, anime (of course, given Sony owns Crunchyroll), news, sports, documentaries and more.
The movie channels include action, sci-fi and horror offerings from the likes of MovieSphere by Lionsgate, 50 Cent Action and Sony One Horror Hits. You'll be able to watch TV shows such as Community, The Walking Dead, Deal or No Deal USA, Fear Factor and Ice Road Truckers. The anime options include Naruto, Sailor Moon, Hunter x Hunter and Death Note, and there are channels showing gaming, esports, podcasts and comedy programming.
Sony said Live TV on PS5 will be updated with refreshed programming and new channels. It plans to bring the service to Canada and other regions.
As with other recent business decisions like largely ending production of game discs, this makes sense on paper for Sony. Nudging console owners to watch FAST channels on a PS5 instead of the likes of Pluto, Roku or Tubi keeps more of their attention on a PlayStation platform. It could put extra cash in Sony's pocket too at a time when the company is focused more on generating extra revenue from existing customers than selling PS5 units to newcomers.
The timing of this, at the very least, could have been better. The backlash against the depreciation of game discs is not going away anytime soon. Sony also recently told customers in Europe that they'd lose access to hundreds of movies they paid for on the PlayStation Store after a licensing deal expired.
Sure, PlayStation does have more games in the pipeline, and we'll see some of those during this week's State of Play doubleheader. But this feels more like the company dragging the PS5 in the direction of the Xbox One. Microsoft infamously pitched that as an all-in-one entertainment hub, in what turned out to be an ill-fated strategy.

This past week, the top health story, without any doubt, is the huge crisis that is brewing out of proportions in Africa - the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. It was first announced as an outbreak on May 15, this year.As per latest data, it has reached over 5,000 cases, making this the one of the worst Ebola outbreaks in history. The outbreak has clearly outpaced response efforts.
Data from Congo’s Ministry of Health showed the outbreak had so far recorded 5,021 cases, including 2,378 deaths as of August 16, 2026, as it rages in some of the most challenging conditions imaginable fuelled by insecurity, displacement and intense population movements. It has officially infected and killed more people at a greater speed than any other outbreak in history. Starting from the first detected case, it has spread about three times faster than an outbreak from 2014 to 2016 across West Africa, which was the deadliest Ebola outbreak on record with more than 11,000 deaths.
The dire situation was underlined as World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus announced: “We must be frank: the epidemic is far from being under control.” Safety concerns have limited the response as health workers are targeted, particularly in Ituri, the province that has been hit the worst by the outbreak. Residents recently attacked a health team in the territory of Aru after a suspected case was reported there. A mob set fire to an ambulance and damaged two other vehicles, according to Michael Wani, president of the Union of Cultural Associations for the Development of Ituri.
Meanwhile, more than 16,000 doses of the new Ebola vaccine Ervebo arrived in the DRC. WHO experts still do not know whether Ervebo protects humans against the Bundibugyo strain, but early data, notably from animal trials, suggest it could offer some protection.The Ervebo vaccine “has already been used several times, and in particular on a very large scale during the 2018-2020 outbreak”, Samuel Roger Kamba, the DRC’s Minister of Health, told the press.
The other big story in India was also about an infectious disease - H1N1. As the cases continue to surge, experts assure that there is no cause for alarm yet. However they do advise that a large number of children were being affected, and that children with asthma and other chronic conditions might require special intervention.
The H1N1 virus, commonly known as swine flu, is a subtype of influenza A, and can cause respiratory illness, with symptoms including fever or chills, cough, sore throat, a runny or blocked nose, headache, tiredness, and muscle or body aches. In some cases, patients may also experience vomiting and diarrhoea. Cases have been rising in Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru and Kerala, and while there are a number of respiratory-like illnesses also about during this season, doctors have warned that early testing is key. Bindu Shajan Perappadan reports that union Health Minister J.P. Nadda reviewed the H1N1 situation, healthcare preparedness in Delhi.
With National Eye Donation Fortnight being observed across India every year from August 25 to September 8 to raise awareness about eye donation we did our bit to highlight issues relating to eye health a little ahead of schedule.
Athira Elssa Johnson writes about the Lazy eye in children, and about squints. In the former, she focuses on how many parents may miss lazy eye among their children. Often called lazy eye, amblyopia may have no obvious signs and can remain undetected during early childhood. Screening, timely treatment and sustained follow-up are important because visual development is time-sensitive. Squints are another condition that impact the development of vision, and therefore need to be addressed on time. Squint, medically known as strabismus, is a condition in which the two eyes do not align properly. It can affect children and adults and, when it develops during childhood, can interfere with the normal development of vision
In the modern age, the field of ophthalmology is among the earliest adopters of AI systems in health care, so here is an article on using AI systems in smartphones to help detect eye diseases. Kathleen Sherwin and Rishi Raj Borah make an impassioned case for more women to lead eye health care systems.
This week we looked at some little explored aspects of cancer care too. Shrabana Chatterjee writes an interesting story on a hardly-spoken about aspect- Navigating the challenges of fertility and breastfeeding after surviving cancer. This story has a positive message for women in this position - that with careful management and supervision, it can be done.
After a cancer diagnosis, women who have not yet started their families, must be given the option for fertility preservation, say doctors. Options such as embryo freezing before cancer treatment is begun may be considered under medical guidance. Other fertility preservations techniques including oocyte and ovarian-tissue cryopreservation may also be explored before treatment begins. When it comes to breastfeeding, doctors say that after surviving cancer it may pose difficulties, but it can be done under the right medical conditions and with guidance from doctors.
Dr. Siddharth Turkar turns the spotlight on sarcomas: Many soft-tissue sarcomas, which are rare types of cancers that form in fat, muscles and blood vessels, initially look like ordinary lumps. However, when a suspicious mass of this sort is removed without appropriate imaging, tissue diagnosis or oncological planning, the opportunity for the simplest and best-planned first operation may already have been lost.
This is by far the most important gene-based analysis that pertains to us, in India. Rupsy Khurana writes the truth: South Asians are missing from global health databases, and why this matters and what needs to change in this scenario. When scientists try to understand why diseases such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease affect South Asians differently, they often have to rely on genetic data drawn from European populations. Advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning are allowing scientists to mine vast amounts of genomic and health data to detect disease earlier, predict risk, monitor patients and tailor treatments to individuals. But at the heart of this changing landscape lies an old, constant problem – the data used to build these tools lack diversity, she points out.
Further, looking the genetic pool, I write about new research that establishes that natural sugar along with meat consumption powered brain development in early humans. It probably explains the human craving for sweets, today. Read Sugar power: the full story of brain development in humans for more.

Singer D4vd pleads not guilty in murder case and switches to public defender
Burke was charged on April 20 with capital murder in the 2025 death of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez
Singer D4vd, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, has pleaded not guilty to murder and other charges stemming from the death of a 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez, whose dismembered and decomposing remains were found in the trunk of his Tesla at a Hollywood tow yard.
Prosecutors allege that Burke killed Hernandez after she threatened to expose their illegal relationship and damage his music career.
The 21-year-old singer appeared in a downtown Los Angeles courtroom Monday morning and stated he had parted ways with his legal defense team and instead wished to be represented by a public defender.
Burke’s new public defender asked that the arraignment be postponed, but a judge rejected the request. The singer's attorney then entered a not guilty plea. Burke is due back in court Oct. 19 for a status conference.
Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Charlaine F. Olmedo found sufficient evidence following more than four days of sometimes-graphic testimony during a hearing in July to allow the case against Burke to proceed to trial.
Burke was charged on April 20 with capital murder in the 2025 death of Hernandez, along with the special circumstance allegations of lying in wait, murder for financial gain and killing a witness in a criminal investigation.
The Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office has not yet announced whether it will seek the death penalty against Burke, who was arrested April 16 by Los Angeles Police Department officers and remains jailed without bail.
Burke is also charged with one count each of continuous sexual abuse of a child under age 14 and mutilation of human remains.
District Attorney Nathan Hochman said the lying-in-wait allegation stems from D4vd's invitation to the teen to come to his Hollywood Hills home on April 23, 2025, while the financial gain allegation stems from the singer's effort to maintain his lucrative music career, which was being threatened by his relationship with Hernandez.
Hernandez was considered the key witness in the investigation into Burke's alleged sexual activity with the underage girl, leading to the allegation of murdering a witness, the district attorney said.
The teen's body was found last Sept. 8, just days after what would have been her 15th birthday, according to a court filing from the prosecution, which noted that the vehicle had been towed three days earlier while parked about 400 feet from his Hollywood Hills home.
The defense lawyer argued that Burke had "repeatedly expressed his love and care" for the girl even after they broke up and that there was no evidence Burke had ever stated he intended to harm her.
Deputy District Attorney Beth Silverman countered there was "nothing about this case that sounds like an accident" and the teen was "obviously dead" within 20 minutes of being dropped off by an Uber driver at Burke's rented Hollywood Hills home on April 23, 2025.
"We have an underage minor who was threatening to expose this relationship," Silverman told the judge, arguing later that the defense has tried to "dirty up" the girl.

It’s safe to say Grand Theft Auto VI is the most anticipated game ever. Thirteen years after the last entry in the series, rampant fervor and speculation about what features the game will include have ratcheted up. Today, Rockstar Games divulged more details through an exclusive livestream event on Netflix called Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look. The spectacle was a 26-minute-long collection of gameplay, cutscenes, and game mechanics.
And boy, does this sure look like a GTA game. The trailer featured Lucia and Jason, the two main characters, driving around Vice City, GTA’s fictional version of Miami. It highlighted all kinds of violence and shenanigans your characters can engage in, and it looks good doing it.
The livestream follows a week of gameplay leaks and story spoilers by the hacker group Cyberleek, which Rockstar called “heartbreaking.” A bevy of other details about the game emerged just a day before the event in a story published by the British magazine Dazed. The piece chronicles the extraordinary level of detail and effort Rockstar has put into GTA VI, including how players control the characters and the unprecedented realism that Rockstar put into its satirical sandbox version of Miami.
It’s bound to be a massive game; today’s reveal shows just how much of a monster it will be. Here are the big takeaways from the livestream.
It Sure Is Pretty
GTA VI is gorgeous. The cityscapes, nightclubs, and lush natural parks shown all seem vibrant and awash in color.
There is a noticeable difference between cutscenes and gameplay, though, as the gameplay clips looked a little flatter and more desaturated than the cinematic cutscenes. That’s kind of a nitpick, though it’s worth noting that in the very first scene—in the dark basement of a crack house—the lighting is so dim it washes out the features of several Black characters around the table.
You Play as 2 Characters Simultaneously
The player can control two characters, Jason and Lucia, a Bonnie-and-Clyde-esque couple who seem to be working out some lingering tension in their relationship as they go about their various criminal activities.
The voice acting for the main characters and other non-playable characters (NPCs) feels tightly written, though that’s based on the select clips Rockstar showed. According to Dazed, the relationship between the characters can change over time, and the player’s actions can affect how that plays out. Keep that in mind if you’re hoping for a particular ending.
GTA VI offers a plethora of options for changing the two main characters’ appearances. Eating too much or too little food affects their weight. Working out can make them swole. The Extended Look also showed off characters eating and working out in minigames. It was a feature in 2004’s GTA San Andreas and in a smaller way in GTA V. Now, that reactivity will be much more fully realized in GTA VI.
There’s also an array of clothes you can equip your characters with, which Rockstar has apparently coordinated with real-life fashion designers to put in the game. Some of these, however, may only come with the $100 Ultimate Edition that people are very mad about.
Maybe Don’t Hit and Run
The NPCs in the game appear much more responsive and interactive than in prior games. According to Dazed, Rockstar has an entire studio in Los Angeles dedicated to working on NPC pedestrian behavior alone.
In the Extended Look, gameplay segments with car chases pointedly avoided streamrolling over pedestrians. But NPCs wore yoga outfits, rode scooters, and seemed to have more personality than the cut-and-paste crowds of past games.
Driving seems greatly improved. When driving, you have a minimap that looks like an actual GPS map guiding you where to go. A car chase saw the main characters running from the police. The player can switch between Lucia and Jason and choose to either drive or shoot at the pursuers. Shooting out tires can cause a car to flip, crash into the sidewalk, and cause environmental destruction.
At one point, a character also body-slams a cop through a wall, which hints at potentially more destructive environments indoors as well. GTA games have been iffy about destructible environments before, though. Sometimes in GTA V you can easily crash through a large light pole but then get instantly stopped by a volleyball net. So we’ll see how reactive everything gets.
So Much Room for Activities
Vice City and the surrounding areas seem absolutely massive. It’s also fully Florida, allowing your characters to fanboat around the Everglades, kayak on the rivers, or scuba dive and jet ski in the Gulf.
One scene from the trailer shows Lucia accidentally kidnapping a livestreaming influencer, then carrying him along through a car chase from the police. Many of the characters use phones and communicate via text. It’s clear that GTA VI has some satirical takes on social media, but we’ll see how relevant it feels in a constantly shifting era.
You Can Pet the Dog
A dog is in at least one scene of the game. Can you pet it? Yes. Yes, you can.
User-Generated Content
In 2023, Rockstar bought the modding marketplace Cfx and reworked it into an official place to share and purchase user-created mods for the game. That service, along with GTA Online’s Rockstar Mission Creator, which lets users make custom levels and modes, indicates that Rockstar has long realized that GTA is fertile ground for user creativity.
The Extended Look didn’t show anything suggesting it would advance those user-creation capabilities, but that’s likely because the game is being released as a single-player title before any multiplayer elements are added.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a type of leukemia or blood cancer that affects the blood and bone marrow (spongy tissue inside the bones that forms blood cells). It is one of the lesser-known types of blood cancers in India. . According to a 2025 paper published in the European Society of Medicine, CLL is one of the least common leukemias in India, accounting for less than 5% of all leukemias, with incidence rates ten times lesser than in the United States.
What is CLL?
The term ‘lymphocytic’ refers to the particular cells that are affected by this type of leukemia. In this condition the lymphocytes or group of white blood cells in the body exceed the normal count and increase in abnormal quantities inside the patient’s body.
The white blood cells form part of the immune system and help the body fight diseases. When the body contracts an infection, the white blood cell count increases, in a defence mechanism to fight against the infection. As the infection gets better, the white blood cell count decreases. But when a person has CLL, the number of white blood cells do not subside even after an infection leaves the body.
CLL has a slower prognosis in the human body than other types of leukemia. According to doctors, CLL does not have any specific cause. . Doctors said most cases of CLL are not linked to environmental exposure, and are believed to arise from inherent oncogenic changes.
How is CLL diagnosed?
According to Aseem Kumar Samar, director - medical oncology, C.K. Birla Hospitals Jaipur, CLL is a type of cancer that is sometimes discovered by chance during a regular blood check, in particular if lymphocyte counts are abnormally high. To diagnose this condition a complete blood count and a peripheral blood film (smear) are the first steps. Blood cell analysis by flow cytometry is key to confirm the disease as this test reveals the typical abnormal B-lymphocytes present in CLL. “Based on the individual situation, other tests, for example, fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH), TP53 mutation analysis and immunoglobulin heavy-chain variable region (IGHV) testing -- all genetic tests -- will be done to understand the disease better, make plans and give a prognosis. In some cases doctors may ask for CT scans,” Dr. Samar added.
According to experts, a bone marrow test is usually not a must for a proper diagnosis, but it can be done if there are certain reasons to justify it or if the doctor deems fit.
Symptoms and prognosis
CLL is usually asymptomatic initially, and presents an increased lymphocyte count, according to Rajib De, head – clinical haematology, haemato-oncology & BMT, Manipal Hospital, EM Bypass, Kolkata. “As the disease progresses, patients may develop swollen lymph nodes, weakness, weight loss and fever, followed in later stages by anaemia and low platelet counts,” Dr. De said.
CLL is broadly classified into Stage A, B and C, with Stage A being asymptomatic, Stage B involving lymph node swelling, and Stage C presenting with symptoms such as weakness, anemia and low platelets.
Treatment for CLL
Treatment for CLL depends on the stage of disease, symptoms, overall health, and specific genetic and molecular characteristics. Many patients with early, asymptomatic CLL do not require immediate treatment and can be safely monitored with a ‘watch and wait’ policy and regular blood tests and clinical evaluations.
Subhasish Chatterjee, who was diagnosed five years ago, said he has not been under any treatment. He only has regular checkups at the Tata Medical Centre - Cancer Hospital & Research Center in Kolkata. “I do blood tests and visit the doctor every six months, and I take a flu vaccine every year in March as a precautionary measure against infections, as was prescribed by the doctors. The doctor has not suggested any other treatment till my blood parameters remain the same,” said the 62-year-old. Mr Chatterjee was detected with CLL incidentally, after going for a check-up following a bout of Covid-19 in 2021.
When treatment becomes necessary, targeted oral therapies such as BTK inhibitors and BCL2 inhibitors, sometimes combined with anti-CD20 antibodies, are commonly used. The choice of therapy is increasingly guided by molecular markers such as TP53 abnormalities. Treatment is individualised, with the goal of controlling the disease effectively while maintaining quality of life and minimising treatment-related side effects, Dr. Samar said.

Crane overturns, bursts into flames at Mumbai port; dramatic visuals show black smoke
The incident took place at around 7:15 p.m. at Green Gate, beside the Cruise Terminal in Ballard Pier Estate, and was reported by the BPT control room.
At least two operators were injured after a crane overturned and caught fire during unloading operations at BPS Port in Mumbai Port on Sunday evening.
The injured have been identified as Ranjit, the crane operator, and Nishant, his assistant. Updates on their condition are awaited.
The incident took place at around 7:15 p.m. at Green Gate, beside the Cruise Terminal in Ballard Pier Estate, and was reported by the BPT control room. The fire was extinguished at around 8:30 p.m., BPT Sub-Officer Shri Shinde said.
The vessel was identified as "Vienna," which was flying the Barbados flag. The incident took place when a 140-metric-ton cargo was being lifted from the vessel with the assistance of two cranes operated by Barkat Company
"At around 19:30 hrs on 30/08/2026, at the BPS port in Mumbai Port, the vessel 'Vienna,' flying the Barbados flag, was undergoing cargo unloading operations. A 140-metric-ton cargo was being lifted from the vessel with the assistance of two cranes operated by Barkat Company," the Mumbai Police said, news agency ANI reported.
Cause of the incident
The police added that the incident occurred following a technical failure during the lifting of the heavy cargo. According to the police, the mishap took place when the load being handled by one of the cranes became imbalanced during the operation, causing the sling attached to the cargo to come loose, which led the load to be shifted to the second crane. As the second crane was lifted off the ground, its front telescopic boom struck the vessel. The impact and resulting friction subsequently led to the crane catching fire.
"During the operation, the sling attached to the cargo on one of the cranes became imbalanced and came loose, causing the entire load to shift onto the second crane. As a result, the second crane was lifted off the ground, and its front telescopic boom struck the vessel. Due to friction caused during the incident, the crane caught fire," the Mumbai Police added, according to ANI.
Following the incident, BPT Fire station staff was mobilised and dispatched to the spot. Fire personnel managed to bring the blaze under control and extinguish it.
Police said the two injured operators were taken to St. George Hospital for medical treatment and added that an investigation has been initiated to ascertain the exact circumstances that led to the accident and subsequent fire.
"An investigation into the incident is currently underway," the Mumbai Police added.

India needs to make up its mind about economic ties with China
New Delhi’s approach has gone from welcoming economic engagement with Beijing to containment to the latest calibrated reopening
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
As India prepares for the Brics summit less than two weeks away, relations with China are warming up. On July 22, Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar met his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi during the East Asia Summit; five days later, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri visited China. Last week, Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval also visited Beijing, for border talks.
But India remains deeply ambivalent when it comes to economic engagement with China: it seeks Chinese capital, technology and expertise while fearing the shocks they may bring. Justifying the latest economic engagement with China, Jaishankar said India’s long-term objective was to compete with China in manufacturing.
After six years of sweeping curbs on Chinese investment, bilateral trade rose to US$151.1 billion in the financial year ended March 31. China remains India’s largest import source and has, after four years, displaced the United States as its top trading partner. India’s approach to engaging with China has evolved: from welcoming participation to containment after 2020 and, more recently, a calibrated reopening.
During Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s first term and the early years of his second, India maintained a broadly open stance. Launched in 2014, the “Make in India” campaign sought to slash bureaucratic hurdles and attract foreign investment. During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit that September, both sides signed a five-year economic cooperation plan. Modi’s 2015 China visit yielded a further US$22 billion in commercial deals.
Economic engagement remained robust even after the 2017 Doklam stand-off. Both sides maintained senior economic dialogue, pursued the “China India Plus One” approach to projects in third countries and planned connectivity projects. Chinese investment in Indian start-ups grew twelvefold between 2016 and 2019, backing at least 18 of India’s 30 unicorns. In 2019, China proposed a manufacturing partnership. By early 2020, the stock of Chinese investment in India was estimated to exceed US$26 billion.
But that was also the year the turning point came. In April, India introduced a requirement of prior government approval for foreign direct investment (FDI) from countries it shared a land border with, ostensibly to block “opportunistic takeovers”. After the deadly Galwan Valley border clash, restrictions against Chinese businesses expanded. India banned Chinese apps on national security grounds, tightened public procurement rules for bidders and required security clearance for directors from border countries. Visa delays, regulatory raids and other pressures suffocated Chinese business.

Meta is testing robots that can plug in cables, reset servers, and handle other tasks inside its data centers, according to several current and former workers familiar with the projects. The ongoing effort, which has not been previously reported, may eventually allow Meta to operate its rapidly expanding data center footprint with fewer humans, keeping labor costs in check as its spending on AI infrastructure soars.
Meta is using robots and related hardware from several different vendors, including Watney Robotics, Kinova, and ABB, according to the same workers, who asked to remain anonymous because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media. Kinova and ABB declined to comment. Watney didn’t respond to requests for comment.
In one experiment, Meta is evaluating whether a Kinova Gen3 robotic arm could be used for power cycling or cutting off electricity to servers. The company is also testing a different robot to swap networking cables. One Meta data center worker estimates that if it’s successful, the bot could replace up to 80 percent of some people’s workloads. “We thought those of us performing the physical tasks were safe for a while, but not anymore,” says the worker. “It’s coming for us all, unfortunately.”
At some facilities, Meta quietly adopted another, relatively simple robot. It looks like a finger—or perhaps a pointy stick—that can press the power button on a Mac Mini or other device to restart it when remotely prompted by a human.
Meta declined to comment on the testing described in this story. Company spokesperson Francis Brennan said in a statement that Meta is investing heavily in training and hiring workers to build and operate its data centers. “America is in the middle of its biggest infrastructure boom since World War II, and there’s a major shortage of skilled workers to fill the roles; we need more workers, not fewer,” he said.
But at a conference last year, Eric Xu, senior manager for robotics at Meta, said the company’s “long-term goals” are to put robots in data centers, arguing they could speed up incident response, monitor the environment, and handle preventative maintenance. “We believe more collaboration and research will be needed, but we have to start, otherwise we don't have a chance to do this,” he said.
Until recently, robots largely weren’t well suited for the delicate work happening in data centers. They were expensive, and in earlier trials in the industry they sometimes crushed servers while attempting simple tasks, a person briefed on the experimentation says. But the hardware has gotten cheaper, and the AI models powering robots are now far more capable than they were a few years ago. Several startups are currently working to build commercial robots capable of assembling servers, swapping parts, and replacing wires.

Robots could offer more consistent output at a lower cost than human labor, especially in less populous regions where data centers are plentiful but qualified workers are scarce. Proponents also rally behind a pro-worker message: Like AI agents promise to do for knowledge workers, they argue robots could take on data center technicians’ most repetitive and dangerous tasks while freeing them to focus on more complex challenges. Longer term, getting workers out of the picture could make it more feasible to run data centers underwater, in space, or in other environments potentially inhospitable to living, breathing species.
“More and more of our customers are telling us ‘we want to run our data centers using humanoid [robots]’ because you can run them at higher temperatures, in the dark, and all these things,” says Paul Golding, who oversees so-called physical intelligence at the chipmaker Analog Devices.
The growing use of robots has received little attention from the activists driving a powerful nationwide movement against data centers. Tech companies often tout jobs for humans as an upside to the developments that can be used to justify tax breaks for them. In Altoona, Iowa, Meta operates what is now its largest data center campus, which employs hundreds of workers. The company opened the facility in 2014 and has several years left of a property tax break that allows it to save tens of millions of dollars annually, which the city has viewed as a worthwhile trade-off for having its cachet upped by having Meta jobs.
In Altoona, Meta worker group chats have taken on a demoralized tone, “saying we’re all going to be gone in a few years anyway because of the robots,” a person familiar with the discussions says. Even if adoption of robots proves slower than anticipated, some worry the quality of jobs available is trending downward. Two of the workers say that Meta is developing AI software and other technologies that they believe will allow it to hire lower-skilled—and thus, lower-paid—workers and centralize some roles in areas such as Denver, Colorado, that are more financially advantageous to the company.
“They no longer want people who can think independently, come up with creative solutions, or perform complex troubleshooting,” one Meta data center worker says. “They want ‘smart hands,’ people who are just capable enough to follow AI instructions and not mess anything up.”
Meta contends its need for skilled workers remains robust. This year, the company launched a long-term program to train thousands of people annually from any background in electrical, mechanical, and plumbing work at no cost to them. Meta is even guaranteeing employment in states such as Louisiana, Ohio, Indiana, and Texas for those who complete the training. It also partnered with building trade unions to fund apprenticeship programs.
But as communities rethink data center tax breaks and weigh putting new rules on the industry, the prospect of robots replacing at least some jobs may need to become a bigger concern. Altoona Mayor Dean O'Connor tells WIRED he hasn’t given much thought to robots taking jobs at Meta’s data center, though he frames automation as inevitable. “We will deal with it as it comes,” he says.
Tripping Cables
In a 2023 YouTube video, Meta touted that it was using a self-driving tugger robot to transport heavy server racks within its data centers as well as a wheeled, barcode-reading robot developed in-house to track inventory. The next year, Microsoft and Google unveiled separate investments in robots for their data center operations, and Amazon last year discussed using robots to help recycle parts at its facilities.
Pursuing robotics for “economically valuable tasks,” like “replacing a faulty server rack,” is “absolutely something we're looking into at Microsoft,” Ashley Llorens, a managing director for the company’s research accelerator, tells WIRED.
Meta’s tugger and inventory robots are now operating in a number of the company’s data centers, including in Iowa and Virginia, according to the people familiar with the projects. They say the robots generally work well, though there are limitations.
The inventory bot is now also being used for failure inspections, but it can’t differentiate between green and red indicator lights on equipment because its camera only detects grayscale, meaning human checks are still required to assess some breakdowns. The device also struggles with corners and traversing the cables that are often in the path of its wheels. Because there aren't that many of them, the robots need to be moved between buildings, which requires a door-opening human who maneuvers the robot with a remote control.
Two sources also describe the inventory bot as too slow. One says Meta previously explored using drones as a faster alternative, but ultimately didn’t pursue the idea.
Inside the Testbed
The Altoona data center campus is often where Meta prototypes new technologies. “What they do here in Altoona, they take to their other sites and put that in place there,” says O’Connor.
Since last June, Meta has been trying out a pair of dual-armed Watney robots for some cabling work at one of its Altoona buildings, according to one of the people familiar with the company’s efforts. The robots are supervised by humans and can’t work as fast as people yet, but they show promise.
After Watney launched in 2023, it put out a demo of a laundry-folding robot that it claimed could also handle janitorial work inside businesses. The San Francisco startup quietly pivoted to data center robots early last year, according to archived copies of its website.
Meta is testing additional robots in New Albany, Ohio, at the company’s newest data center campus known as Prometheus. Four-wheel robots “with a scissor-lift-style riser and a six-axis arm on top” made by the automation giant ABB are being used there to reseat parts and, eventually, they may take on other tasks with diminishing human oversight, a person familiar with the product says.
But the idea that robots will prevail over humans isn't guaranteed. “There's been a lot of pilots and demos, but no provable working solution,” says Helen Oleynikova, CEO of Exclaim Robotics, which is developing prototypes to replace broken parts and reset cables in data centers.
At Meta’s data centers, some workers have complained about the amount of downtime the robots need to recharge their batteries, according to the people familiar with the matter. Meta has also acknowledged internally that robots aren’t equipped for certain tasks, such as the intense cabling work required to run an Nvidia GB300 supercomputer. “Things have been designed for human hands forever to make everything a five-minute repair,” says one former Meta employee. “Redesigning everything will take time.” But the robots are getting prepared.

Tornado touched down near Elkhorn, Man., on Sunday: Environment Canada
1 confirmed, 1 possible tornado also reported in eastern Saskatchewan
A tornado touched down near a community in southwestern Manitoba on Sunday, Environment and Climate Change Canada has confirmed.
A tornado was observed near Elkhorn, Man., 300 kilometres west of Winnipeg, around 6:30 p.m. Sunday, Environment Canada said. Reports of the tornado were made via the RCMP and social media.
The weather agency is collaborating with the Northern Tornadoes Project to investigate further and will provide more information once a preliminary assessment is done.
Storm damage was reported in the Manitoba community of Kola, just south of Elkhorn, Environment Canada meteorologist Shannon Moodie told CBC News on Monday.
The Northern Tornadoes Project said it's possible the tornado near Elkhorn began near Kola, Moodie said.
"So we're not sure if it's two tornadoes [or] if it's one. There could be more."
'Lost almost all our buildings'
A farmer near Kola said his family will be deciding Monday whether to rebuild, after the storms damaged most of their buildings, including a hay shed that "blew away."
It was raining "like crazy" when Kelvin Siemens said he heard a roar outside the farm on Sunday.
"We lost almost all our buildings," but their house was spared, Siemens said Monday.
He's going to speak with his insurance company before a family meeting to discuss next steps, he said.
"I'm not a young man anymore, and how much do we, or will we, rebuild?"
Siemens said he's certain they will rebuild to some extent.
"I'm not quite ready to give up."
It's been a summer of wet weather in the area, with parts of southwestern Manitoba were previously walloped by torrential rains earlier this summer.
Kola received about 74 millimetres of rain on Sunday, while St-Lazare got about 41 mm and Duck Mountain Provincial Park got 37.8 mm, Moodie said.
Another confirmed tornado was seen near Maryfield, Sask., around 4 p.m. Sunday, the weather agency said. A possible tornado was also reported near Kelso, Sask., on Sunday, but there's insufficient evidence to prove that so far.
Parts of Manitoba will see some showers and non-severe, isolated thunderstorms on Monday, as the "pretty big" system over the Prairies that produced Sunday's storms has begun to settle down, she said.
Kurt Fuchs, who lives in Fleming, Sask., said he was driving home from his job in Virden, Man., when heavy rains forced him off the highway and into Elkhorn around 6:30 p.m. Sunday.
He took images of the town after the storm ripped the roof off a store's shed, which littered the streets alongside broken tree branches.
"It was really, really shocking," Fuchs told CBC News on Monday.
Dwayne Hohmann, division manager of the Twin Valley Co-op on the west side of Elkhorn, which is near where Fuchs took photos, said part of the roof of the store's lumber shed ripped off in the storm.
There's damage to some stock and the lumber shed is closed to customers, but Hohmann says the main store is open.
"It was a positive that nobody was injured, so that's what we're taking out of it," he said.
"We'll band together as a community and move forward."

How 'Book Queen' Dolly Parton inspired millions of children with gift of reading
- Published
One child in Denver called her "The Book Queen".
Another in Alabama calls her "Ms Dolly".
Across the globe in Australia, a toddler with speech delays delighted her family with her first word - "orange" - after she and her twin sister received a free book in the post about colours. It came from Imagination Library, the literacy programme begun by late global superstar Dolly Parton.
Parton, who died this week aged 80, launched the philanthropic effort in 1995 to honour her father - whose difficult Appalachian upbringing never allowed him to finish school or learn to read and write.
"He was the smartest man I have ever known, but I know in my heart his inability to read probably kept him from fulfilling all of his dreams," wrote Parton in an open letter on Imagination Library's website.
"Inspiring kids to love to read became my mission."
Imagination Library sends one free book a month to children from birth to age five. It first launched in Tennessee's Sevier County, where Parton grew up, before expanding across the US in 2000. The programme, which partners with local organisations, launched in Canada in 2006, the UK the following year, then Australia in 2013 and Ireland in 2019.
By 2025, as Imagination Library celebrated its 30th anniversary, it had distributed more than 300m books - equating to one book mailed every 78 seconds, according to the organisation.
And for the families in receipt of the storybooks, the impact has been invaluable.

  - Published16 hours ago
"It just blows my mind that it's readily available for every family that lives in my borough," said London mother-of-two Harriet Anscombe, whose four-year-old daughter has been receiving Imagination Library books since she was three months old.
The free books helped Anscombe establish a reading-focused nighttime routine.
"I think that, if I didn't get those books, maybe I wouldn't have started doing bedtime stories till she was two - but because we were getting them so early, it embedded story time into our routine from when she was just a couple of months old," Anscombe said. "She probably doesn't remember a time when we weren't reading stories."
Imagination Library became part of the family routine for Ciara Fernandez Faber, too, after she signed up her son about eight years ago in Colorado. His favourite book for years was one written by Parton herself: I Am A Rainbow.
"We read it almost every night, and I never got tired of reading it to him," said Faber, 42.
"It's a book about different emotions, and so we would act out the different emotions, the different faces," she said. "At the back of the book, there's a little excerpt by Dolly talking about how everybody has a rainbow of feelings, and we would read that - and he would always point to her picture and say, 'There's the Book Queen.'"
Families like Faber's repeatedly remarked on how well curated the books were - detailing how topics helped their children not just with reading, but also with social and emotional development.
"There were themes that were addressed in a lot of the books that would have really helped us navigate issues," said Helen Cashell, of Dublin, Ireland.
She signed up both of her children, now aged seven and five, for the scheme. "Whether it was same-sex families or just different types of families, things about bravery, courage, bullying, things about different identities."
Author Selina Brown, whose book My Rice Is Best was selected for distribution through Imagination Library, noted how the plotline features a black protagonist.
The programme also helps promote authors like herself; because of the selection, it "means 14,000 copies of my book have been sent to children in the UK".
"To choose between gas, electric, food or a book, you're going to choose a core need - but with the Dolly Parton Imagination Library, you don't have to do that," she said.
In inner-city Sydney, Australia, first-time mum Paige Stewart was astounded as she watched her children's progress with the programme.
Her twin girls, now four, "had a speech delay and some learning difficulties" - but Stewart noticed a change after just the second book.
"Not only did they learn their colours from that book… it kind of set the tone for them speaking and their joy for books."
She's become a vocal advocate for the programme, telling others: "It's so helpful, honestly."
Alabama grandmother Kristina Hadley also promotes the programme to friends and family - even incorporating Imagination Library into baby gifts.
"I'll pull up the Imagination books website, and I'll print that, and I'll put it in a picture frame, and I'll get little newborn books and stuff like that, and I'll put it with that for like a suggestion for new mothers," said Hadley, 53.
She signed up her nearly three-year-old granddaughter, Eillie Elaine, "before she was actually born". Now the child has her own bookshelf in their shared household - "and one whole shelf is for her Dolly books".
"She likes to go to go to the mailbox, and she's like, 'Ms Dolly! Ms Dolly!' and I'm like, 'Well, let's go see if Ms Dolly sent you a book!'"
A lifelong Parton fan, Hadley chokes up while detailing how she was at work when a friend texted to say the singer had died.
Imagination Library, she says, "is going to keep her memory going with the younger generation, and I hope and I pray that this is something that goes on for years and years and years."
It's a legacy that Parton built quietly in the background as she presided over pop culture for more than six decades.
"The biggest thing that I like is the fact that she didn't do anything for recognition," said Geoff Blacklin, 67, of Manitoba, Canada.
He and his wife signed up their grandchildren for Imagination Library after a local doctor brought the programme to their region.
"She gave families more than books," Blacklin said. "She gave children a love of reading, precious moments with loved ones, and opportunities to learn and dream."
Such family stories and gratitude would undoubtedly have been music to Parton's ears; the expansion of the programme was truly a realisation of her own dream.
"In the beginning, my hope was simply to inspire the children in my home county, but here we are today with a worldwide programme that gives a book a month to well over 3 million children," she wrote on the Imagination Library site - also taking care to thank the partners "who have embraced my dream and made it their own".
At the centre of it, always, was her love for children - and her love for her father.
"Before he passed away, my Daddy told me the Imagination Library was probably the most important thing I had ever done," Parton wrote.
"I can't tell you how much that meant to me, because I created the Imagination Library as a tribute to my Daddy."

Algeria president seeks death penalty for arsonists after deadly forest fires
- Published
Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has said he wants to reinstate the death penalty for arsonists, following a wave of forest fires that have killed at least 12 people.
The president ordered the justice ministry to introduce changes to the criminal law introducing capital punishment for arsonists. Capital punishment remains in the country's penal code for some offences, but no execution has been carried out since 1993.
More than 100 wildfires have been recorded in recent days in the north-east of the country, most of which have been extinguished.
On Saturday, Tebboune said he did not rule out foul play.
The Algerian president said necessary investigations would be carried out especially in view of the intensity of the fires.
On Sunday, he gave a 15 September deadline for amendments to provide for the death sentence for anyone convicted of intentionally starting a fire in forested areas.
Under the current law, deliberately starting forest fires is punishable by up to 30 years in prison, or life imprisonment in certain cases.
Deadly blazes swept through large swathes of northern Algeria last week, causing widespread destruction, injuring dozens and displacing thousands of people.
The fires erupted amid an intense heatwave in northern Africa, with Algeria and Tunisia particularly affected.
Algerian civil authorities were on Sunday afternoon still battling to battle some of the fires, with the Algerian Press Service noting that 18 out 19 fires that had broken out in the previous 24 hours had been extinguished
The Algerian president ordered that compensation be paid to the families who have been affected, as well as repairs to damaged homes and essential services.
He said there would be investigations into the extent of the damage and losses caused by the fires.
While Algeria regularly experiences forest fires around the summer months, climate change has exacerbated the intensity and severity of recent wildfires in the country.

AI and robotics drive an IPO boom in China as Shein lists in Hong Kong
Chinese markets are booming with new public share listings driven by the craze for artificial intelligence
HONG KONG -- Chinese markets are booming with new public stock offerings, energized by the craze for artificial intelligence and other advanced technology and a growing preference to list shares in Hong Kong and Shanghai.
In the latest big stock listing, shares in China-founded e-commerce and fast fashion giant Shein are due to debut Tuesday in Hong Kong in a blockbuster initial public offering raising $1.7 billion, in one of the city’s biggest new share sales this year.
In July, CXMT, China’s largest memory chipmaker, raised more than $8.6 billion in Shanghai in the second-largest IPO for its Nasdaq-style STAR market, mainland China’s second-largest IPO. Its shares jumped 466% on the first day of trading.
Unitree, one of China’s leading humanoid robot makers, also made its listing debut in Shanghai in August. Shares rose 460% on the first day of trading.
“The current IPO boom is powered by investor appetite for AI and robotics,” said Ruiying Zhao, a senior research analyst at S&P Global Market Intelligence. Trading in Shanghai's stock market, for one, is heavily driven by retail investors.
CXMT’s IPO in Shanghai “placed China in a strategically significant position in tech manufacturing related to AI,” said Perris Lee, head of APAC equity capital markets for ION Analytics. “It’s also a testament to China’s tech self-sufficiency ambitions.”
Founded in China in 2016, the company's revenue surged more than 700% year-on-year to 50.8 billion yuan (about $7.5 billion) in the first three months of 2026 on a spike in demand for computer chips needed for AI.
IPO proceeds in Hong Kong and Shanghai so far this year have already surpassed the funding raised last year, according to the financial data platform LSEG.
It says IPOs and secondary listing activities on the Hong Kong and Shanghai exchanges raised a total of over $54 billion from so far in 2026, surpassing last year’s total of more than $46 billion.
Combined Hong Kong and Shanghai proceeds so far this year accounted for roughly 21% globally, ranking them only behind only the Nasdaq’s roughly 55% global share, LSEG said. There, the mega $75 billion IPO by SpaceX in June made the U.S. exchange the world’s biggest IPO market this year.
Since China limits foreign purchases on mainland exchanges, many Chinese companies do parallel listings in Hong Kong to help raise international capital.
Stricter U.S. and Chinese regulatory scrutiny in recent years of big Chinese companies listing in U.S. markets, especially those in strategically important sectors like advanced technologies, has led some Chinese companies to stick closer to home.
Listing overseas typically takes more time compared with doing IPOs in China, said Howie Farn, a capital markets partner at the law firm Freshfields.
In Hong Kong, recent public stock listings of Apple-supplier Luxshare Precision Industry, and Zhongji Innolight, which makes optical transceivers used in data centers, were among this year’s largest deals and were also a reflection of investor demand for advanced technologies.
More companies are looking to hold their IPOs in Hong Kong or Shanghai, like robotics firms AGIBOT and Deep Robotics.
Shein also explored the possibility of listings in the U.S. and London before opting for Hong Kong.
After massive oversubscriptions and huge gains in their share debuts, some companies have seen their market value shrink.
Chinese robot maker Unitree’s share price had fallen more than 40% as of Friday from its peak share price on the day of its trading debut.
"The critical question remains: is the AI sentiment enough?” said Zhao from S&P, as the similar question that raised worries among investors in the U.S. also now also applies to China. “For a durable market cycle, investors will demand sustainable revenue, visible profit margins, and realistic valuations.
The global AI frenzy also has also drawn attention away from companies like Shein. “The AI investment cycle is absorbing much of the risk appetite that would have otherwise flowed to a company like Shein,” said Jacob Cooke, CEO of WPIC Marketing + Technologies.
Shein’s IPO puts the company’s value at around $27 billion, a fraction of its peak valuation a few years ago, though that is partly due to U.S. and EU moves to restrict de minimus tax-exemptions for imports of small packages.
