Body odour is a normal part of life. Contrary to popular belief, sweat in itself does not usually smell. The familiar odour develops when bacteria and fungi that live on the skin break down substances in sweat, particularly secretions from glands in the armpits and groin. In most cases, body odour is harmless and may vary depending on factors such as heat, physical activity, diet and hygiene.
However, a new or persistent change in body odour should not always be dismissed as a hygiene issue, doctors say. In some cases, an unusual odour may be linked to an underlying health condition and may need medical evaluation.
Heat, food and hormones
Several everyday factors can alter body odour. Hot weather and physical activity increase sweating, while tight or synthetic clothing can trap moisture. Garlic, onions, spicy foods, alcohol and certain medicines can also affect body odour.
Hemanath M. J., consultant, internal and family medicine, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, says the apocrine glands in the armpits, groin and scalp contribute more to odour than the eccrine glands, which cover most of the body. Stress can stimulate the apocrine glands and intensify odour.
Hormonal changes can also play a role. Puberty, menstruation and menopause may temporarily alter sweating and body odour. Puberty is one common situations in which changes in body odour are routinely seen. An overactive thyroid, which can cause excessive sweating, may also make odour more noticeable.
A change is more likely to be temporary when there is a clear trigger and the odour settles after the trigger passes. “If somebody develops an odour after eating a particular food, drinking a particular drink, starting a medication or strenuous exercise, or during a period of hormonal change, and it returns to normal after some time, the context helps explain the change,” says Narayanan A., consultant, dermatology, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai..
Body odour as a health clue
A persistent or unexplained change can sometimes be associated with a skin condition or an underlying medical problem. Skin infections in the armpits, groin or other moist areas can alter odour. These may be accompanied by redness, soreness, itching, peeling or discharge.
“An infection in the groin or axilla (armpit) or excessive growth of bacteria or fungi can alter the odour,” says Dr. Narayanan.
Dr. Hemanath says conditions such as erythrasma and fungal infections can produce a distinct smell, particularly in warm, moist areas. Excessive sweating, or hyperhidrosis, does not itself cause odour but can provide more moisture for bacteria to act on.
Certain metabolic conditions have also been associated with distinctive smells. Uncontrolled diabetes can produce fruity or sweet-smelling breath because of ketone build-up. A rare condition called trimethylaminuria can cause a fish-like odour because the body is unable to break down certain compounds properly.
Odour changes have also been described in advanced kidney and liver disease. But doctors caution against treating these smells as diagnostic tests.
“Some distinctive smells have been described with complications of diabetes, liver disease or kidney disease, but these are clues rather than reliable diagnostic tests,” says Dr. Narayanan. The overall clinical picture, including symptoms, examination and biochemical investigations, is what guides diagnosis.
Need for evaluation
The first step when there is a change in body odour is to look for an obvious trigger. Regular washing, changing sweaty clothes, washing clothes properly and using an antiperspirant can help determine whether the problem responds to routine measures.
But a sudden change in body odour without a clear cause is reason to consult a doctor.The physician would first consider what changed at the same time as the odour. If there is no obvious trigger and the change persists or keeps recurring, a deeper evaluation may be required.
A sudden unexplained increase in sweating, night sweats without an obvious reason, or sweating that interferes with daily activities should also prompt medical attention. Experts list other warning signs such as unexplained weight loss, excessive thirst or urination, fatigue, swelling, fever, night sweats or skin changes. A fruity odour with excessive thirst, frequent urination, nausea, vomiting or confusion requires urgent assessment.
Depending on the symptoms, a doctor may conduct a physical and skin examination and consider tests such as blood glucose and HbA1c, kidney and liver function tests and a thyroid profile. Skin scraping or culture may be considered if an infection is suspected.
Doctors say, body odour should not be used to self-diagnose a disease. Most changes have an everyday explanation, but a smell that is new, persistent, unexplained or accompanied by other symptoms is worth discussing with a doctor

New Delhi, Aug 31: At the invitation of the Prime Minister of India Narendra Modi, the Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Belgium, H.E. Bart De Wever, will undertake an official visit to India from 02 - 04 September 2026. Prime Minister De Wever would be accompanied by the Belgian Minister of Defence, H.E. Theo Francken.This will be Prime Minister De Wever’s first visit to India since taking office in February 2025.
During the visit, Prime Minister De Wever is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Prime Minister Modi on 03 September to discuss the entire spectrum of bilateral relations, as well as, regional and global issues of mutual interest. Former Republican congressman George Santos has received a first-of-its-kind lifetime ban from the prediction market platform Kalshi, which has also fined him $71,356 for violating its rules around insider trading and market manipulation.
According to the notice of disciplinary action Kalshi posted today, the former politician placed trades in markets related to whether he would attend President Trump’s State of the Union address in February 2026. He then “began making a series of public statements regarding his attendance at the event in an attempt to influence the price” of certain contracts, some of which were “false or misleading,” per the notice.
The day before the address, Santos posted, “I'm going to be there for the State of Union in the gallery, guys” on X. During the speech, he sent a follow-up noting that he was actually at an airport watching the address on television. “FML,” he wrote.
Kalshi’s enforcement team flagged the trades, froze Santos’ account, and referred the case to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that oversees prediction markets. This summer, he settled with the CFTC for $35,000 over these suspicious trades; a little over $17,500 was returning the profit he made, with an additional $17,500 fine. At the time, his lawyer issued a statement stressing that Santos settled to “put this matter behind him” and that he had done so “without admitting the Commission’s allegations, findings or conclusions.”
Through his legal representative, Santos declined to comment to WIRED. However, on social media, he already weighed in, sarcastically thanking Kalshi “for the lifetime ban from your gambling platform,” adding, “Let’s see how much longer you guys are around for 💋,” a nod to the prediction market’s ongoing battles with state authorities over how it is regulated.
Once upon a time, Santos had a rosier relationship with the industry; he was once paid for promoting Kalshi’s rival Polymarket, but Polymarket severed ties with him once federal regulators began looking into his behavior around February’s State of the Union.
This is far from Santos’ first brush with the law. He was expelled from Congress following an ethics investigation in 2023, and eventually pleaded guilty and served time in federal prison for embezzling from campaign donors, lying to Congress, and defrauding campaign contributors. He was released from prison in 2025 after President Trump commuted his sentence.
According to today’s notice, the prediction market found that Santos successfully influenced the pricing of several markets. Kalshi also issued four additional notices of enforcement actions today, but Santos was the only person penalized who did not settle with the company.
“He wouldn’t talk to us, and actively dodged us,” Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana tells WIRED.
In the past year, Kalshi has issued a number of other enforcement actions against politicians who it found had broken its rules. In this most recent round of enforcement actions, it fined North Carolina Congressional candidate Laurie Buckhout, California gubernatorial candidate Stephen Kloobeck, and Maine gubernatorial candidate Ben Midgley for attempting to trade on contracts related to their races; they are all temporarily suspended.
“I bet on myself. Literally. It was a dumb mistake, and as soon as I learned there was an issue, I worked to make it right. Safe to say my career as a Kalshi trader was short-lived,” Buckhout, a retired military officer, told WIRED in an email. Kloobeck and Midgley did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
Previously, it fined US Senate candidate Mark Moran for insider trading; at the time, Moran told WIRED that he “did it on purpose” and did not intend to cooperate with Kalshi.
Kalshi’s Diana says that Santos can expect “legal action” if he does not pay.

A common way to deal with emotions is through food, says Lakshmi Venkatraman, consultant psychiatrist and assistant director of Psychosocial Rehabilitation Services at SCARF (Schizophrenia Research Foundation). Dieting and restrictions on food are also culprits. The vicious circle begins when people tend to eat more, end up feeling guilty at their act, reduce their self-esteem, because of which they binge eat and feel more guilty.
Simple measures such as eating regular meals with all foods, including favourites in moderation, helps. “When we realise emotions are pushing us (to eat), finding ways to tackle the emotions will help,” Dr. Lakshmi explains. “Be mindful while eating, focus on what we are eating, take it quite slow while eating which helps to prevent binge eating,” she points out.
R.M. Anjana, managing director of Dr. Mohan’s Diabetes Specialities Centre, cites the various studies done by the Foundation at various intervals of time, to explain the importance of regulating “what we put into our mouth”. When a person finds that they binge once a week and this persists for three months then it should trigger an alarm, she says. “Diet and physical activity alone can prevent 50% of diabetes,” she said and cited studies that state that binge eating contributes to about 15 to 20% of type 2 diabetes.
A bariatric surgeon aims to moderate the gut hormones, says P. Praveen Raj, consultant and head of the Department of Minimal Access Bariatric and Robotic Surgery in the Department of Surgical Gastroenterology, GEM Hospital and Research Centre, Coimbatore.
The first step is to take a thorough history of the person’s issues. There are various hormones in the gut that regulate satiety, trigger appetite and aid digestion. An imbalance in any one of them could be the cause for obesity. The aim is to treat the cause, he explains. “You rule out the psychological reasons, and the pathological abnormality. Once this is understood we can start to treat it (the condition),” he adds.
The specialists were panelists at a webinar on “The Binge: Learning to handle addictive behaviours,” organised on Sunday by The Hindu. The webinar can be viewed at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Cl4wxf7_HRI

Most people know that Labor Day is one of the best times of the year to buy tools (get it? Labor?), but if you’re a newly minted homeowner or DIY-er, the landscape can be intimidating. When I bought my first home, I owned only two screwdrivers, a pair of pliers, and a hammer; I had no clue what I was in for.
Now that I’ve been a homeowner for 17 years, I agree with WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson that unless you’re a professional tradesperson or really love large projects, you don’t need a garage full of specialty tools. Just the basics will do: a drill, a saw, a set of manual screwdrivers, and a stud finder, for example.
Luckily, early Labor Day deals are pretty decent this year. In fact, after examining all the major sales, I was able to find a rather encyclopedic house-repair kit for any new homeowner or DIY-er for under $375 (minus tax and shipping) with deals from Home Depot, Lowe’s, and Walmart. Any of these would also be great to stash away for a holiday gift.
Here’s what I chose:
Power-Tool Workhorses: Ryobi 4-Tool Kit for $199
Look, you’re not going to take Ryobi tools to a jobsite or use them to build a house from scratch (a former WIRED editor once deemed them “the Kia of tools”), but if you’re just using them for basic, casual home use, they’ll do the job. Ryobi’s 18V ONE+ batteries (this set comes with one) are fully backward compatible with all Ryobi tools ever made, and this set has a three-year warranty. I live in a DeWalt household, so I don’t have a lot of firsthand experience with Ryobi, but my brother, a contractor, says the brand is great for the average DIY homeowner and offers a much broader range of tools than competitor Bauer from Harbor Freight.
This set packs a ½-inch drill/driver, an impact driver (which WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson said had a profound 'I can't believe I didn't own one sooner' impact on him, though his is Milwaukee), a circular saw, and an LED light. The impact driver packs 1,800 pounds of torque, which is pretty decent for a consumer-level tool. If you need a sander, there's also another kit with a sander plus drill/driver and circular saw, which may be worth a look if this set sells out.
The Hand-Tool Essentials: Workpro 408-Piece Set for $144
I don't have this exact set, but I do have remnants of a similar one. Again, you're not going to bring these to a construction site, but this kit is a knockout deal for everything you get—pliers, screwdrivers, Allen keys, wrenches, sockets, bits, tape measure, knife, hammer, wire stripper … there's even a metal box in which to store everything. A lot of the “pieces” are doodads like screwdriver heads and drywall anchors, but it still contains pretty much any non-power tool you might need for light home repairs and even basic car maintenance. (There's no level, but you can always use an app on your phone for that.) However, note that this is a flash deal, so it's likely only live for a limited time.
Wall-Hanging Must-Have: Franklin Sensors Stud Finder for $22
No household repair kit is complete without a stud finder. (And if you're a dad, it will give you years of built-in dad jokes.) In fact, you can't—or, at least, shouldn't—hang anything even slightly heavy on your wall without one. I have a Franklin Sensors stud finder, though not this exact model, and it's done well to help my family hang pictures, shelves, mirrors, and pretty much everything else for the past decade or so. This is the best deal I could find, though it's not technically on sale. However, Lowe’s is having a sale on plenty of other tools, including outdoor furniture, appliances, and grills.

In Summary
- As concerns around smart glasses and privacy grow, Meta has ensured that users cannot use the cameras on its smart glasses if they cover or tamper with the LED that lights up during recording.
- While Meta’s move is a step in the right direction, it still does not go far enough to address the privacy issues posed by smart glasses.
- Smart glasses brands need to do more to prevent misuse. This includes informing and educating not just users, but also the public, who could unknowingly end up in footage shot on these devices.
Smart glasses have existed for a while but have attained a whole new dimension of popularity since Meta invested in them. For those of you who might not be aware (welcome to high-tech planet, folks), smart glasses look like regular glasses but come with a number of tech add-ons, such as displays, speakers, and most notably, cameras. These smart glasses can take photos, record videos, handle phone calls, play music, let you speak to an AI assistant, figure out your way around town, get recommendations, and more.
Table of Contents
Smart glasses? Pervert glasses, more like!
Sound uber cool, cutting-edge and futuristic, don’t they? Unfortunately, this tech rose comes with a stack of thorns that would make a cactus turn even more green with envy. While the tech world and content creators may be going gaga over all these smart glasses can do, more and more people are beginning to refer to them as “pervert glasses.” There is a sound reason for this – these glasses are increasingly being used to record people (often women) without their consent and knowledge, resulting in a massive breach of a person’s privacy. There have been a number of incidents in which people have been recorded without their knowledge and the footage shared in public or private groups, causing severe trauma to those who appeared unknowingly in the footage.
What’s worse, the onus of figuring out that they are being recorded fell on the person being recorded. Being vigilant, actively looking for signs of someone wearing smart glasses, and catching up on tech cues were all part of the package – we also did a story on ways one could find out if they are being recorded as smart glasses moved from being content creators to destroyers of privacy. As incidents of “secret recordings” through these glasses increase, pressure has finally started building on the brands making these devices to make them safer not just for their users, but also for those in their vicinity.
Meta finally moves, but is it enough?
Recently, Meta finally fixed a flaw that was making it easier for users to covertly record others. In a post made on Threads (https://www.threads.com/@ahimel/post/DcjTatTGyn-), Alex Himel, Vice President of Wearables and Vice President of Augmented Reality at Meta, said that the camera on the glasses would stop working if the LED on the glasses was covered.
He was referring to a small LED indicator on the glasses that lights up when the glasses are recording. While the cameras on the glasses would not allow users to record if the LED was covered, many users found ways around this. One method was as simple as covering the LED light after starting to record the video. Following Himel’s announcement, an update will ensure that if the LED is covered at any stage (before or after starting a video recording), the glasses will automatically stop recording the video or taking photos. What’s more, if users tamper with the LED light and destroy or disable it, the glasses will now disable the camera feature permanently.
While this is definitely a step in the right direction, it does not really solve the biggest issue around these glasses. We have seen Meta’s glasses in public, and it is very difficult to spot when they are recording, especially in daylight or if the person is some distance away. The LED light is bright, but can easily be missed if one is not looking for it. What’s more, one can place a hand in front of it to stop others from seeing it, without actually covering it. We really think more needs to be done to safeguard the privacy of users in the vicinity of these devices. Brands need to come up with stronger measures that can help people spot those who may be wearing smart glasses and steer clear of their line of vision, if they so wish.
Making smart glasses safer: five more things brands can do
Given how limited the LED indicator can be, here are five measures that tech brands can take to make smart glasses safer for those in front of them:
Just make them look different…VERY different
One of the reasons why it is extremely difficult to find out if a person is wearing smart glasses is because they look exactly like usual glasses. Clear, tinted, or even running smart glasses all come with designs/frames that make them look like “normal” glasses. This makes them difficult to spot and enables users to record footage without being noticed.
We think that, given the privacy nightmares they can potentially pose, smart glasses need to look fundamentally different from everyday glasses. Visible badging, colors, even frame size or design should make them easy to spot. Who knows, this might even catch on as a style statement, but at least it will alert those in the vicinity that the person is walking around with a camera literally on their eyes!
Better, brighter (and maybe even more) LED lights
An LED light blinking while recording or taking photos is currently the only way to find out if someone is recording video or taking photographs from their smart glasses. As we have said before, a single light can be missed or even discreetly covered. The solution? Brands could perhaps use multiple LEDs of different colors, and which are of larger size, to pretty much advertise that a smart glasses’ camera is in use. Something like Nothing’s Glyph UI would be very handy!
Pump up the volume
Smart glasses should also give clear audio signals when their cameras are functioning. It should not be possible to take photographs without a loud camera shutter sound, and adding low but constant beep sounds when video is being recorded would also alert people to the presence of a camera in their vicinity.
Mandatory identifying apps
There are already apps like Zuckoff in the market that notify users if they are around someone wearing smart glasses. But these are unofficial and a little hit and miss. We think it would be wonderful if smart glass manufacturers took the initiative to come up with an app that can alert people in a small radius (say, 10 meters if based on Bluetooth), letting them know that they are in the presence of someone wearing smart glasses. Yes, it does violate the privacy of the person wearing smart glasses, as it is likely to make people in their vicinity notice them, but then that’s the price one pays for wearing such a device.
Better marketing and awareness
Brands have been pouring sackfuls of money into normalizing and promoting smart glasses. It would be great if they could allocate some of these funds to also highlight the dangers they can pose, and how they can be misused. Some might think this is counterproductive, but we feel this is the socially responsible thing to do – to make people aware that the device has its dark side too. And it is best that the brands do it themselves before they are forced to do it by Governments around the world.
The Government needs to step in as well. While new tech does make lives easier, there are always people who can find ways to misuse it. It happened with the Internet, it happened with smartphones, it is happening with AI, and it is happening with smart glasses too. To make sure that technology is not misused, there need to be strict privacy laws that are implemented effectively and come with stringent punishments. Perhaps statutory warnings on devices, advising consumers not to misuse them, might be an option worth considering. People need to realize that with great tech comes great responsibility.
Smart glasses need a Meta-morphosis, pun intended. They do not need to blend in, but to stand out and make people realize that they are present in a room. People need to know that they could be on camera. And the onus for this lies not just on those doing the recording, but on the brands who facilitate this.

The Terrible Movie That Chinese Audiences Can’t Stop Watching
Viewers are flocking to a new film that captures the pleasure of bad art.
One of the only compliments I can offer the new Chinese animated film Niu Lai is that it certainly qualifies as a film. There is sound. The pictures move. But beyond the basics of what makes a movie a movie, Niu Lai, which translates to “The Ox Comes,” contains little artistic merit. The plot, about a calf coming of age with the help of a leopard, a bird, and his mother, is thin, and the characters have been so nightmarishly rendered on a rudimentary computer program that they might as well be sleep-paralysis demons.
Yet Niu Lai has become a bona fide box-office hit in China. Since a small distributor unceremoniously dumped it in theaters in early August, the film has become one of the most lucrative movies in Chinese history, making more than $7 million off a reported budget of no more than $500 and outperforming recent blockbusters such as The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Much of its success is thanks to Chinese social media, where clips of it first went viral: Some users have embraced Niu Lai as a meme, purchasing tickets so they could ridicule the baffling work with an audience. Others have championed the project as anti-AI art, arguing that it deserves to be appreciated as a purely human creation. As flawed as Niu Lai may be, to the fans, it’s at least better than AI slop.
I’m not so sure about that. Watching a bootleg version of Niu Lai felt painful but apt: What better way was there to see a jankily made film than in potato quality on my computer at home? Instead, what’s distinctly human about Niu Lai comes from everything around it: how it was made, how it became a sensation, and how it has inspired further creativity in turn. Theater workers have drawn posters by hand to help advertise the movie. Businesses have made plush toys of the bovine hero. Fans have donned cow masks for screenings, and although the film isn’t available in the United States, underground viewings have popped up in major cities. As such, Niu Lai is the rare passion project that has attracted audiences not because it’s so bad that it’s good, but because it’s an occasion to celebrate the ability to have an original idea at all.
Never mind that the idea was apparently underdeveloped from the start. The first-time director, Xin Yumeng, explained in an interview that he wanted to write about an ox because that’s his father’s zodiac symbol; the year he began working on it also happened to be 2021, the year of the ox. Production took five years, as the then-29-year-old Xin and his mother, Sun Lifang, wrote the screenplay together and made up the entire crew and cast: Sun sang the theme song, and Xin animated the 86-minute film frame by frame on SketchUp, an architectural-modeling program. The process was grueling, Xin said, adding that he kept going in part because he saw the story as a way to inspire viewers to not tang ping, or “lie flat,” referring to a societal trend in 2021 where young people in China rejected overworking by cheekily glorifying the act of lying down.
In some ways, the movie is a deeply Chinese phenomenon: Fuzzy cartoon characters tend to become popular in the country—Zootopia 2 is the highest-grossing Hollywood film ever released there—and the words niu lai could also refer to the coming of a bull market, which has led some Chinese stock investors to purchase tickets for good luck. Plus, Niu Lai’s threadbare plot is rooted in the principle of filial piety, as the titular protagonist learns to respect and care for his mother.
The Niu Lai phenomenon also seems to embody a phrase that’s gained traction lately in China: huo ren gan, which, translated literally, means “alive-human feeling.” The film expresses this quality, but not only because Xi didn’t use AI to help create it. What makes Niu Lai stand out most is its unabashed sincerity. It is an earnest attempt to tell a fable about a naive cow, and the story of its making is deeply charming: Here is a mother-son duo, total outsiders to the entertainment industry, trying their best to turn their quixotic idea into reality. Making a movie anywhere requires overcoming so many hurdles that have nothing to do with art or creativity; there are budgets to be balanced and business expectations to be met. But Niu Lai is a modest reminder that any film simply begins with an idea and an irrepressible urge to see it through.

Excel Entertainment co-founder and producer Ritesh Sidhwani has opened up about the challenges of bringing Mirzapur from streaming to the big screen with Mirzapur: The Movie. The upcoming film marks the theatrical transition of the popular franchise and is set to bring its established characters and world to cinemas on September 4, 2026.
Mirzapur: The Movie: Ritesh Sidhwani reveals why the film needed its own story; says “It needed its own midpoint, emotional journey and payoff”
With the series having already completed three seasons, one of the key challenges for the makers was creating a feature film that could offer something new to existing fans while also functioning as a standalone cinematic experience.
During an interview, Sidhwani was asked what Mirzapur: The Movie could do in a theatre that the series could not, particularly given the challenge of fitting the franchise’s extensive story into a three-hour feature. Explaining the approach, he said, “We are taking an IP created as a series and turning it into a feature film. We have seen the reverse happen many times, where films are turned into series. So, in a way, we are breaking the format again and trying something different. Mirzapur has a very loyal fan base, and we are giving those fans something new to experience in theatres. We are essentially saying, ‘You already love these characters. Now come and experience them in a completely different way’."
Sidhwani further explained that the film does not attempt to compress the three seasons of the series into one theatrical outing. Instead, the makers developed an untold chapter set within the timeline of the first season.
He said, “The idea was to take an untold chapter from Season 1 (between two or three episodes) and bring it to the big screen. We also wanted to bring back beloved characters, including Munna Bhaiya and others who were no longer around by Season 3. The first challenge was to tell a story without affecting the narrative of the later seasons. Secondly, we had to ensure the film didn't feel like three stitched-together episodes of the series. It had to work as a film, with its own beginning, middle and end. It needed its own midpoint, emotional journey and payoff so that audiences could enjoy it as a complete story without affecting Season 4, which will follow. However, if anyone has not watched any season of the series, he/she would still be able to enjoy the film.”
The film’s theatrical format is being positioned as a new way for audiences to revisit the Mirzapur universe, while retaining its established characters and tone. The return of characters such as Munna Bhaiya has further added to the anticipation surrounding the film.
Presented by Amazon MGM Studios and Excel Entertainment, Mirzapur: The Movie is directed by Gurmmeet Singh and written by Puneet Krishna. The film is produced by Ritesh Sidhwani and Farhan Akhtar under the banner of Excel Entertainment, with Kassim Jagmagia and Vishal Ramchandani serving as co-producers.
Mirzapur: The Movie is scheduled to release in cinemas on September 4, 2026.

A deep-sea search and rescue vessel is on its way to Cyprus as Turkey joins efforts to retrieve the 20 people still missing after a passenger ferry capsized off the island’s northern coast.
The TCG Isin will join the vast operation to find survivors after the high-speed ferry sank on Sunday barely four nautical miles outside the port town of Kyrenia.
Authorities confirmed late on Monday – the first of three days of national mourning in Turkish-held northern Cyprus – that the tragedy had claimed eight lives, increasing the number of passengers still unaccounted for from 17 to 20.
A total of 241 of the 267 people aboard the Filo Jet, bound for Taşucu on the Turkish mainland when it began to take on water, had been rescued, they said. Almost all were either Turkish or Turkish Cypriot.
International sympathy for the victims was highlighted as the Anglo-Cypriot founder of easyJet, Stelios Haji-Ioannou, offered €260,000 (£223,000) in support for the families of the deceased and missing, in a move hailed by Turkish Cypriot officials.
Visiting Kyrenia’s new port, where relatives gathered for news of loved ones on Monday, Tufan Erhürman, the self-styled state’s president, vowed search efforts would “continue with the same intensity, with no interruption, through the day and night”.
The Isin, capable of searching up to 3,000 metres below the sea surface, was due to arrive on Tuesday, he said, as he comforted the families of those still missing.
The ship is expected to play a vital role in recovering the ferry’s voyage data recorder, or black box, now viewed as key in deciphering the cause of a maritime disaster not seen since the breakaway territory declared independence in 1983.
Turkish Cypriot officials told the Guardian it was likely “all those responsible” would be charged with gross negligence as the seaworthiness of the 26-year-old ferry was also questioned.
The owners and shareholders of the privately owned company operating the passenger vessel have also been ordered to appear in court.
It remained unclear whether those still missing had been trapped on board.
“Nobody is saying it publicly, but the hope of any survivors being found at this point is very slim,” one official confided. “Those who weren’t rescued very likely didn’t find a lifejacket. We believe many were elderly people and mothers with babies and young kids.”
In testimony – and video footage – that emerged on Monday, panic-stricken passengers could be seen desperately looking for lifejackets and screaming before the double-hulled ferry flipped over. One mother, Ayten Biçer, described feeling her 12-year-old daughter slip from her hands and disappear as the ferry capsized and sank in a matter of minutes. “She was saying, ‘Don’t let go.’ And I didn’t let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn’t let her go,” she sobbed. Two of Biçer’s other children are among the 20 still missing.
The captain of the ferry and seven crew members were detained on Monday as judicial authorities launched an inquiry into the tragedy amid claims they had been among the first to abandon ship.
Appearing before a local magistrate, the crew attributed the disaster to the bow of the catamaran-style ferry breaking apart in turbulent seas. But eyewitness accounts contradicted that version of events, with passengers telling officials that appeals to turn back to port had fallen on deaf ears as the ferry began to take on water.
Ünal Üstel, the northern Cyprus prime minister, told reporters the Filo Jet was lying on the seabed at a depth of 514 metres and that he foresaw the Turkish salvage ship “reaching [it] tomorrow afternoon”. Boats, helicopters, aircraft and other search and rescue teams had joined the operation, he said, adding that search efforts were continuing “on a 24-hour basis”.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when a coup aimed at union with Greece – engineered by the military junta then in power in Athens – prompted Turkey to invade and seize the island’s northern third. Ever since, as many as 45,000 mainland Turkish troops have been stationed in the north.
In 1983, the territory unilaterally declared independence, but in the absence of a settlement, decades of international isolation have ensued.

A Greenlandic commission is to present a highly anticipated report Friday to determine whether Denmark's forced contraception of thousands of the Arctic island's indigenous Inuit constituted a "genocide".
The forced contraception campaign between the 1960s and 1990 is one of the darkest chapters in Greenland's history with its former colonial master, Denmark.
Once the conclusions are presented, Greenland's government will decide how to move forward.
"For us, it's about trying to understand our history," Naaja Nathanielsen, a member of parliament representing Greenland in Denmark's parliament, told AFP.
"Others may feel that we should simply keep quiet about this and try to be conciliatory, because of the United States' aggressiveness toward Greenland."
Nathanielsen announced the creation of the commission, tasked with shedding light on the legal implications of the campaign, in August 2024 when she was Greenland's minister of justice and gender equality.
During the 1960s to 1990, more than 4,000 Greenlandic women were forced to wear a contraceptive coil -- or intrauterine device (IUD) -- in the vast majority of cases without their consent or that of their parents if they were minors.
Greenland, a Danish colony for three centuries and now an autonomous territory, still has a complicated relationship with Copenhagen.
Despite many thorny issues between them, both Copenhagen and Nuuk have presented a united front rejecting US President Donald Trump's threats to take over Greenland.
He has repeatedly accused Denmark of treating Greenland badly.
"Everything that is happening between Denmark and Greenland now is scrutinised," said historian Astrid Andersen, a researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS).
"There's this pressure on the relationship so of course, when we start talking about genocide, that increases the pressure.
"But everyone in Greenland has been very clear that this tragic case should not be used to legitimise other political purposes internationally."
The commission's four appointed experts were unable to agree on which approach to take and ended up writing two reports, submitted nearly six months behind schedule.
Not just about history
One of the victims, Henriette Berthelsen, told AFP the conclusions, regardless of what is decided, were skewed from the start since no Greenlandic Inuit were appointed as experts.
"For me, this is not just about history or politics. It's my body, my life, and my right to self-determination," she said.
"And once again, I see that it is others who will investigate and define what was done to me and to other Inuit women."
The campaign affected girls as young as 12, some of whom were never able to have children afterwards.
Nuuk and Copenhagen are also shedding light on several other painful chapters from the past, including children adopted without parental consent or torn from their families.
On Thursday, the Danish parliament agreed that women affected by the forced contraception campaign can claim compensation from Copenhagen, an initiative pushed by Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen who presented Denmark's official apology last year.
Beyond imagination
Media coverage of the case has revived trauma that had been buried for decades.
"I realised everything it had cost me -- all those hospitalisations, those surgeries, the schooling I missed and, above all, those pains I had never associated with that damn IUD," said Kirstine Najarak Berthelsen.
"It was buried so deeply in my subconscious... Everything that happened to people is beyond imagination if you haven't experienced it yourself," she added.
By the late 1970s, one in two Greenlandic women of childbearing age -- at least 4,070 women -- had been fitted with an IUD, according to an investigation presented in September 2025.
The scandal came to light when one of the victims spoke out in the media about the trauma she experienced.
A podcast series in 2022 then revealed the full extent of the campaign.
Henriette Berthelsen has called for a "Truth and Reconciliation" commission to be established. The Danish government is considering the idea.
According to the 68-year-old psychologist, that would make it possible to "acknowledge what happened".
"I believe that only then will we be able to begin to heal and move forward -- not as adversaries, but as human beings and as peoples equal in dignity."

Asset management giant BlackRock has purchased nearly 26 Lakh shares of electric vehicle (EV) maker Ather Energy via an open-market transaction worth ₹445.3 Cr. As per NSE data, BlackRock, via BlackRock Global Funds, bought 25.9 Lakh shares at ₹1,713.02 apiece. The asset management major lapped up the shares at a premium of 2.1% to the stock’s last closing price on Monday. The stake purchase came on the same day as Ather was added to the MSCI India domestic small cap index. The stock also touched an all-time high of ₹1,704.1 during the intraday trading yesterday following the company’s launch of Konarc escooter. Launched at its annual Community Day, the new escooter has been priced at ₹99,999 for the entry-level variant, placing it in the mass-market electric two-wheeler segment. Built on Ather’s new EL platform, the Konarc will be available across the S and Z product lines, with claimed IDC range between 100 km and 200 km. Besides, the EV maker also unveiled an advanced electronic braking system, a 450-watt onboard charger, and other charging and convenience features at the event. Following the launch, brokerage Emkay Global Financial Services raised its target price for the stock by 37.5% to ₹2,200 per share from ₹1,600 earlier. However, the new launch is not the only factor driving Ather’s rally. Just days ago, auto giant Hero MotoCorp also acquired an additional 3% stake in the EV maker for up to ₹1,758 Cr. What is also helping is Ather’s improving financials. The listed OEM managed to narrow its consolidated net loss by 71% to ₹51 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹178 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. Meanwhile, operating revenue jumped 79% YoY to ₹1,227 Cr during the quarter. As a result, shares of the company have been on an upward swing. The stock has zoomed 78.2% in the past three months, and is up 127.6% on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. Shares of Ather closed Monday’s trading session 4.11% higher at ₹1678.2 on the BSE.

South African airline defends low-altitude aerial stunt over packed stadium
- Published
The South African airline behind a dramatic stunt that saw two of its aircraft in close formation fly reportedly within feet of the top of a stadium has defended itself in the face of some criticism.
The jets roared over Cape Town's DHL stadium as flares shot up before the start of a rugby match featuring fierce rivals South Africa and New Zealand.
Some labelled the manoeuvre reckless, while others have praised the precision and expertise required to pull it off.
In response, Airlink said it was carefully planned with the support of the aviation authorities.
"Planning. Precision. Performance," was the airline's message in social media posts, external accompanied by the footage.
In a statement reproduced on a government news site, external, Airlink went into more detail.
"The two aircraft were flown by highly experienced crew, with each comprised of three senior captains operating in the roles of commander, co-pilot and safety/technical officer," the airline said.
It added that the flights were performed with the "approved and rehearsed safety altitude and speed limits for the flypast".
The flight tracking website Flightradar24, external said that according to its analysis "the lead aircraft passed less than 50 feet (15 metres) above the top of the stadium".
Questions have been raised over the risk and potential for disaster involving two planes and a packed stadium, but many South Africans have responded with expressions of national pride that its country's pilots could pull this off.
The low-altitude flyby has become a feature of the build-up to some big matches.
The most notable was when a South African Airways jet flew over a Johannesburg stadium before the start of the 1995 rugby World Cup final which saw South Africa beat New Zealand.
The match, immortalised in the Hollywood film Invictus, was highly symbolic as the country's first black president, Nelson Mandela, donned the jersey of the national side, which had been closely associated with the apartheid government and previously excluded players who were not white.

Ecuador intelligence chief and five Americans killed in Kenya helicopter crash
- Published
Ecuador's intelligence chief and his wife have been killed in a helicopter that crashed at Mount Ololokwe in central Kenya.
Michele Sensi-Contugi, 44, and his wife, fashion designer Stephany Hollihan, 42, were among the group of seven people - six tourists and the pilot - killed in Samburu county at approximately 09:13 (06:13 GMT) on Wednesday.
Five of victims were Americans, a US State Department spokesperson said. The Reuters news agency reports that Hollihan also held US citizenship.
The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) said the helicopter was on a scenic flight from a wildlife conservancy in Loisaba to Ewaso Nyiro, a river that flows along several national reserves.
Samburu county is a popular tourist destination with many private wildlife conservancies and is renowned for its stunning landscape.
Images from the scene show smoke at the wooded crash site on Mount Ololokwe, as members of the Kenya Red Cross approach the still-burning wreckage.
Ecuador's President Daniel Noboa named Sensi-Contugo director of the country's Centre of Strategic Intelligence (CIES) in January 2024.
The office of the president and Ecuador's National Assembly expressed their condolences over his death and that of Hollihan.
The Italian-Ecuadorean businessman had had close links to Noboa even before he was chosen to lead the intelligence service and was considered a close ally of the president.
Shortly before being named head of the CIES, he had served for four months as a minister in his cabinet.
Noboa has declared three days of national mourning starting on Thursday.
Newspapers in Ecuador have also run obituaries of Hollihan. The Guayaquil-based designer founded Sensi Studio, a brand praised for incorporating traditional Ecuadorean elements and materials in its designs.
Lady Lori Helicopters, which operated the Eurocopter EC130 B4 aircraft, said it was "deeply saddened" by the accident.
"Our deepest sympathies are with the guests, crew, their families and loved ones, and all those affected by this tragic accident," a statement read.
According to a memo seen by the BBC's US partner CBS News, external one of the Americans killed in the crash was NBCUniversal journalist José Alberto Suárez.
In the memo, NBCUniversal called Suárez "a deeply respected leader and beloved friend and colleague.
"José was an exceptional colleague and mentor to many," the memo read.
Miami restaurateur Roger Duarte was among the Americans killed in the crash, according to local and US media.
Commenting on his death on X, US Rep Carlos Antonio Gimenez wrote: "Our prayers are with their loved ones during this incredibly difficult time. May their memories be a blessing."
The other victims have not yet been identified.
Helicopter crashes are not uncommon in Kenya.
In February, a helicopter crash in the Rift Valley county of Nandi killed six people, including a member of parliament.
In 2024, the military chief, Gen Francis Omondi Ogolla, died after an army helicopter that was carrying 11 people crashed in the west of the country, with only two survivors.
In June 2021 at least 10 soldiers were killed when their helicopter crashed while landing near the capital, Nairobi.

Partey signs for Al-Shabab in Saudi Pro League
- Published
Saudi Pro League side Al-Shabab have confirmed the signing of Ghana international Thomas Partey.
The former Arsenal midfielder, who made 167 appearances for the Gunners between 2020 and 2025, became a free agent this summer when Villarreal decided against extending his expiring contract.
The 33-year-old is scheduled to stand trial next year after pleading not guilty to seven charges of rape and one count of sexual assault relating to allegations by four different women between 2020 and 2022.
During this summer's World Cup, Partey was denied entry to Canada before Ghana's opening match of the tournament against Panama because of ongoing criminal proceedings in the UK.
Partey wrongly told officials he had never been arrested or charged with a crime. He went on to play in Ghana's other three games at the tournament as they lost in the last 32 stage to Colombia.
Al-Shabab, whose squad contains former Burnley captain Josh Brownhill and ex-Wolves winger Daniel Podence, finished 13th last season in the Saudi Pro League and lost their opening match this term.

South Korea court sentences Unification Church leader to jail
Unification Church leader Han Hak-ja arrives for a sentencing hearing over political funding and bribery offenses linked to efforts to gain influence with former President Yoon Suk Yeol's administration, at Seoul Central District Court in the South Korean capital on Monday.
| Pool / via REUTERS
Seoul – A South Korean court on Monday sentenced Unification Church leader Han Hak-ja to a combined two years in prison over political funding and bribery offenses linked to efforts to gain influence with former President Yoon Suk Yeol’s administration.
The Seoul Central District Court found that Han, 83, was involved in providing money to politicians and luxury goods, including Chanel bags and a diamond necklace, to former first lady Kim Keon Hee, according to the ruling.
Han, head of the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification, widely known as the Unification Church, was indicted in October 2025 by a special prosecutor team investigating allegations involving Yoon and Kim.

What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?
- Published
The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is now the deadliest of the 17 the country has faced as it continues to spread. United Nations experts have described it as the fastest growing outbreak on record in terms of new infections.
Getting the spread of the deadly virus under control is challenging because it involves a rare species of Ebola for which there is no vaccine - though some are being tested - and the epicentre is in an area affected by conflict.
What is Ebola and what are the symptoms?
Ebola is a rare but deadly disease caused by a virus.
Ebola viruses normally infect animals, typically fruit bats, but outbreaks among humans can sometimes start when people eat or handle infected animals.
It takes two to 21 days for symptoms to appear. They come on suddenly and start like the flu or malaria, with fever, headache and tiredness.
As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
Ebola outbreaks used to be small and contained to remote rural areas. However, urbanisation is pushing larger populations closer to these natural reservoirs of Ebola and increasing the risk of transmission.
Why is this Ebola outbreak different and is there a vaccine?
This outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which had not been seen for over a decade.
Named after a district in Uganda where it was first detected, Bundibugyo has only caused two previous outbreaks - in 2007 and 2012.
One study showed that it killed about a third, external of those infected, far less than the more common Zaire (66.6%) and Sudan (48.5%) species. About 48% of those known to have been infected in the current outbreak have died.
Initial blood tests for Ebola in the affected areas were negative as they were designed to identify the more common form of the disease.
In July, the UK's medicines regulator, the MHRA, said it had given permission for the first human trials of a vaccine for Bundibugyo to go ahead.
It was created by a team from the University of Oxford based on the same technology used in the Oxford-AstraZeneca Covid vaccine.
It took scientists just eight weeks to develop the new jab after plugging in genetic code from the Bundibugyo species of Ebola.
The vaccine is being tested on 50 volunteers from Oxford aged 18 to 55 to see whether it triggers the correct antibody response without causing significant side effects.
Three other groups are also developing different vaccines for Bundibugyo although they have not yet entered clinical trials.
While treatments are available for other species of the Ebola virus, no drugs have been specifically approved to treat those infected with Bundibugyo.
DR Congo is currently preparing to roll out the Ervebo vaccine - which helps protect against the Zaïre species of Ebola - as part of a trial to see if it is effective against the Bundibugyo species.
The World Health Organization (WHO) is also sponsoring a separate clinical trial in the country to see whether two existing antiviral therapies can improve survival rates.
The two drugs selected as the most promising are an experimental monoclonal antibody called MBP134 and remdesivir, an injection into a vein, which is also used to treat Covid.
A further complication is that the outbreak is taking place in a conflict zone, with a quarter of million people displaced from their homes and people moving across porous borders into neighbouring countries.
How did the current Ebola outbreak start?
The first known case was a nurse who developed symptoms on 24 April, which means the virus had been spreading undetected for weeks.
The nurse died in Bunia, the capital of eastern DR Congo's Ituri province, according to Congolese Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba.
The victim's body was repatriated to Mongbwalu.
Kamba said one of the reasons the virus spread so quickly was the number of people exposed to the body during the funeral ceremony.
But researchers believe that it may have been spreading since February but it was initially misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid.
How many Ebola cases have been reported and where are they?
On 23 August, officials said there had been 5,514 confirmed cases and 2,642 confirmed deaths from the virus in DR Congo.
There have also been 1,200 recoveries from Ebola so far, including four nurses whose discharge from hospital was celebrated at a special ceremony.
Ituri province is the epicentre of this outbreak and accounts for the vast majority of confirmed infections.
Cases have also been confirmed in North Kivu (714) and South Kivu (3), provinces partly controlled by the rebel AFC-M23 alliance. These discoveries signalled the outbreak's spread from its epicentre.
The last patient being treated for Ebola in neighbouring Uganda was discharged from hospital on 16 July. Up to that point, the country had recorded 20 confirmed cases - with most having travelled from DR Congo - and two deaths.
Uganda has since announced it is Ebola-free, going against the protocol of waiting 42 days - until 27 August - from when the last patient recovers to declare an outbreak over.
What is being done in DR Congo to tackle the current Ebola outbreak?
Mass gatherings have been banned in the six provinces with confirmed cases - Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Tshopo, Haut-Uele and Bas-Uele.
The capital city, Kinshasa - which has no confirmed cases and is located some 1,800 km (1,100) miles from the outbreak - has also been ordered to ban mass gatherings.
The government has now established four laboratories in Ituri - in Bunia, Mongbwalu, Beni and Aru - which can test blood samples for Bundibugyo and deliver results within 24 hours, removing earlier delays.
Surveillance systems, contact tracing and the treatment infrastructure, with dedicated centres in several affected towns, have also been expanded, according to the health minister.
The WHO has dedicated $3.9m (£2.9m) to tackling the outbreak, while Africa CDC has announced a $319m budget.
A toll-free number, 151, has been provided for reporting symptoms and people are being reminded to:
- avoid contact with bodies of people who died with symptoms, or with dead animals
- not eat raw meat, as undercooked food may transmit the virus
- practise social distancing.
How have the rebels responded to the latest Ebola outbreak?
The AFC-M23 group has created an Ebola response team in an effort to prevent transmissions in the areas it controls.
In late June, the rebel authorities had declared their zones Ebola-free, but introduced new restrictions in August, following two travellers testing positive in North Kivu.
Shared taxis and passenger boats between government-held and rebel-held areas of the province, have been suspended, highlighting the hostilities between the two sides.
The region's Ebola response co-ordinator Dr Freddy Kaniki, told the BBC in July that while UN agencies such as the WHO and Unicef - for children - had been helping, there has been no co-ordination with the Congolese government.

What are Rwanda and other countries doing about the Ebola outbreak?
Rwanda closed its borders with DR Congo earlier on in the outbreak. According to Congolese media, authorities began to reopen parts of the border late in June following a lull in local infections.
Uganda has temporarily suspended flights, buses and all other public transport crossing the border with DR Congo.
Several other African countries have tightened border screenings and bolstered health facilities.
The US has extended travel restrictions on its citizens who have been to DR Congo. Anyone who wants to return home must spend 21 days in a third country before being allowed into America.

Donald Trump announced Friday a new US oil agreement with Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez, saying the US will have “majority” control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves.
The terms of the agreement remain to be seen, but the US president said on his social-media platform that it had been brokered “through a partnership with private business” by his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and defense secretary, Pete Hegseth.
The administration, Trump wrote, has “secured majority U.S. control of more than 65 BILLION BARRELS of proven Oil Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the American Taxpayer”.
Trump said the agreement would more than double American oil reserves.
“This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people,” Rubio wrote on social media.
Trump’s announcement provided few details on the structure of the agreement, the fields or companies involved, or how the US would exercise majority control over the reserves.
Venezuela has an estimated 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves, the world’s largest.
Since the US captured and removed former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro from power in January, Washington has been trying to secure a stable flow of Venezuelan crude oil for US refineries while promoting American investment into the Opec country’s deteriorated energy industry, which produces 1.25m barrels per day of crude.
Trump is under pressure before November’s midterm elections over rising gasoline prices, which could be eased through cheaper oil supplies and expanded output.
The US also has been looking for solutions to replenish its strategic petroleum reserve, the oil stockpile, including the possibility of crude swaps with US producers.
Earlier this week, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration was “in advanced talks with Venezuela for the U.S. to take a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields that house nearly one-third of the country’s massive energy reserves”. Axios also reported on the negotiations, quoting a US official who claimed the deal would be “massive”.
The discussion was reportedly over a US stake in Venezuela’s most promising oil-and-gasfields, with some 90bn barrels of proven reserves.
The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro.
“It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticizing the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States.”
The announcement comes as Chevron and other US energy companies are expected to sign a deal next week investing billions in Venezuela’s oil fields, according to the Journal.
Tom Phillips and Reuters contributed reporting

Paperwork, lines, hours on hold: There's a 'Time Tax' on Americans who need help most
How much of your life do you spend waiting, either in line, on the phone or while filling out government forms? Annie Lowrey, a journalist with The Atlantic, says all that waiting amounts to what she calls a "time tax," paid most often by those applying for government benefits like unemployment, disability and food assistance.
"I really saw this as a tax, because there's this understanding that, with the government, we should be getting what's ours," Lowrey explains. "How much time, how much effort, how much emotional strain, how much do you have to give up to receive something that you're trying to either purchase or obtain or a right that you are supposed to have?"
In her new book, The Time Tax: How the Government Wastes Our Time — and How to Fix It, Lowrey argues that excessive red tape in many, but not all, government agencies often acts as a barrier to people receiving benefits. She notes that new paperwork and work requirements have already cut millions of Americans from food assistance, and the numbers are still growing. She points to our current unemployment insurance system as an example of how administrative hurdles prevent people from collecting benefits they are owed.
"Unemployment insurance is a contributory benefit. You have to be paying into a trust fund in order to get it," she says. But, she adds, some people don't collect unemployment, either because they can't figure out how to complete the paperwork or "the state, frankly, can't figure out how to deal with all of the paperwork that it's receiving."
In addition to lost benefits, Lowrey says living with such a time tax contributes to what she calls a "low-trust society."
"When the government treats us like this, we don't trust it. And if we don't trust it, we're not going to trust it to do more and better things for our life. And I think that it leads us not to trust each other, too," she says.
Interview highlights
On the administrative burdens faced by the Americans with the greatest need
If you are looking at the programs that are targeted at the most at-risk Americans — Supplemental Security Income [SSI], which is used by very low-income seniors with disabilities; TANF [Temporary Assistance to Needy Families] or cash welfare, which is used by very low-income, primarily mothers of small children; WIC [Women, Infants & Children], which is a nutrition support program that is also used by quite low-income mothers and their kids. They tend to come with really significant time burdens. ...
SSI, for instance, it makes these folks comply with an asset test, right? So how much exact money is in your bank account? Or do you have any little pockets saved away somewhere? ... And I think that everything that we know about being very sick, very at risk, very poor, homeless, vulnerable in some fashion, those programs should be easier, not harder.
On the hurdles people seeking food assistance face
I see it in moral terms. Food assistance should not be a program for low-income, at-risk Americans who might not be able to eat enough, who are also good at paperwork. That's not what that program should be, right? ... Do we want all of these programs to [say] this is assistance for lower income Americans, provided that they have a smartphone and a wifi connection? That's not what these programs are about.
On how the time tax relates to voting
We vote on Tuesday, because back when we were an agrarian society, the days were limited ... by the need for people to go to church on Sunday. And often, [voters] would have to travel for, like, a day to get to their polling place, because they might be going on foot or they might be by horse. And you had to avoid market days also. And so it ended up being that Congress, in I believe the 1840s, decided that Tuesday was the day. And this is not a holiday. ...
[As a result] We do not have high voter participation rates. And so that means that the voting public is not representative of the actual American public. That's not good for (small d) democratic reasons. And I would say that vote by mail has started to change this. But there's now real attacks on vote by mail, and I think precisely for that purpose. What you are doing when you hold elections in a really complicated fashion is you allow politicians to pick their voters instead of allowing the American public — as big as we can make it — to pick their politicians.
On why Social Security works relatively well
[It's the] biggest government program that we have, pretty much. It's huge. It's overhead cost 1% and it works really well. The payment error rate [is] extremely low. I think there's this idea of, "Oh, it's easy to calculate somebody's social security benefit." No, it isn't. They have to monitor your income and whether you're employed throughout your whole life. So yeah, it is pretty easy for them to get you your benefits when you elect them. They've already done all of the work, but that was a lot of work in the background. They just don't impose it on people. And I'm not saying Social Security is perfect, right? Like there are absolutely problems with it. But nevertheless, people really like it. It works really well.
We have tremendous overhead because we have duplicative programs, programs that people have never even heard about, that we bother to set up and then nobody uses. ... The way I see it, you can make the government smaller by making the rules easier, giving the government a little more budget to update these systems and giving it the express goal of reducing burden on citizens and taxpayers.
Anna Bauman and Susan Nyakundi produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

Zerodha’s core business is no longer growing. Regulatory curbs and changing investor behaviour are cooling trading activity and squeezing brokerage revenue. Broking revenue fell 10.4% from ₹3,066 Cr in FY25 to ₹2,738 Cr in FY26. Net transaction charges (income earned from exchange-related transaction fee rebates) also fell to zero from ₹400 Cr in FY25 due to SEBI’s true-to-label norm framework. In a blog post, CEO Nithin Kamath hinted that its overall top line remained almost flat in FY26 versus ₹8,847 Cr a fiscal year ago. Despite the revenue squeeze, Zerodha kept its bottom line largely intact, with profit rising marginally to ₹4,283 Cr in FY26 from ₹4,231 Cr in FY25. So, with its core revenue engine slowing, what is keeping Zerodha’s profits afloat? The answer: Zerodha is increasingly making money from sources other than brokerage. Interest income (₹2,269 Cr): The discount broker earns interest on its cash balances and other interest-generating assets. Delayed payment charges + MTF (₹448 Cr): It earns money when customers delay paying for trades and, through MTF, when customers borrow money to buy stocks. AMC charges: Zerodha’s asset management business is also generating more fee income, though it is still relatively small. In Q1 FY27, the discount broker said that nearly 40% of its gross revenue came from the businesses outside its core trading platform. While these revenue streams are cushioning the impact of falling brokerage income, are they large enough to replace the core business entirely, especially when its arch-rival Groww now has an active client base almost twice the size? Zerodha’s User Problem Is Bigger Than It Looks Regulatory changes have added to the pressure on Zerodha’s core brokerage business, particularly by curbing derivatives and currency trading activity. SEBI’s derivatives clampdown and RBI’s tighter rules around currency futures and options (F&O), introduced in 2024, reduced trading activity across segments. According to Zerodha, these regulatory changes led to a 20-30% drop in F&O activity across exchanges and brokers. INR currency F&O volumes fell 90% after the RBI introduced rules requiring trades to be backed by an underlying foreign currency exposure. But regulations do not fully explain the divergence between Zerodha and Groww, which has almost twice as many clients as Zerodha. In July, Groww added 70,119 active clients, taking its base to 13.12 Mn and its NSE market share to 28.88%. Zerodha lost 38,725 clients, leaving it with 6.76 Mn and a 14.88% share. The entire broking industry added only around 8,000 net active clients during the month. The divergence is visible in revenue as well. Groww’s operating revenue rose from ₹ 2,609 Cr in FY24 to ₹4,645 Cr in FY26, an increase of about 78%. Zerodha, by comparison, saw its revenue decline from nearly ₹9,994 Cr in FY24 to around ₹8,847 Cr in FY26. However, according to Rahul Sharma, head of office research at Equity99, Groww and Zerodha are not competing for the same customer or the same kind of revenue. While Groww has focused more on mass-market equity, mutual funds and SIPs, Zerodha continues to derive a significant portion of its revenue from active F&O traders. Even CEO Nithin Kamath argues that the active-client market is not the most important metric. This, however, does not answer the fundamental question: if Zerodha is not trying to win on users, can it extract enough value from its existing base? MTF Rescue Boat Margin trading facility (MTF) is helping Zerodha build a new revenue stream, but it is not the only one trying to reduce its dependence on trading-led revenue. Angel One has been moving aggressively in the same direction, with client funding, wealth management, asset management and distribution becoming a larger part of its business. Zerodha launched its MTF offering in December 2024, after years of debating whether to enter the segment. At the time, Zerodha said it made little business sense to remain the only large broker without the product. The product has since scaled. Zerodha’s MTF book has reached around ₹9,000 Cr, with customers borrowing about ₹6,000 Cr. Per Kamath, MTF contributes roughly 10% of the startup’s revenue. The financials show the change clearly. Delayed payment charges and MTF generated ₹448 Cr in FY26, compared with ₹22 Cr in FY25. The reason this matters is simple: Brokerage revenue depends heavily on customers trading. MTF allows Zerodha to earn interest from customers who borrow to invest, creating a revenue stream that is less dependent on the number of trades. The bigger issue is that MTF is being built against a business that remains heavily exposed to derivatives. Avinash Gorakhshar, founder of Avinash Mentor Research, said continued regulatory pressure on F&O could make Zerodha’s slower diversification into mass-market wealth products a growth constraint. But MTF is not yet large enough to replace the revenue lost from Zerodha’s traditional business. It puts Zerodha in an interesting position. Angel One, which had a broadly similar active client base to Zerodha at the end of FY26, has also been building its client funding business; its average client funding book stood at ₹5,305 Cr for FY26 and rose to ₹6,783 Cr by June 2026. It is pertinent to note that Angel One’s client funding book includes MTF loans and period-end trade receivables, net of non-interest-bearing receivables. Then there is also a limit to how aggressively Zerodha can push the product. Kamath has acknowledged the risks associated with leveraged investing and said the startup does not want to encourage customers to borrow simply because it generates revenue. The Diversification Dilemma Zerodha remains profitable, its AMC is scaling faster than Groww's AUM, and its MTF book has grown rapidly. But the timing of some of these moves is tricky. Zerodha had a significant first-mover advantage in digital broking, but MTF came only in late 2024, while it launched AMC in 2023. It is now bringing mutual fund transactions to Kite, after keeping the trading and mutual fund experience separate for years. The gap is more visible in wealth management. Groww has moved into the affluent investor segment through W, its wealth management platform, which offers access to Portfolio Management Services (PMS), Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) and private market opportunities. Lalit Keshre’s Groww entered the segment after acquiring Fisdom in October last year, a deal that brought wealth management and distribution capabilities into its business. Zerodha, by comparison, remains largely a self-directed investment platform through Kite and Coin. Its Zerodha Fund House gives it an asset management business, but that is different from offering personalised wealth management. However, not everyone believes Zerodha’s slower customer growth means it has been slow to respond to changing market realities. Sharma of Equity99 argues that the startup is making a deliberate trade-off, prioritising profitability and capital efficiency over aggressive customer acquisition. But with Groww moving faster into wealth and adjacent products, Zerodha risks falling behind if its diversification does not scale quickly enough. All in all, Zerodha is not a troubled business. It remains highly profitable, has a strong brand, a sizeable customer base and growing businesses beyond brokerage. But the economics of digital broking are changing, and the company can no longer rely on its traditional F&O-heavy model to drive growth. Therefore, it will have to diversify fast enough before its core business shrinks further. Edited By Shishir Parasher Creatives: Varshita Srivastava

It took three years, but Coyote vs. Acme is finally in theaters and delighting audiences of all ages with its irresistible blend of slapstick humor, pointed satire, and even a warm fuzzy here and there. We’re happy to report that the film was worth the wait.
(Some spoilers below but no major reveals.)
The film is based on a well-known satirical piece by Ian Frazier (also titled “Coyote vs. Acme”) published in The New Yorker in 1990. Development of a film version didn’t start until 2018, but some pretty talented people worked on the script, including James Gunn. Small wonder that Warner Bros.’ bizarre 2023 decision to shelve the film in order to take a tax write-off sparked outrage both within the industry and among fans online.
The concept alone is sheer brilliance: Wile E. Coyote, after decades of ACME equipment failing him in his efforts to catch that darned Road Runner, decides to sue the corporation. He chooses Albuquerque personal injury lawyer Kevin Avery (Will Forte) to represent him against Acme’s hotshot corporate lawyers, led by Buddy Crane (John Cena)—who just happens to be an old law school buddy of Kevin’s.
Kevin has made a number of personal injury claims against Acme over the years on behalf of his cartoon clients, usually settling out of court for small sums. That’s what he expects will happen with Wile E.’s case—until a clerical error results in filing a massive lawsuit against every Acme product. Acme unexpectedly (and suspiciously) offers a very generous settlement. But the coyote has other plans and rips it up, forcing the matter to trial.
The problem is that Kevin is not a trial lawyer and only has his intern niece Paige (Lana Condor) and partners Sal Maltese (Tone Bell) and Dottie Jones (Martha Kelly) to assist him. The Road Runner is the only eyewitness to Wile E.’s many Acme-related mishaps and unlikely to show up in court, given that it is well-nigh impossible to catch. Acme also has a deep, dark secret related to something called “Project Sisyphus” and the disappearance of an Acme product development scientist back in 1992. And they will do anything to protect that secret.

Singapore to invest US$173m over 3 years to boost fintech innovation
The money will help co-fund at least 1,000 internships under the Financial Sector Technology and Innovation Scheme to build young talent
The funds come under the latest iteration of the Financial Sector Technology and Innovation Scheme (FSTI), which aims to strengthen the country’s fintech space and accelerate innovation and technology adoption in the financial sector.
The latest edition of the scheme, known as FSTI 4.0, includes a manpower track that will support firms in building young talent by co-funding an internship stipend. This will be facilitated through a new internship portal managed by the Singapore FinTech Association to connect students with internships across business, technology and other roles.
MAS said it aimed to support at least 1,000 fintech internship opportunities over the next three years.

Ex-congressman George Santos banned from betting platform for life
- Published
Prediction-market operator Kalshi has permanently barred former US congressman George Santos from trading on its platform.
The company alleged that Santos, who was expelled from Congress following a series of fraud and identity-theft charges, placed bets in February related to his own attendance at US President Donald Trump's State of the Union address, according to a notice of disciplinary action.
Kalshi said its compliance team concluded his activity showed signs of insider dealing, prompting the lifetime ban. It said it was acting independently without waiting for external enforcement action.
Santos on X thanked Kalshi for the ban and said "Let's see how much longer you guys are around for".
The BBC has contacted Santos for comment.
In 2025, Trump ordered the release of Santos, who had been sentenced to a seven-year prison term for wire fraud and identity theft. He had served three months.
In July, Santos agreed to pay $35,000 to settle a federal investigation by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission into his State of the Union trades.
Kalshi, alleging Santos used non-public information to place bets, issued a penalty of $71,356 (£38,000).
The disciplinary moves come at a moment when prediction markets – which allow users to wager on outcomes ranging from elections to economic indicators – are facing heightened scrutiny.
Both Kalshi and rival Polymarket have reported an uptick in unusual trading patterns, forcing platforms to strengthen monitoring systems and respond more aggressively to potential misconduct.
Kalshi said Santos's case was referred to federal authorities earlier this summer after internal systems flagged suspicious behaviour linked to his account.
The company said the case centered on his trades in a market tied to whether he would attend Trump's address – an event he could directly influence.
Its compliance team found he placed a series of sizeable bets between 2 and 25 February, some of which were based on false or misleading public statements about his plans, according to the company.
His comments moved contract prices, and he ultimately earned $17,839.57 from the trades.
Santos has denied wrongdoing in various matters but has admitted to stealing identities of nearly a dozen people, including next of kin. He pleaded guilty to wire fraud and aggravated identity theft and served three months in prison before Trump commuted his sentence last year.
He embellished much about his biography in the run-up to his election to Congress in 2022. The former lawmaker was only the sixth in US history to be expelled from Congress.
The Kalshi episode underscores the growing compliance burden facing prediction markets as they attract more users and move closer to mainstream products. Regulators have signalled that platforms will be expected to meet higher standards as the industry matures, particularly when political or economic events are involved.
