SC panel picks new Rajasthan HC chief justice amid allegations against acting CJ
The Supreme Court collegium's recommendation came on a day Rajasthan HC's acting chief justice Sanjeev Prakash Sharma opted out of judicial work until Sept 5
The Supreme Court collegium on Monday evening recommended Chhattisgarh High Court judge Sanjay Kumar Agrawal as the full-time chief justice of the Rajasthan High Court, a move that comes amid an escalating controversy over allegations of “corruption”, “nepotism” and “favouritism” levelled against the high court’s acting chief justice Sanjeev Prakash Sharma by Supreme Court judge Justice Sandeep Mehta.
The recommendation came on a day Justice Sharma opted out of judicial work until September 5, as lawyers in Jaipur and Jodhpur stepped up protests demanding that he be removed as acting chief justice and a regular chief justice appointed.
Justice Agrawal was elevated as an additional judge of the Chhattisgarh High Court in September 2013.
The collegium comprised Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and justices Vikram Nath and BV Nagarathna.
The recommendation to appoint Justice Agrawal as chief justice of the Rajasthan High Court comes as the controversy over Justice Sharma’s functioning is being considered at the institutional level.
Justice Mehta, in three letters to CJI Kant Kant dated August 2, 10 and 17, repeatedly urged the appointment of a regular chief justice from another high court and sought Justice Sharma’s transfer out of Rajasthan.
Justice Mehta has alleged that Justice Sharma misused his powers as master of the roster, selectively shifted cases from other benches to his own court and passed orders that raised “serious question marks” over the integrity of the decision-making process. He has also accused the acting chief justice of favouring influential and rich litigants and described the cumulative conduct as amounting to “brazen misuse of powers” that “smack of corruption”.
In his August 10 letter, Justice Mehta cited two cases as “living proof” of what he described as Justice Sharma’s attempt to “hit longer sixes” ahead of his retirement on September 26. One concerned “priceless lands” in Udaipur, while the other involved a mining magnate whose delayed appeal, according to Justice Mehta, was improperly registered and heard by Justice Sharma’s bench.
Justice Mehta has also levelled allegations of nepotism and favouritism, alleging that Justice Sharma backed the elevation of the daughter-in-law of a senior advocate and went out of his way to support lawyers close to him. He has further alleged vindictive treatment of judicial officers and questioned several administrative decisions concerning the Jodhpur principal seat.
The Supreme Court judge also claimed that judges of the Rajasthan High Court expressed “anguish” to him over Justice Sharma’s conduct and alleged that the acting chief justice frequently threatened colleagues with retaliatory transfers by invoking his alleged proximity to the CJI.
In his August 17 letter, Justice Mehta alleged that Justice Sharma delayed the inauguration of the new Jodhpur District Court building despite it being operationally complete for about a year, saying the resulting loss to the institution was “unpardonable”.
Justice Mehta also criticised the functioning of the high court under Justice Sharma, alleging that a full court meeting on July 31 was used to push the designation of around 96 advocates as senior advocates without a uniform criterion.
According to his letter, the proposal could not ultimately be passed after other judges resisted it. He further questioned the organisation of a three-day conference in Jaipur, alleging that almost ₹80 lakh was spent from the public exchequer while the Jodhpur principal seat remained without a functional court for two working days and around 20 to 22 district judges were nominated to attend the event.
In response, a statement issued by CJI Surya Kant on August 26 said that he and other collegium members have taken note of Justice Mehta’s concerns but stressed that allegations against a sitting judge must be dealt with through the established institutional mechanism. The statement added that the concerned judge must be given an opportunity to respond and that allegations cannot be treated as findings merely because they have been made. CJI Kant had further said that he and the other members of the collegium were already working on appointments of regular chief justices to the remaining high courts.
The row triggered protests by lawyers at both Jaipur and Jodhpur. The Rajasthan High Court Lawyers Association on Monday announced a complete strike till September 6, demanding that Justice Sharma be divested of his administrative charge and a regular chief justice appointed. The association also decided to send representations to the CJI and President Droupadi Murmu.
At Jaipur, police were called to the high court premises to disperse protesting advocates, while lawyers at Jodhpur also raised slogans and demanded action against the acting chief justice.
Following an emergency general house meeting, the lawyers’ association said the situation was “against the sanctity of justice”. Its president, Dilip Singh Udawat, said the lawyers had unanimously concluded that they needed to raise their voices.
Justice Sharma, meanwhile, opted out of judicial work from Monday. A modified roster issued under his endorsement said he would not sit on any bench till September 6, with matters earlier assigned to his bench distributed among other benches. The high court website attributed the change to the “non-sitting of Hon’ble the acting chief justice”.
Justice Sharma has been serving as acting chief justice for more than 10 months following Justice S Shriram's retirement as chief justice in September 2025.
Justice Mehta had repeatedly urged the collegium to appoint a regular Chief Justice from another high court, arguing that the prolonged arrangement had adversely affected the institution.

New Wolverine video game features Squamish Nation's language, B.C. locations
Sḵwx̱wú7mesh sníchim displayed on 2 Sea-to-Sky Highway signs
A sign featuring the Squamish Nation's language is on display in a new Wolverine video game that’s expected to draw millions of players globally.
The game, Marvel’s Wolverine, will be released on Sept. 15 on PlayStation 5 and shows off several slices of B.C., including North Vancouver, the Lions Gate Bridge and the Sea-to-Sky Highway.
At one point, while the main character Logan (aka Wolverine) is driving a motorcycle along the highway, the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh sníchim (Squamish language) is displayed on two signs, spelling out the words for Whistler — Sk̲wik̲w — and Squamish — Sḵwx̱wú7mesh.
"It's something that I felt we absolutely had to do," said senior art director Gavin Goulden, who's based in Vancouver. "I worked with the team to get like the proper signage for it."
He said it was also critical to have real parts of Canada represented in the game, since Wolverine's character was born in Alberta.
"Wolverine is a Canadian hero, arguably the most famous Canadian superhero that there is," Goulden said.
It’s rare for British Columbia to be displayed in video games, and having the Squamish Nation's language included is being considered a big win, according to gaming experts.
Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish Nation) chairperson Sxwíxwtn (Wilson Williams) said having Wolverine ride through their territory and past the highway sign proudly displaying their language is "more than just a cameo."
"It’s a moment of visibility and proof that our language and our presence on this land are not something of the past, but something living, spoken and seen today," Sxwíxwtn said.
"We are proud that in a game about a Canadian hero, it's our language on the sign that welcomes him home."
‘This is where we live’
Cary Brisebois has been making video games for more than 25 years.
He’s also on the game development advisory board at Vancouver Film School and said its great to see the subtle nod of Indigenous inclusion in the game.
"I love that they didn't shy away from it, but I love that it's also not really tokenized," Brisebois said. "It's saying, ‘Hey, look, this is where we live. This is the land that we're on, and we're not afraid to show it.'"
Simon Fraser University assistant professor Sarah Christina Ganzon, who specializes in game studies and digital fandom, said it's refreshing to see Canada featured in a game.
"It's wonderful to see it; the fact that Logan is Canadian, you don't really see him in Canada," she said.
Representation in pop culture
Aliki Marinakis, an Indigenous language programs manager at the University of Victoria, said the sign is "definitely a win."
While not Indigenous herself, she's raising two Indigenous children who are trying to learn their language.
"We have 35 different Indigenous languages in B.C. alone, and I mean, how many Canadians could name one or two?" she said.
Her 16-year-old son dressed up as Wolverine a couple of years ago for Halloween and she knows he’ll be excited to see Sḵwx̱wú7mesh sníchim in the game.
"Indigenous kids need to see themselves being represented in pop culture just the way they need to see themselves being represented in education and in health," Marinakis said.
The Sea-to-Sky region is a hot spot for filming, according to Nikki Johnston with Tourism Squamish.
"A lot of films and TV shows tend to come to Squamish because of the beautiful natural landscape," Johnston said. "We're seeing that same effect here with the cinematic action game."
Previous Marvel games like Spider-Man have been played by millions of people globally, according to an account manager with PlayStation.
"A cinematic action game like Wolverine might increase destination exposure for Squamish, but at this point, I think it's a little too soon to see," Johnston said.

John Galliano exhibition at New York Met cancelled after backlash
- Published
John Galliano has cancelled an upcoming major exhibition celebrating his work as a fashion designer after it prompted criticism due to his previous conviction for making antisemitic remarks.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York had announced an exhibition titled John Galliano: Horizons that was due to open in May 2027.
But Galliano said on Monday: "After much reflection and discussion with the Met and all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time."
The British designer was sacked as creative director of Dior in 2011 and found guilty of abusing a Jewish curator in a restaurant in Paris.
A court also heard that he hurled racist insults at her friend, who is of South Asian origin, and in a separate incident declared a love for Hitler.
'I remain deeply sorry'
At the time, he apologised for his behaviour and his lawyer blamed it on "work-related stress and multiple addictions".
Galliano said in his statement on Monday: "I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it.
"I understand that meaningful atonement is not achieved through an exhibition, institutional recognition or a single public gesture.
"It is a continuing responsibility, demonstrated through listening, learning and one's conduct over time."
Galliano added that he did not want "to distract from the remarkable work" of the Met's Costume Institute and said he recognised and respected that "an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some".
Galliano's new statement noted his "15 years of sobriety and recovery from alcoholism and addiction".
As well as being the focus of the exhibition, Galliano and his work in fashion would have provided the theme for the next Met Gala.
The star-studded event is due to take place on 3 May, coinciding with Yom HaShoah (Holocaust and Heroism Remembrance Day).
Vogue global editorial director Anna Wintour, a trustee of the Met and co-chair of the Met Gala, gave her support to Galliano on Monday.
"John's decision that the exhibition devoted to his work should not take place at this time is very courageous and a measure of the man he is," she said.
"I believe this is the right decision, and both he and the Museum have my full support."
'Misguided'
Others had previously voiced their opposition to the Met's plan to commemorate Galliano.
Julie Menin, speaker of New York City Council, said, external: "After my numerous and lengthy meetings and conversations with the Met, I am pleased that they have agreed to not honour John Galliano.
"From the beginning, I have told them that I strongly disagreed with this decision, and at this rising time of antisemitism, it had served as a gut punch to the Jewish community.
"This is the correct decision, as the harm and pain this was causing was simply unacceptable."
Meanwhile, Jonathan Greenblatt, chief executive of the Anti-Defamation League, which aims to counter antisemitism, said that with antisemitism at "crisis levels", honouring Galliano would be "misguided".
"Even Galliano ultimately recognised what the Met should have done from the start," he added. "This was the wrong move at the wrong moment. Timing matters."
Galliano is regarded by some as one of the greatest fashion designers and returned to the fashion industry following his conviction, serving as creative director of Margiela for a decade until 2024.

'Like fighting a dinosaur': Sydney woman recalls how she punched shark during attack
- Published
A Sydney woman who survived a shark attack has described the moment she came face-to-face with a 4m great white before repeatedly punching it.
Leah Stewart, 34, was dragged under the water at Coogee Beach in June as the shark bit into her thigh and arms, leaving her with extreme blood loss and injuries so severe that doctors had to amputate her left arm.
In an interview which aired on Sunday, the mother-of-one said she was determined to live for the sake of her baby daughter.
"In my head, I was like, ... 'You are not taking me away from my daughter', and I twisted myself around and I just started punching it over and over and over again - it was like fighting a dinosaur".
Moments earlier, Stewart had just finished her regular Saturday morning swim and was heading back to shore when she was alerted to danger.
"I heard a girl behind me… a shrill shriek. I turned and there was a huge, huge fin behind her. It was massive," she told Nine Network's 60 Minutes.
"I looked at the size of it and I realised that's not a dolphin."
Stewart turned around and realised the shark was "right there … and it just was getting closer and closer and closer."
The shark's face was "horrific" with "black little beady eyes" and its "teeth and its mouth was massive".
"We were looking face-to-face," Stewart said, and at one point, the shark was just 30cm from her own.
Even in that moment, Stewart's thoughts remained calm.
"I'm right-handed, so I thought 'let's do a left hook'," she said.
"I just kind of throw my left arm and it just grabs onto my forearm and rips, rips away my skin, my muscle, everything... there's a big gap between my forearm and the hand."
The shark started to pull Stewart under the water, grabbing her leg.
"I had the thought, 'this is it, this is how I die' and then I just thought of [my daughter] August and I thought she's not going to have a mum, she's gonna grow up without a mum," she said, fighting back tears.
"I just knew I couldn't leave her... I know it sounds strange but I sort of willed myself back."
Fighting the shark felt "like punching a brick wall" but she kept going.
"I must have got a really good one in and so it let me go. It was the hardest thing in the world, but I fought my way out of there."
Stewart was pulled to the shore by other swimmers and rushed to hospital, where she was placed in an induced coma and underwent almost a dozen surgeries.
Despite her harrowing experience, Stewart said she doesn't want to be remembered as "a girl that got mauled on the beach".
"I'm the woman that punched the shark in the face," she said.

Mount Fuji pics, life-changing ramen and a weak yen - why young Brits are going to Japan
- Published
As I open up Instagram, I see another person in their late-20s has been to Japan.
It shouldn't come as a surprise any more.
"I cannot scroll through TikTok or Instagram without seeing videos of people in [convenience store] 7-11 and trying all the different skincare and trying all the snacks and the viral sandwiches and the viral drinks and going to all the viral restaurants," says Alex Baker, who has been to Japan three times.
There's been growing hype about Japan as a travel destination among young British people.
Data from the Japanese National Tourism Organization, external shows that 483,157 British tourists visited Japan in 2025, up 24.8% on 2024 and up 40.8% on 2019, the benchmark year used by travel companies to compare with pre-pandemic trends. Provisional data for 2026 suggests numbers are continuing to grow.
This reflects the boom in total tourism to Japan since the pandemic, with a record number of foreign visitors in 2025.
The Brits in their 20s and 30s I spoke to gave a long list of reasons for wanting to go to Japan - the cityscapes, food, anime, nature, history, gaming, temples. But they largely agreed that social media was the main driving force behind so many young people heading there.
When Maitri Sanghvi scrolled through TikTok, "Japan just kept popping up," she says.
It was a big reason why Maitri, 24, and her boyfriend went for three weeks earlier this year. "Seeing [Japan] on social media restarted my urge of wanting to go," she says.
Search #japantravel on TikTok or Instagram and you'll see countless videos of Mount Fuji, bowls of steaming ramen, itinerary suggestions, small villages in the Japanese Alps, the Fushimi Inari torii gates in Kyoto, the neon lights of Osaka's Dotonbori, and the chaos of Shibuya Crossing.
"Seeing other people's Japan videos definitely influenced my decision to go," says Aden Ibrahim, 29.
Since he went with friends last July, Aden has posted dozens of TikToks of his trip, and he's still uploading them more than a year later. One captioned "Japan made it out the group chat" has 1.1 million views.
Travelling to Japan isn't cheap - return off-peak flights with a layover in China start at about £450 with a budget airline. But the yen is weakening, making it cheaper for tourists when they're actually out there - even as rising prices hit residents. In July, the yen fell to a 40-year low.
"You can literally get a bowl of life-changing ramen for £3/£4 compared to a rubbish one here for like £20," says Faye Jawad, 26, who reviews restaurants on TikTok and visited Japan last year.
"When the yen was weakening, I thought 'actually this is a good time to go, things are going to be cheap'," says Vivek Haria, 26, who has a trip planned for this autumn. His interest in Japanese culture means he's wanted to visit for years - he has been learning the language and even sings in the UK-Japan Choir - but he says the value of the yen made it even more attractive.
The low prices have led to many tourists splashing out on souvenirs when they're out there. Videos of people showing off their Japan "haul" of flavoured KitKats, stationery and clothes have become popular on social media.
When Sam Corbett, 23, was in Japan in May he bought so many souvenirs - including snacks, matcha, clothes and skincare - that he had to buy an extra suitcase, which he stuffed full. Everything was "really affordable," he says.
Almost all the Brits I spoke to had stuck to the same route known as the Golden Route: Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka, often with day trips to nearby destinations like Nara, Hiroshima and Mount Fuji.
It's easy to see why so many tourists pick this route. These cities are easy to travel between and packed with some of Japan's biggest attractions.
But complaints about badly-behaved tourists are sparking debate about overtourism.
Chiyuki Izumii, a tour guide for the Japan Guide Agency, feels tourist behaviour has got worse in recent years. She says that while her customers are respectful, she's seen other tourists jumping queues for buses, blocking space on board with big suitcases, carving their initials on trees in Kyoto's bamboo forest, speaking in loud voices at night and entering restricted areas to take pictures.
Some authorities are cracking down. Fujikawaguchiko, a town near Mount Fuji, cancelled this year's cherry blossom festival after repeated issues with misbehaving tourists, while Tokyo's Shibuya ward, home to the famous Shibuya Crossing, started issuing on-the-spot fines for littering in June.
In July, Japan increased its international tourist tax, external - typically incorporated into flight and boat tickets for people leaving Japan - from 1,000 yen (£4.60) to 3,000 yen, which it says will be spent on things like improving public transport and restoring historic sites.
Some visitors were surprised just how crowded major cities in Japan were.
"I was prepared for it to be busy but I didn't expect it to be as busy as it was," says Millie Dring, a huge anime fan who went in November with a friend to celebrate her 21st birthday.
The DisneySea theme park near Tokyo was so busy that Millie and her friend only went on one ride, which had a three-hour queue, and felt overwhelmed by the crowds.
Sam blames some of the crowds at tourist hotspots on social media hype and he says he regrets going to some places just because they were popular online. One dessert spot he went to in Kyoto after seeing it "all over social media" was very busy "and there wasn't a single local person in the queue," he says.
Sites like the Hakone torii gates and Arashiyama bamboo forest had huge crowds of people trying to get Instagram-perfect photos, he says.
But for some visitors, the hustle and bustle of the tourist destinations are all part of the attraction.
"I think there's a snobbiness around being a tourist over the past couple of years where people want to avoid looking like one," says Laura McGregor, 29, who's spending two weeks in Tokyo and Osaka in November for her honeymoon. Her plans include going to Disney and Universal, attending a sumo event, visiting Fuji and Hiroshima, and hiring go-karts to drive around Tokyo.
"Of course I want to experience an authentic side of Japan but I'm excited to embrace the tourist side too and go along with it," she says.

Norway's late King Harald's casket moved to lie in state
King Harald V lies in state at the royal palace chapel until his September 9 funeral, as Norway enters a national mourning period.
OSLO: The casket of Norway's late King Harald V was transferred on Monday (Aug 31) to the royal palace chapel, where the late regent will lie in state until his funeral on September 9.
The casket was escorted by Harald's children and grandchildren, with televised images showing a procession through the palace halls that included Marius Borg Hoiby, the 29-year-old stepson of the new King Haakon VIII, who is under house arrest pending his appeal of a four-year sentence for two rape convictions.
Earlier on Monday, Norwegian police confirmed that Hoiby would also be allowed to leave his house arrest to attend next week's funeral.
The casket, draped in Norway's royal standard, had been in the palace's Red Salon state room since Friday, after being transported from Oslo University Hospital where he died earlier that day.
The same ritual of moving the king's casket to the chapel was performed when Harald's father, King Olav V, passed away in 1991.
Queen Mette-Marit and Harald's wife, Queen Sonja, also took part in the procession, holding hands and walking behind the casket.
A national period of mourning has been declared until the funeral.
The public will be able to view the casket in the palace chapel from Tuesday at 2:00 pm (1200 GMT) until September 8 at 6:00 pm.
The late king enjoyed massive support despite the slew of scandals that dogged his family in the final stretch of his 35-year reign.
On Tuesday, King Haakon will swear an oath of allegiance in parliament.
King Haakon and Queen Mette-Marit are not expected to be ceremonially crowned as Norway abolished coronations in 1908.
But, like his father and grandfather before him, Haakon could opt for a consecration ceremony at Trondheim Cathedral, where Norwegian monarchs were crowned between 1814 and 1906.
Harald enjoyed broad popularity, seen as the embodiment of an open and tolerant Norway. He was praised for leading a monarchy that was modern and modest.
He faced mounting health problems in his final years, forcing him to scale back his official schedule.
He had been in hospital in Oslo since August 17, suffering from haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells that leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.

Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?
- Published
A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks.
When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; £205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to thousands of prospectors arrived in Cheporor.
And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps.
It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.
Even a small amount of the precious metal can transform the futures of these men and women - from Kenya and neighbouring Uganda - many of whose precarious lives rest on an unreliable farming income.
People do sometimes pan for gold in these parts - but rarely find anything significant.
Lomachar's says his discovery came about purely by chance. While he was searching for a missing goat he encountered a group of women panning along a riverbed.
"I joined them, and that's how [the village] realised there was gold in this area," he says.
Farmer and herder Patrick Lokolia, from neighbouring Napawoi village, joined the gold rush hoping to earn some extra money to support his family.
"I have children in school, and paying school fees has been a big problem for me," he tells the BBC wearing an old Chelsea football top and standing amid the mining activity.
Eighteen-year-old Abigael Chelengat says she had never mined before coming to Cheporor from a nearby district, but arrived hoping to find enough gold to pay her school fees and help keep her younger siblings in school.
Behind her hundreds of people work side by side, hacking into the rocky ground with hoes and shovels.
Others carry the earth to a nearby seasonal river, where mostly women crouch in the murky water, washing and sifting mud and sand hoping to detect a tiny trace of the element.
Some of the more experienced miners are deep in holes excavating the earth and drilling at rocks with the same goal.
Hope is kept alive by stories of those for whom the effort has paid off - like Lomachar.
Samuel Kiarie, the deputy commissioner of West Pokot county, says he thinks the rush began after two notable discoveries.
"Young men found what appeared to be a substantial amount of gold. The following day, women made another significant find in the same area," he tells the BBC.
Kiarie explains that women have been finding small quantities of alluvial gold along the same seasonal riverbed for years, typically earning $8-$23 a week.
But the uncovering of larger quantities at the beginning of August is what caught the attention of many people.
Kiarie reckons as rumours spread, the number and size of the discoveries were exaggerated - drawing in ever larger groups of people with little or no mining experience who hoped to replicate the reported early successes.
Since the initial rush, the number of prospectors has gone down to around 2,500 as some have given up the search.
While there is little doubt that some gold has been found in the area, questions remain about the size of the deposit in the earth and its commercial potential.
"I can confirm that small-scale gold traders told us they received an average of about 100 people every day," the deputy commissioner says - though whether the finds were actually gold is not known.
Individual discoveries reportedly range from amounts worth a few hundred Kenyan shillings to one find valued at approximately 78,000 shillings ($600).
West Pokot county borders Uganda, and communities on both sides have long-standing social and family ties.
Mugisha Godfrey, an artisanal miner from Busia in eastern Uganda, travelled to Cheporor after hearing about the discovery from a friend.
He immediately set out for the village spending about 100,000 Ugandan shillings ($27) to get there.
However, the living conditions in Cheporor are not favourable, he says.
"We sleep under the trees, and when morning comes, we continue working. Sometimes we work both day and night," Godfrey tells the BBC.
So far, he has found nothing. But he is not discouraged.
"We can't return unless we find something. Only when we have found what we need can we go back home," he says.
For others, the gold rush has created opportunities without requiring them to dig.
More than 200 businesses have emerged around the site, according to local officials, selling food, water and other essentials to the village's new population.
Irene Ameja travelled from neighbouring Baringo county to cater to the crowds. She sells bottled water, soft drinks, bread, milk and other foodstuffs.
"I am hoping that when I leave, I will have made enough money to continue with my business and expand it," she says.
But the rapid growth of the settlement has also exposed the area's lack of basic services.
"This is a forest and we are in the middle of the mountains," she says. "We don't have clean water to drink or even to bathe."
For women, she adds, the challenges become greater after dark: "You have to find somewhere safe to stay because most of the people sleeping here are men."
Local officials admit the influx has placed enormous pressure on an area with little infrastructure, no piped water and limited sanitation.
Public health officials have been deployed to monitor conditions and help prevent disease outbreaks.
The authorities say they have also increased security patrols amid concerns over sexual violence and the vulnerability of women and girls at the site.
Officials are also worried that children could be drawn into mining activities as schools prepare to reopen in September.
Measures are being put in place to discourage young people from remaining at the site once the new school term begins.
Those still searching are increasingly turning to deeper excavation.
Several truckloads of material have already been transported to nearby Ortum town for processing, with the authorities awaiting the results.
Until then, the size and commercial viability of any mining remain uncertain.
For Lomachar, the answer is not to stop the mining, but to make it more organised.
He wants the government to help local miners establish safer and more effective ways of finding and extracting the gold.
"We would ask the government to help us with things like metal detectors, which could help us find out whether there are other minerals here, so that our community can develop," he says.
He points to the homes nearby as evidence of the area's poverty.
"If you look around, there are hardly any houses with iron-sheet roofs; most are just thatched houses."

PM Modi highlighted that the ongoing warfare negatively impacts humanity, reinforcing the urgent need to cease hostilities and pursue peaceful solutions to geopolitical conflicts.
“Every day of war sets humanity back,” PM Modi said, emphasising the need to work towards ending the hostilities.
India has maintained a cautious position on Russia’s war in Ukraine since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. New Delhi has repeatedly called for an end to the conflict.
Putin, meanwhile, said relations between Russia and India were becoming stronger, attributing the deepening ties in part to Modi’s personal attention.
The two countries have maintained close political, economic and defence ties despite pressure from Western countries over Russia’s war in Ukraine.
When Putin visited India in December, his first trip to the country in almost four years, the two sides said their relationship “remain resilient to external pressure.”
Putin is also expected to travel to New Delhi next month for the BRICS summit.
India and Russia have emerged as major trading partners since 2022, when New Delhi sharply increased purchases of Russian oil following Western sanctions on Moscow.
Bilateral trade stood at nearly $60 billion in India’s 2026 fiscal year, although that was around 13% below the record level achieved in 2024-25.
The two countries have set an ambitious target of expanding bilateral trade to $100 billion by the end of the decade.
Defence cooperation continues to be a major pillar of India-Russia relations. Despite efforts to diversify defence procurement, Russia remains an important source of military equipment and technology for India.
The Indian military operates hundreds of Russian-made fighter aircraft and several S-400 surface-to-air missile systems. The S-400 systems were used during India’s four-day conflict with Pakistan in May 2025.
The SCO summit also saw PM Modi meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. The meeting marked their first talks since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran.
PM Modi said India remained committed to strengthening its longstanding friendship with Iran across multiple sectors.
“We want to expand and diversify our trade basket in the times to come,” PM Modi said in a post on X.
India is expected to host Pezeshkian again next month at the BRICS summit, with New Delhi holding the grouping’s rotating chairmanship this year.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin also met on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Bishkek.
Founded in 2001 by China, Russia and Central Asian states, the SCO has expanded considerably and now includes India, Pakistan, Iran and Belarus as members.
Afghanistan and Mongolia have observer status, while countries including Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, Egypt and the UAE are dialogue partners.

'This star is for Africa' - Angélique Kidjo on making Hollywood Walk of Fame history
- Published
Five-time Grammy award winner Angélique Kidjo, who made history on Tuesday to become the first African musician to get a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, has told the BBC she wants to dedicate the accolade to the continent of her birth.
"This star is for all the continent of Africa. Because if I was not African, would I be here?" said the 66-year-old musical icon from Benin.
She reiterated her message, made at the ceremony in Los Angeles to mark her four-decade career, about the importance of Africans to the world of music.
"Without the blues brought by the slaves in America, there's no R&B, there's no rock and roll, there's no soul music, there's no jazz. All of it comes from Africa."
- Angélique Kidjo's secret to success: Being hangry 
  - Published17 November 2023
Kidjo told BBC Focus on Africa TV that Africans themselves needed to appreciate what they had given the world, and nurture talent at home.
"Let's celebrate our artists in their own right on the continent. Let's give them visibility, strength, because music creates economy," she said.
Most African artists - besides mega stars who have a global fanbase - struggle to make a living as they rarely get paid the royalties they are owed.
"We need to recognise our artists and create a system for them to make money on their continent and to participate also in creating jobs."
As her illustrious career was immortalised in Los Angeles, Kidjo became emotional - wiping away tears.
"At that moment, I'm like, dad, mum, I wish you were here with me to see [this]" the songstress explained to the BBC.
"I couldn't take the emotion. They were not here to taste the fruit of what they've created. How they have nurtured my curiosity, my love for music."
Kidjo - who has taken African sounds to global audiences, blending influences from home with funk, jazz and pop - grew up in Benin and then went to Paris aged 23, citing oppression from the country's then-communist government.
At her Walk of Fame ceremony, she was joined by other family, friends and stars such as Hollywood actors Willem Dafoe and Djimon Hounsou, who is also from Benin, and Nigerian musician Adekunle Gold.
The gathering was filled with singing and dancing in celebration of her career, which has included collaborations with big names such as Burna Boy, John Legend, Bono and Alicia Keys.
Her latest album, HOPE!!, was released earlier this year with tracks produced by Pharrell Williams, and collaborations with Ayra Starr, Quavo, Nile Rogers and Diane Warren.
Kidjo has released 18 albums in total and has been nominated for 17 Grammy awards, which she has won five times.
She also won the 2023 Polar Music Prize, and two years earlier was named as one of Time's 100 Most Influential People.
"She is without a doubt the hardest working woman in showbusiness," Dafoe said at the ceremony.
"The first time I saw Angélique perform live, I thought her music, her dancing, her commitment were incredible."
The Spider-Man star likened her energy to that of soul singer James Brown, who he called the "hardest working man in showbusiness".
"She's not only an incredible performer... songwriter and musician, but also an incredibly kind and giving person and a real deal activist."
Kidjo is a Unicef and Oxfam goodwill ambassador, and is the co-founder of the Batonga Foundation, which helps vulnerable young girls and women in Benin.
At the Los Angeles gathering she was also praised by Harvey Mason Jr, the CEO of Recording Academy - the organisation that also oversees the Grammy awards.
"She's connected cultures, she's crossed borders, she's reminded audiences everywhere that while we may come from different backgrounds, her music unites in a way that few other things can," he said.
During her interview with the BBC, the musician's phone kept ringing with those wanting to congratulate her.
"Yesterday I received the call of the president of Benin," she said.
"Today I received the call of Chris Blackwell, the founder of Island Records, the producer of Bob Marley, the maker of U2 and so on and so forth."
Kidjo explained how fundamental Blackwell, who signed her in the 1990s, had been to her success - launching her breakthrough album Logozo.
"I said to him at that moment… 'Can I do the music I want to do and keep my cultural identity without anyone imposing any other music on my shoulder?' He said… 'It's no brainer.'"
Kidjo joins Charlize Theron, a white South African actress, in representing Africa on the Walk of Fame, which comprises more than 2,800 stars.
She said she was amazed to hear a year ago that she had been nominated for a Hollywood star, telling Focus on Africa she did not believe the news given to her by her husband until she said she had seen it on the BBC.
And when asked about the significance of becoming the first African musician with a star, she replied: "Changes that last take time."

లోక్సభలో ప్రతిపక్ష నేత రాహుల్ గాంధీకి సంబంధించిన ఒక వీడియో సోషల్ మీడియాలో వైరల్ అవుతోంది. ఈ వీడియోలో ఆయన మహిళలు, అత్యాచారాలకు సంబంధించి వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలు చేసినట్లు ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారు. వైరల్ వీడియోలో రాహుల్ గాంధీ, “80 శాతం అత్యాచారాలకు మహిళలే కారణం. భారతదేశంలో అత్యాచారాలు జరుగుతాయి, కానీ ‘భారత్’లో అత్యాచారాలు జరగవు.” అని చెప్పినట్లు వినిపిస్తోంది. అయితే, ఈ వీడియో నిజంగా రాహుల్ గాంధీ చేసిన వ్యాఖ్యలను చూపిస్తుందా? ఈ వైరల్ వీడియో వెనుక ఉన్న నిజమేంటో ఈ కథనంలో తెలుసుకుందాం.
క్లెయిమ్: లోక్సభలో ప్రతిపక్ష నేత రాహుల్ గాంధీ “80 శాతం అత్యాచారాలకు మహిళలే కారణం. భారతదేశంలో అత్యాచారాలు జరుగుతాయి, కానీ ‘భారత్’లో అత్యాచారాలు జరగవు” అని అంటున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియోను ఎడిట్ చేశారు. అసలు వీడియోలో రాహుల్ గాంధీ స్వయంగా ఈ వ్యాఖ్యలు చేయలేదు. ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ చీఫ్ మోహన్ భగవత్, మాజీ హర్యానా ముఖ్యమంత్రి మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ గతంలో చేసిన వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలను ప్రస్తావిస్తూ, వారి అభిప్రాయాలను రాహుల్ గాంధీ విమర్శించారు. అయితే, వైరల్ వీడియోలో ఆయన ఎవరి వ్యాఖ్యలను ప్రస్తావిస్తున్నారో చెప్పిన భాగాన్ని తొలగించి, ఆ వ్యాఖ్యలు రాహుల్ గాంధీ స్వయంగా చేసినట్లుగా చూపించారు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేస్తున్న వాదన తప్పు.
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీలక ఫ్రేమ్లను ఉపయోగించి రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, కాంగ్రెస్ పార్టీ అధికారిక యూట్యూబ్ ఛానల్లో 22 ఆగస్టు 2026న అప్లోడ్ చేసిన అసలు వీడియో మాకు లభించింది. అదే రోజు పుణెలో జరిగిన కాంగ్రెస్ “ఛాత్రోన్ కీ గూంజ్” కార్యక్రమానికి సంబంధించిన వీడియో ఇది. అసలు వీడియోలోని 1:00:12 టైమ్స్టాంప్ వద్ద వైరల్ క్లిప్లోని దృశ్యాలు కనిపిస్తాయి. అయితే, అసలు వీడియోలో రాహుల్ గాంధీ ఆ వ్యాఖ్యలను స్వయంగా చేయడం లేదు. ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ చీఫ్ మోహన్ భగవత్, మాజీ హర్యానా ముఖ్యమంత్రి మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ గతంలో చేసిన వ్యాఖ్యలను ఆయన ప్రస్తావించాడు. అత్యాచారాలు “ఇండియా”లో జరుగుతాయి కానీ “భారత్”లో జరగవని మోహన్ భగవత్ చెప్పారని, 80 శాతం అత్యాచారాలకు మహిళలే కారణమని మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ వ్యాఖ్యానించారని రాహుల్ గాంధీ పేర్కొన్నారు. అనంతరం, ఇలాంటి వ్యాఖ్యలు తాము వ్యతిరేకిస్తున్నానని ఆయన తెలిపారు.
మోహన్ భగవత్, మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ పేర్లను ప్రస్తావించిన భాగాన్ని వీడియో నుంచి తొలగించారు. ఆ వ్యాఖ్యలను రాహుల్ గాంధీ స్వయంగా చేసినట్లుగా కనిపించేలా వైరల్ వీడియోను రూపొందించారు. దీంతో వైరల్ వీడియోను ఎడిట్ చేసినట్లు స్పష్టమవుతోంది.
తదుపరి, గూగుల్లో కీవర్డ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) ఉన్న వీడియోలు లభించాయి. వీటి ప్రకారం, 4 జనవరి 2013న ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ చీఫ్ మోహన్ భగవత్ అసోంలోని సిల్చర్లో పర్యటించిన సమయంలో అత్యాచార ఘటనలపై వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలు చేశారు. “ఇండియా”లో ఇలాంటి నేరాలు ఎక్కువగా జరుగుతాయని, “భారత్”లో తక్కువగా జరుగుతాయని ఆయన చెప్పినట్లు వార్తలు వచ్చాయి. ఈ వ్యాఖ్యలు అప్పట్లో వివాదానికి దారితీశాయి. తర్వాత అప్పటి ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ అధికార ప్రతినిధి రామ్ మాధవ్ వివరణ ఇచ్చారు. మహిళలను గౌరవించే భారతీయ సంప్రదాయాల గురించి మోహన్ భగవత్ మాట్లాడారని, ఈ విలువలకు దూరమైనవారు నేరాలకు పాల్పడే అవకాశం ఉందని ఆయన చెప్పినట్లు రామ్ మాధవ్ వివరించారు.
అదేవిధంగా, 2018 నవంబర్లో అప్పటి హర్యానా ముఖ్యమంత్రి మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ అత్యాచారం, వేధింపుల ఘటనలపై వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలు చేశారు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ). వార్తా కథనాల్లో ఈ వ్యాఖ్యలకు సంబంధించిన వివరాలు ఉన్నాయి. అత్యాచారం, వేధింపుల ఘటనల్లో 80–90 శాతం వరకు ఒకరికొకరు తెలిసిన వ్యక్తులే ఉంటారని ఖట్టర్ అన్నారు. అలాగే, కొన్నిసార్లు చాలా కాలంగా సంబంధంలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తుల మధ్య వివాదాలు తలెత్తిన తర్వాత ఇలాంటి ఘటనలు జరుగుతున్నాయని ఆయన సూచించారు.
చివరిగా, అత్యాచారం, మహిళలపై రాహుల్ గాంధీ వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలు చేసినట్లు చూపిస్తున్న ఈ వైరల్ వీడియో ఎడిట్ చేసినది.

Topline
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito holds between $175,000 and $545,000 in fossil fuel-related investments, according to his 2025 financial disclosure, reporting the holdings Monday as the justice comes under pressure to recuse from an upcoming case being brought by oil and gas giant Exxon and Suncor Energy.
Key Facts
Alito’s 2025 financial disclosure was released on Monday, which revealed the justice’s broader stock portfolio last year, including investments in the oil, gas and energy sector.
Alito held investments last year in ConocoPhillips, Woodside Energy Group and AES Corp that were each valued at up to $15,000, his disclosures show, and investments in Phillips 66, OGE Energy Corp, Black Hills Corp, BHP Group and Fortis Inc that were each valued between $15,001 and $50,000.
He and his wife also own a mineral interest in land in Grady County, Oklahoma, valued between $100,001 and $250,000, as the Alitos reportedly receive a percentage of oil and gas sales made off of fossil fuels that are extracted on their land.
The disclosure comes as watchdog and left-leaning groups have urged the justice to recuse himself from the upcoming case Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, in which Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil are asking the court to decide whether claims can be brought in state court that attempt to hold oil and gas companies liable for the effects of climate change.
Alito has refused to recuse himself in the case because he doesn’t directly hold investments in Exxon or Suncor—he sold his Exxon shares a decade ago—with a spokesperson for the court telling NBC News that Alito “does not have a financial interest in any party” involved in the case and was advised by legal counsel that “his recusal is not required.”
What to Watch for
The court will hear oral arguments in the Suncor Energy case on Oct. 5. The dispute will not decide whether Suncor Energy and Exxon are liable for the impacts of climate change, but rather whether those claims can be brought in state court to begin with. It comes after the Colorado Supreme Court ruled that the city of Boulder could bring claims against the companies in state court, and that those legal claims were not overruled by federal law.
Forbes Valuation
Forbes values Alito’s net worth at approximately $10 million, making him the second-richest justice on the court, behind Chief Justice John Roberts. (The chief justice is also the only other justice on the court who holds stocks in individual companies.)
Big Number
Up to $2.9 million. That’s how much Alito made from his interests in the fossil fuel industry between 2005 and 2024, according to an analysis of his financial disclosures by judicial watchdog group Court Accountability.
Surprising Fact
Alito’s decision not to recuse in the Suncor case this term comes after the justice previously recused himself when the court considered an appeal in the case in 2023. A spokesperson for the court told NBC News the justice “inadvertently recused” himself in 2023 because the case “was considered at the same time as other cases where the justice did have a financial interest in the parties.” Critics argued to NBC the Suncor case was intertwined with those similar lawsuits, which are also trying to hold other companies liable for climate change, including ones Alito is invested in. The Suncor lawsuit should still be viewed in connection with those other cases, they argue, rather than only concerning Suncor and Exxon. “The oil company petitioners in these cases have been explicit in court filings that they view the cases as linked; there is no reason for Justice Alito to view them otherwise,” Hannah Story Brown, deputy research director at the left-leaning watchdog group Revolving Door Project, told NBC in May.
Tangent
Beyond his significant investment portfolio, Alito’s financial disclosure, which was signed on Aug. 11, also reported the justice was reimbursed for traveling to speaking engagements in Arizona, Italy and the United Kingdom in 2025, by the organizations hosting the events he spoke at. He did not report receiving any gifts. Alito also reported $33,000 in income for his upcoming book “So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country,” which will be published in October. SCOTUSblog noted that $33,000 falls far below what some of his colleagues have earned for their books, with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson reporting an advance of more than $1 million for her memoir and Justice Amy Coney Barrett reporting nearly $850,000 for her 2025 book “Listening to the Law: Reflections on the Court and Constitution.”
Key Background
The controversy over Alito’s participation in the Suncor Energy case comes as scrutiny has intensified in recent years on the Supreme Court’s justices and perceived ethical issues. Alito and Justice Clarence Thomas have faced the most criticism, with Thomas coming under fire for not disclosing numerous trips he received from friend and GOP megadonor Harlan Crow, while Alito was slammed for him and his wife flying flags outside their home associated with the “Stop the Steal” movement, among other controversies. The justices have denied any wrongdoing or ethical conflicts. Unlike lower federal judges, Supreme Court justices are not forced to follow a code of ethics, and while there are rules in place governing issues like avoiding conflicts of interest, there are no set punishments if those rules are broken. The Supreme Court has declined to take up a binding code of ethics amid the outcry over its alleged ethical issues, and Alito has previously opposed efforts by Democratic lawmakers to impose an ethics code on the court.

New Zealand's government introduced legislation on Monday to ban under 16s from using social media, joining a number of countries seeking to keep youngsters off sites such as Instagram and TikTok.
Australia implemented world-first legislation banning children from social media in December, with the UK, France and others following suit.
Under New Zealand's proposed law, firms like Meta could be fined up to 10 percent of their global revenue if they fail to comply.
"We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said.
"One in three children aged between 13 and 17 are now spending at least five hours on social media a day," he said.
"Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with, and it's affecting their family life, mental health, sleep and education."
Luxon specifically called out platforms Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Facebook, saying they would be required to take "reasonable steps to check users are over the age of 16".
They would have to use "existing account information, facial age estimation, digital ID services and formal ID" to verify age.
Platforms would also be required to assess the risks they pose as well as report on how those dangers are being reduced, with penalties slapped on companies that fail to comply.
Education Minister Erica Stanford said the Bill "places legal obligations on platforms".
"No penalties are proposed for children, their parents or caregivers," Stanford said.
It's unclear whether the bill will pass, as both National Party's coalition partners, the libertarian ACT party and populist NZ First, have said they oppose it.
In a statement, the populist NZ First said they could not support the law given the "colossal failure" of the legislation in Australia, while ACT said they believed the law "won't work" and that teenagers would easily get around the ban.
The main opposition party Labour has submitted a list of dozens of questions it wanted answered before deciding whether it would offer support, including how age verification will work and which platforms will be affected.
"We take this legislation very seriously," spokesman Reuben Davidson said.
"The safety of young people in Aotearoa New Zealand is at stake and the risks they face in increasingly complex online environments are significant," he added, using the Maori-language name for the country.
Australia banned under 16s last year from the likes of Facebook, Instagram and TikTok, in a crackdown designed to protect children from online bullying and "predatory algorithms".
A team of Australia-based researchers in a peer-reviewed study published in June found little evidence to suggest teenagers have turned away from social media as a consequence, however.

About 1,600 federal employees who work at the General Services Administration have been forced to relocate from their office on F Street in Washington, DC, to the Theodore Roosevelt Federal Building, roughly two blocks away. Workers say the new building, which also houses staff from the Office of Personnel Management has mice, a caved-in bathroom ceiling, and drinking water that needs to be run for five to 10 seconds before it is clear.
The federal workforce has been rocked by changes made by Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) since January 2025. DOGE effectively fired tens of thousands of workers and forced those who remained to commit to in-person schedules and, in some cases, zero-based budgeting. GSA, the agency in charge of the federal government’s IT services and real estate assets, was hit early by DOGE, and in addition to major workforce cuts also rolled out plans to sell hundreds of federal office buildings. A year after the cuts, GSA announced it planned to hire about 400 workers.
“We’ve all been through a lot, but this really made me finally understand that they don’t care about us,” says one GSA employee who asked to remain anonymous, as they aren’t authorized to speak to the press. “We’re left wondering what else is going to collapse or break—do we need to look at the ceiling before going to the bathroom? Can we actually trust the water is safe to drink?”
Photos obtained by WIRED show a toilet in a men’s room on the third floor covered in debris from the ceiling, a gaping hole in said ceiling, and a dead mouse caught in a trap. Workers said the mouse wasn’t “entirely shocking” since many federal buildings allegedly have vermin, but the ceiling pushed them over the edge. An additional sign in the office recommends workers filling up water bottles to “run the water without your bottle for 5-10 seconds and wait for the water to run clear.”
GSA and OPM did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
GSA leadership, including administrator Ed Forst, has told employees they should expect to work in the OPM building—which is slated for “accelerated disposition,” or a quick building sale—until December 2028. Their prior building, located at 1800 F Street, is undergoing extensive renovations. The initiative is part of a “government-wide effort to reduce underutilized space and fortify the federal real estate footprint,” according to a GSA press release.
While Musk himself has stepped back from his public role in the Trump administration, DOGE affiliates have continued working in government, embracing austerity measures and AI initiatives. Others have gone back to the private sector, working in AI, data centers, and manufacturing.

Prediction markets have priced the Trump-Xi summit. Do the bets have any value?
Trump has announced a September 24 meeting, but Beijing has not. As prediction market bets multiply, they may begin to shape diplomacy
US President Donald Trump has already announced the date: September 24.
That is when, Trump says, Chinese President Xi Jinping will come to the White House for a visit following the “America first” leader’s own three-day trip to Beijing in May.
But there is a diplomatic wrinkle.
The Trump administration has publicly put the date on the calendar. Beijing has not formally announced Xi’s Washington visit.
Traders are already pricing the odds of the visit. As of August 27, Polymarket contracts on whether Trump would meet Xi in September and whether Xi would visit the US by September 30 were both priced at about 95 per cent.
Polymarket put the probability of Xi visiting the US by the end of September at 94 per cent. At Kalshi, another prediction market, the chance of a visit before October stood at 88 per cent.

Norwegians in emotional memorials remembering the late King Harald V
Norwegians have gathered for memorial services honoring the late King Harald V, who died at 89
OSLO, Norway -- Norwegians across the country lined up early Sunday in front of cathedrals and churches for memorial services held for the late King Harald V, who died at 89.
“This Sunday is different. His Majesty King Harald is dead. A family has lost their spouse, father, grandfather, father-in-law,” said Dean Pål Kristian Balstad as he opened the funeral service in Oslo Cathedral, Norway's public broadcaster NRK reported.
The royal family attended the service at Asker Church, southwest of Oslo.
Since Harald's death Friday morning, tens of thousands of Norwegians have expressed their grief by laying flowers, writing cards and lighting candles in front of the royal palace in Oslo, where the coffin arrived late Friday from the hospital.
A date for the funeral has not been set, but the country is in a state of mourning and some people decided to postpone celebrations such as weddings and baptisms until after the mourning period has passed, NRK reported.
Harald's son, who became the new King Haakon VIII, eulogized Harald on Saturday night. He expressed his pain over the beloved father's death and promised to lead the country with the same dedication.
“I’m going to miss him. I’ll miss his laughter. His good-natured way of dealing with people and situations,” Haakon said in his first speech as new king that was broadcast live on public Television.
Trying to hold back his tears, he vowed to give everything for the country in the future as its new king.
“That means — in the ultimate sense — being willing to risk everything, even one’s life, for Norway’s freedom and independence,” Haakon said.
The new king adopted the motto “All for Norway,” which dates back to his great-grandfather. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne.
His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction.
Norway’s monarchy has old roots, tracing its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. Today, the role is largely symbolic as power lies with an elected parliament, but the country’s royal family retains celebrity and a role in promoting the wealthy nation around the world.

Zambian opposition leader charged with treason
- Published
Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile has been charged with treason, his lawyer has said amid heightened political tensions in the country.
Mundubile was arrested on Thursday, after a deadly raid by the authorities led the opposition politician to go into hiding.
He had disputed the results of the country's recent presidential election, which saw incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema securing a second term.
The authorities then accused Mundubile's NRPUP party of planning an armed insurgency, which it denied.
On Saturday night, Mundubile's lawyer Milner Katolo announced that his client had been charged with treason. The opposition leader looks forward to answering the accusation in court, Katolo told the Zambian Eye, external.
The lawyer said 17 others, including Mundubile's running mate Makebi Zulu, had also been charged with treason.
Mundubile gained 38% of the vote in the 13 August election, while Hichilema secured 60%, official results show.
The day after the poll, security forces raided a property in the capital, Lusaka, linked to Mundubile, killing a former cabinet minister and arresting a number of other politicians.
Following the raid, Mundubile and Zulu took refuge at a United Nations building in the city. The pair were detained after the president put pressure on the UN to hand them over.
The opposition was unable to mount a legal challenge to the election outcome as the courts were sealed off by the authorities on Monday, the final day that a case could be filed.
Hichilema is due to be sworn in for a second term on 1 September.
Regional and international observers described the election day as largely peaceful, but Zambia's Human Rights Commission has called for accountability over people whose whereabouts remain unknown following arrests and security operations around the elections.

Leader of the Opposition in the Keralam Assembly Pinarayi Vijayan on Monday (Augut 31, 2026) accused former leader of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) [CPI(M)] and Independent MLA T.K. Govindan of betraying the CPI(M) and contributing to its defeat in the Taliparamba Assembly constituency in the recent Assembly elections.
Mr. Vijayan was addressing a rally organised by the CPI(M) at Taliparamba to explain the party’s stand following its defeat in the constituency.
Mr. T.K. Govindan had left the party following differences over the decision to field CPI(M) State secretary M.V. Govindan’s wife and CPI(M) leader P.K. Shyamala as the party candidate in Taliparamba.
He later contested as an Independent candidate with the support of the United Democratic Front (UDF) and emerged victorious in the constituency, considered a CPI(M) stronghold.
Mr. Vijayan said the Left Democratic Front (LDF)’s vote share had declined by more than 11% compared to the previous election, leading to its defeat. “The reason for our defeat is that we lost more than 11% votes compared to the ones we received in 2021. This is what led to the defeat,” he said.
Mr. Vijayan said the candidacy of Mr. T.K. Govindan, whom he accused of taking a stand that amounted to betraying the party, had resulted in some votes shifting away from the LDF.
“The opponent who contested here was T.K. Govindan, who became a candidate by taking a stand of betraying the party. When T.K. Govindan came as a candidate, it can be seen that following that candidacy, a few votes were lost from the LDF,” he said.
He said it was unfortunate that some people who had supported the CPI(M) at various stages had taken a different stand in the election. “The fact that a lot of people who stood with the CPI(M) at all stages thought differently at this stage was something that should not have happened. Only if a mistake is recognised as a mistake can it be corrected. Those who took such a stance should conduct proper introspection regarding that matter,” Mr. Vijayan said.
Govindan’s reaction
Addressing a meeting, Mr. T.K. Govindan alleged that the CPI(M) leadership was destroying the party in pursuit of its own interests. “The leadership is destroying this party for your own selfish interests. To you, the party is not what matters most; your other spin-off deals are what matter to you. Those need to be protected. That is why you are destroying the party,” he said.
Mr. T.K. Govindan questioned whether the party leadership was impartially examining the reasons for the CPI(M)’s decline. “However, are you impartially examining why the party has fallen into such a state? If you attack V. Kunhikrishnan (Payyannur MLA) and me, will this party be saved?” he asked.
Referring to the killing of Revolutionary Marxist Party leader T.P. Chandrasekharan, who was allegedly hacked to death by CPI(M) activists in 2012, Mr. T.K. Govindan questioned whether his elimination had strengthened the party. Chandrasekharan was a CPI(M) leader who formed the RMP after leaving the party.

Reports that the US is preparing to claim a big stake in Venezuela’s massive energy reserves have sparked an outcry, with critics describing the move as “predatory” and a “rapacious” land grab.
Several media outlets this week reported that the Trump administration – which abducted Venezuela’s authoritarian president, Nicolás Maduro, in January and has steered the South American country ever since – hopes to secure long-term access to its oil and gasfields.
Venezuela has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves with an estimated 303bn barrels, compared with Saudi Arabia’s 268bn and Iran’s 208bn.
On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal said Trump officials were in “advanced talks” with Venezuelan officials to take “a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields” containing 90bn barrels, nearly a third of Venezuela’s energy reserves.
“This is real and being discussed at the highest levels of the US and Venezuelan governments,” a source told Reuters, which said the fields being negotiated were in the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo regions.
Axios claimed the deal would be “a legacy-defining moment for President Trump”, with one unnamed official telling the US outlet: “Calling this deal huge would be an understatement … It is massive.”
Bloomberg, citing sources familiar with the negotiations, said one deal under discussion was a 100-year lease on several oilfields.
The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro.
“It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticising the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States,” they added.
Since January’s special forces raid on Caracas, Venezuela has been led by an interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president and minister of petroleum. Other key members of Maduro’s regime have also retained positions of power, including the interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, who has been collaborating with Trump officials – despite having a $25m (£18m) US bounty on his head for alleged drug trafficking. Meanwhile, the exiled opposition leader, María Corina Machado, whose movement is believed to have won the 2024 presidential elections, has been sidelined.
Ricardo Hausmann, an exiled former minister and opposition supporter, wrote on X: “An illegitimate interim government with an illegitimate hydrocarbons law has no legitimacy to strike this unconstitutional deal. It will be a fiasco for all involved.”
The economist Francisco Rodríguez urged Venezuela’s national assembly to reject what he called a “predatory deal”. “Handing over Venezuela’s oil wealth to the US contravenes the constitution and is not in the interest of the Venezuelan people – much more when it is done at gunpoint,” Rodríguez said.
Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent journalist and government critic, sarcastically called the “surrender” of Venezuela’s natural riches “the deal of the century”.
Gregory Brew, an energy historian and Eurasia Group analyst, anticipated “quite a lot of suspicion and rejection of any deal that would hand the United States government effective control over Venezuelan resources”.
Brew said the reported deal reminded him of how BP, then the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, controlled the oil resources of Iraq and Iran at the start of the last century.
“Anglo-Persian was given a concession by the shah of Iran in 1901 … in exchange for what was essentially a bribe to the Persian government, and it gave the company sweeping rights. The company was essentially in total control of any oil it found and would be able to retain virtually all the profits of any other oil it found and exploited and exported,” Brew said.
“From Trump’s point of view, the control over oil is something of an end in and of itself,. But if you do try to rationalise it, I think US dominance over Venezuelan oil reserves allows the US to regard Venezuelan reserves as its own reserves: a source of oil from which the United States can draw and that nobody else has access to. I think that’s how the administration is conceiving of this – excluding China, excluding Russia, but I think also excluding other potential customers for Venezuelan oil,” he said. “It sounds colonial, because it is.”
Venezuela’s post-Maduro conversion into what many call a US protectorate is the most dramatic play in Trump’s push to reassert Washington’s influence over Latin America as part of the so-called “Donroe Doctrine”.
That policy is a 21st-century adaptation of the 19th-century Monroe doctrine by which President James Monroe sought to keep European powers out of the Americas. Trump’s version is about countering China’s growing footprint in the region and imposing US will through economic and military pressure.
Maduro’s downfall has brought some change to Venezuela, with hundreds of political prisoners freed under Rodríguez and talks about reforming the regime-controlled supreme court taking place.
But no date has been set for a fresh presidential election and Machado has been unable to return from exile. “Delcy’s been doing a fantastic job,” Trump told reporters last month, claiming Venezuela was “not really ready” for a vote.

Shivraj reviews watershed scheme, calls for faster implementation to achieve drought-free India
New Delhi, Rural Development Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan on Monday reviewed the progress of the watershed development component of the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana and called on states to expedite projects and ensure measurable outcomes on the ground.
Chouhan said watershed development is an important tool in achieving the goal of a "drought-free India" for a developed India, according to a statement issued by the Rural Development Ministry.
"Watershed development is not merely a programme to create water structures; its real objective is to bring water to farms, increase land productivity and strengthen farmers' incomes and livelihoods," he said.
Under WDC-PMKSY 2.0, 1,220 projects covering 52.93 lakh hectares have so far been sanctioned at a total cost of ₹12,404 crore, including a central share of ₹8,134 crore. Of the central share, ₹6,955.75 crore, or 85 per cent, has been released, the ministry said.
Chouhan said the impact of watershed interventions was visible in increased cropping intensity, with nearly 1.40 lakh hectares of land that previously supported barely one crop now producing two crops and, in several places, three crops.
The expansion of horticulture, vegetable cultivation and high-value crops has also contributed to improved livelihoods, he said.
The programme has resulted in the construction and revival of 1.24 lakh water-harvesting structures, including check dams, nala bunds, percolation tanks, village and farm ponds, field bunding, trenches and reservoirs, according to the ministry.
These structures have helped conserve rainwater locally, recharge groundwater and improve water availability for agriculture, it said.
The interventions have provided protective irrigation to an additional 3.08 lakh hectares, helping farmers in rain-fed areas protect crops during periods of low rainfall or drought, the ministry said.
As many as 28.50 lakh farmers have benefited from the programme so far, while afforestation, horticulture and plantation activities have been undertaken across 1.45 lakh hectares. The programme has also generated 2.85 crore person-days of employment, it said.
Chouhan urged states and implementing agencies to adopt transparent, technology-enabled, performance-based and people-centric approaches and complete projects within the stipulated timelines.
He said watershed projects should not be assessed merely on the basis of expenditure, but on actual improvements in land development, water availability, irrigation, cropping intensity, land productivity and farmers' livelihoods.
Chouhan also said the government had sought to turn watershed development into a people's movement through the 'Watershed Yatra' and 'Watershed Mahotsav'.
He called for taking watershed development forward not merely as a scheme but as a national campaign for water and land security, agricultural security and rural prosperity.

A purported statement by Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke is circulating on social media. In the viral post, Dipke is quoted as saying, “We are demanding responsibility, not resignation from the chief minister (of Jharkhand), so that problems don’t arise regarding papers in the future.”
The apparent statement was shared by a verified Instagram handle named ‘indians’ on August 14. The post received has over 74,600 reactions till date. The page has around 9 million followers. (Archive)
The caption of the post reads:
“… Dipke said he does not want Soren to resign, but wants accountability to ensure such incidents do not happen again. His stand has sparked questions among citizens over why accountability is being sought instead of resignation in this case, while Dharmendra Pradhan faced demands to resign.”
After Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned following CJP’s Delhi protests, a similar protest erupted in Ranchi over alleged paper leaks and irregularities in Jharkhand’s government recruitment exams. Protesters, including students and activists, demanded chief minister Hemant Soren’s resignation.
It was against this backdrop that the quote attributed to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke went viral. The viral posts reinforce the key BJP charge that CJP was comparatively restrained when allegations of exam irregularities emerged in Opposition-ruled states, particularly Jharkhand. BJP leaders have used this argument to accuse the group of selective outrage. In comments to the above Instagram post, many users replied saying Dipke’s stance showed his ‘hypocrisy’ or ‘double standard’.
The same quotation was also shared by Facebook pages named The Youth – India and Saale Dost Ko Thanks Bolta hai. The follower counts of the two pages are 141,000 and 4.9 million, respectively.
Fact Check
To find more on the purported statement by Dipke, we first went through his X timeline, since the CJP founder regularly posts about his media interactions and public statements on his X account. We could not find any post corroborating the viral claim.
We, however, found a post from August 2 where Dipke is speaking to the protesting students in Jharkhand on a video call. “The CJP stands with all the students in Jharkhand and support their demands,” he wrote. He makes the same point in the video as well.
Spoke to the students who are protesting in Jharkhand over irregularities in JPSC and JSSC recruitment exams.
The CJP stands with all the students in Jharkhand and support their demands. pic.twitter.com/lLSRhFVpv1
— Abhijeet Dipke (@abhijeet_dipke) August 2, 2026
Next, we performed a keyword search on Google, looking for news reports on the said statement. We used the keyword combination: “Abhijeet Dipke Jharkhand Hemant Soren resignation”.
We could not find a single report which mentioned that Dipke had said they were only seeking accountability and responsibility, and not the Jharkhand chief minister’s resignation. Instead, we found several reports on the CJP and its founder supporting the Jharkhand students’ stir. For instance, this report in The Hindu states that Abhijeet Dipke “was in touch with the protesters and supported their demands, and they will go to Ranchi to express solidarity.” Similar reports were carried by outlets like The Print and The Times of India.
None of the articles mentioned anything similar to what the purported quote claims.
We also found an ANI post containing Dipke’s detailed response to the Jharkhand situation. He says, “… We offer our full support. Our delegation has visited the area, and our people are distributing food there. We stand firmly with them and support all their demands… I, too, intend to go… Although, I am currently dealing with some health issues…”
#WATCH | Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar, Maharashtra | On students’ protest in Jharkhand, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Founder Abhijeet Dipke says, “We offer our full support. Our delegation has visited the area, and our people are distributing food there. We stand firmly with them… pic.twitter.com/R3XbAv5jaT
— ANI (@ANI) August 7, 2026
In another interview with PTI, Dipke said CJP would support demands for educational reforms, irrespective of which state was in question and which party was in power.
Alt News then reached out to Abhijeet Dipke and asked him whether he had made the statement shown in the viral posts. Dipke replied: “Never said this. These people (the social media pages) are running anything they want.”
To sum up, the viral post quoting Abhijeet Dipke as saying that they were seeking accountability but not Jharkhand CM Hemant Soren’s resignation is baseless. There is no credible evidence of the CJP founder having made such a statement. Dipke himself refuted the claim.

Clean tech startup YOGa Clean Air has raised ₹20 Cr (around $2.1 Mn) in its Series A round, in a mix of primary and secondary deals, led by Info Edge Ventures. The round, which marked the startup’s first external funding, also saw participation from Zomato founder Deepinder Goyal and Three Words Capital. While ₹10 Cr was raised via primary capital, the remaining ₹10 Cr came from secondary transactions. The startup plans to deploy the fresh capital to deepen its presence in existing markets and expand its footprint to new Tier I and tier II cities. YOGa Clean Air also said that a chunk of the capital will also be utilised to deploy its clean air solutions on public transport and at other outdoor spaces. Speaking with Inc42, YOGa founder and CEO Sachin Panwar said that the startup is eyeing ₹100 Cr in revenue this year. Founded in 2010 by Panwar and formally established as YOGAN Solutions Pvt Ltd in 2019 with cofounders Deepak Raina and Gaurav Nagar, YOGa builds indoor air-quality systems. The startup claims that its systems clean the air across an entire room or building, instead of treating only a limited area like a conventional air purifier. Its Clean Air Bubble system filters outdoor air before bringing it indoors and uses positive air pressure to keep polluted air from entering through doors, gaps and other openings. The system also monitors and manages carbon dioxide (CO2) levels to keep indoor air fresh. The system can be installed through a small opening in a wall or glass and is designed to maintain positive air pressure across an entire indoor space. YOGa claims that its system can deliver equivalent air quality across a house in about 55 minutes, while using roughly 70 watts of electricity during continuous operation. According to Panwar, YOGa follows a service-led model instead of a one-time hardware sale. The startup added that its systems are already operational across 11 Indian cities and serve around 5,000 families, schools, offices, hospitals and gyms. It also claims to have undertaken projects for government institutions, including deploying its systems in parts of the Delhi High Court. The startup also claims to have signed projects with real estate players to deploy its solutions. “Earlier, we were mostly doing retail. Now B2B is actually shifting. Orders are coming from large real estate projects and institutions,” Panwar said. YOGa Clean Air competes with the likes of domestic startups such as Airth, Clairco, Ubreathe and Atovio, which offer indoor air-purification solutions ranging from AC retrofitting to plant-based technology. The fundraise comes as persistent pollution is pushing the demand for indoor air-quality solutions beyond conventional air purifiers. As per reports, India’s air purifier market is projected to become a $1.2 Bn opportunity by 2030.
