On 26 August 2026, massive flash floods struck parts of Nepal and Tibet, causing widespread destruction as rivers including the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli overflowed and swept away homes, roads, bridges, and other infrastructure. Experts said the disaster was likely triggered by the collapse of a glacier and a massive ice-and-rock avalanche in the Himalayas, which sent huge amounts of debris and water into the river systems. As of 28 August 2026, the death toll in Nepal had risen to 469, according to Nepal Police, while nearly 1,000 people remained missing as search and rescue operations continued (here, here, and here).
Amid the disaster, multiple visuals are being shared on social media with the claim that they show visuals of the August 2026 Nepal floods. Let’s verify the truth behind these visuals in this article.
Claim: The visuals show the August 2026 Nepal floods.
Fact: None of the videos are related to the Nepal floods in August 2026. They are either old videos from other locations or AI-generated videos that are being shared as visuals of the disaster. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
This video is being shared on social media with the claim that it shows a Chinese helicopter reaching the site where a glacier had broken, causing a massive amount of water to be released and resulting in widespread destruction in Nepal.
In our investigation, we found that the video was originally uploaded (archived) on the Instagram account of Leigh Coates, an American commercial helicopter pilot based in Valdez, Alaska. She posted the video on 22 August 2026 and specifically identified the location as Columbia Glacier in Alaska. She explained that a Jökulhlaup, also known as a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF), occurs when water trapped by glacier ice suddenly finds a way out, causing the water to drain rapidly beneath the glacier and rush downhill with immense force. She further stated that such events have been occurring annually at Columbia Glacier since 2014, although they are rarely captured because they generally occur in remote areas.
Video 2
The video is being shared on social media with claims that it shows the largest lake in the mountains whose embankment breached, causing the massive Nepal-Tibet floods.
We found that the video was uploaded by Leigh Coates on her official YouTube channel on 16 August 2026, before the Nepal floods. The video is titled “Before and After a Jökulhlaup Glacial Outburst Flood” and shows an example of the glacial outburst flood that occurred in Juneau, Alaska. This confirms that the video is unrelated to the August 2026 Nepal-Tibet floods.
Video 3
The video (here, here, and here) is being shared with claims on social media that it shows vehicles and buildings being swept away by flash floods in Nepal.
However, we found (archived) that this video has been available on the internet since 04 August 2026, at least 22 days before the Nepal floods. Moreover, upon examining the video, we noticed that the movement of the water and vehicles appeared unnatural.
We also analysed the video using AI detection tools such as Hive, which indicated that the video was AI-generated.
Video 4
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows vehicles being swept away by heavy floods during the August 2026 Nepal disaster.
We found that this video is related to the flash floods that occurred in the Chamoli region of Uttarakhand on 10 August 2026. Media reports (here, here) from the time also carried the same visuals and reported that vehicles were swept away after a bridge collapsed amid the flooding.
Video 5
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows a mudslide rapidly turning into a torrent of muddy floodwater during the August 2026 Nepal floods.
We found that the video is not related to the August 2026 Nepal floods. The video was actually recorded in Hpakant, Myanmar, in January 2024 (here, here).
Video 6
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows water and debris rushing down from a mountainous area and sweeping away homes during the August 2026 flash floods in Nepal.
We found (here, here, and here) that this video is from Dharali village in Uttarkashi, Uttarakhand, and dates back to August 2025. It shows flash floods that occurred following a cloudburst in the upper catchment area of the Kheer Ganga River. The resulting floodwaters, debris and silt surged through Dharali, washing away houses and other structures. At least four people were confirmed dead, while more than 50 others were reported missing.
Video 7
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows a massive landslide occurring during the August 2026 Nepal floods.
We found (here, here) that this video has been available on the internet since at least 11 August 2026, predating the recent Nepal floods. Several users have claimed that the landslide was triggered by an earthquake that struck Colombia on 10 August 2026.
Video 8
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows a power plant being devastated amid the August 2026 Nepal floods. News outlets like NDTV, Dainik Bhaskar, and Divya Bhaskar also shared the video, claiming it was from Nepal.
We found (here, here, and here) that this video has been available online since at least 2022 and is not related to the August 2026 Nepal floods.
Video 9
This video is being shared with the claim that it shows people in Nepal running ahead of fast-moving floodwaters during the severe floods on 26 August 2026. Dainik Bhaskar, Punjab Kesari TV, and News18 Tamil Nadu also shared the video in the context of the Nepal floods.
We found that the video was available online as early as 04 August 2026, well before the 26 August 2026 Nepal floods, and therefore predates the disaster. The original post stated that the video showed rainfall in Yafa, a mountainous region of Yemen (here, here).
Video 10
The video (here, here) shows an elephant rescuing a man during the August 2026 Nepal floods.
We found that the video shows an elephant rescuing a man in Assam, India. The video was filmed several weeks before the August 2026 Nepal floods and is therefore unrelated to the disaster.
To sum up, none of these visuals are related to the Nepal floods in August 2026.

Russia is rattling NATO’s nerves, but how far will Moscow go?
Incursions may be aimed at testing Western military alliance's resolve
It would be fair to say this summer has been the season of fear and loathing in Eastern Europe, as more signs emerge that Russia could be ready to further test NATO solidarity in the hopes of breaking it.
Poland and Romania have witnessed a series of Russian drone intrusions and at least one missile strike since the spring.
The idea that the Kremlin is preparing some kind of incursion drove speculation surrounding the CIA director's surprise visit to Moscow last week.
What is worrying officials in Poland and the Baltic states is not the prospect of Russian armoured divisions suddenly crossing the frontier.
The concern is that Moscow may believe it can carry out a deliberately ambiguous, limited act of violence — large enough to frighten or destabilize NATO, but small and deniable enough to make invoking the Western military alliance's self-defence clause, Article 5, politically difficult.
In late July, a Russian cruise missile crashed into Poland's Lublin province after travelling deep into Polish territory during a massive strike against Ukraine. Multiple drones have also approached or tested Polish airspace in the weeks since.
A Polish defence expert who specializes in the Russian military and politics said the war in Eastern Europe is rapidly approaching a critical turning point where the Kremlin has reached the conclusion that the only way to defeat Ukraine is to politically break NATO.
"There is frustration [over the] inability to break Ukrainian armed forces and to defeat Ukrainians in the field," said Withold Rodkiewicz, a security expert at the Center for East European Studies at the University of Warsaw.
The Russian "elite," as Rodkiewicz calls them, know they're not winning the war, and Ukraine's increasingly effective attacks on oil and commercial infrastructure have the potential to destabilize the Kremlin's grip on power.
"The analysis that's around in Moscow is that the main reason that Ukrainians are able to resist is because they are supplied from the West," he said, adding that nothing short of total victory in Ukraine will satisfy the Kremlin.
"They're not looking for a way out. They are not looking for … an off-ramp," he said. "When they are thinking what to do next, an escalation is an obvious thing."
Rodkiewicz said he believes the time will be right for Moscow sometime in September, either before or after Russia's parliamentary elections.
There is mounting evidence of Russian risk-taking, but there is no consensus that Russian President Vladimir Putin has decided to start a conventional war with NATO. Estonia’s foreign intelligence service, for example, still assesses that Russia does not presently intend to attack a NATO country militarily in the coming year.
Do I think they'll do something that is so clearly aimed at shaking NATO decision-making and political cohesion? Absolutely.- Kerry Buck, Canada's former ambassador to NATO
At the same time, throughout the summer, U.S., Polish and Baltic warnings about a provocation have become considerably more specific.
In late June and July, reporting emerged that Western intelligence services had picked up indications that Russia could be preparing some form of action against Poland or the Baltic states, designed specifically to test NATO cohesion.
The Guardian newspaper in the U.K. reported that intelligence received by Latvia pointed toward a possible Russian military provocation, and subsequent reporting said the United States had warned Poland about the possibility of an armed incident on Polish territory.
By early August, the warning sharpened even further. U.S. intelligence was reportedly telling Poland and the Baltic countries that Putin could be prepared to authorize provocative action against NATO while the Ukraine war is still underway, rather than waiting for Russia to regenerate its conventional forces after the war.
That is a significant change in the threat conversation.
Canada's former ambassador to NATO, Kerry Buck, said Russia has been out to destroy the alliance since its invasion of Crimea in 2014, and the conditions have only improved since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to power last year.
The constant berating of allies, the new fiscal demands placed on them, the cutting of U.S. forces earmarked for an emergency, and now Washington's review of American troop posture in Europe have created the conditions for a major political crisis, should there be a provocation.
It is, Buck said, "a window of opportunity where Russia was emboldened to poke NATO more, poke NATO territory, airspace and space more."
While she doesn't believe an outright attack on NATO is in the offing, she also believes Russia is prepared to try something ambiguous.
"Do I think they'll do something that is so clearly aimed at shaking NATO decision-making and political cohesion? Absolutely," Buck said.
Trump told reporters last week that he's "not concerned at all" about Russia attacking NATO territory. He said he's spoken to Putin and has been assured he "is not going to be attacking a NATO territory."
At a meeting of the North Atlantic Council in Brussels last week, U.S. defense policy chief Elbridge Colby insisted Washington is not abandoning Europe. He said it wants a new vision of NATO built around European-led conventional defence.
Buck said most of what Russia is likely planning falls below the threshold of a direct attack. She also accepts at face value what Colby has said. Rather, her concern lies within the reality of NATO politics.
In the past, whenever there's a crisis, the U.S. has stepped up to organize the allied response. Will that happen under the current administration?
"All signs from President Trump are that they are not as committed as they used to be, so who would step in and lead the preliminary response?" Buck asked.
"And would it be held up by U.S. reluctance? So we're dealing not just with a lack of U.S. leadership, but potentially U.S. reluctance to fall into whatever it is NATO is doing or might contemplate doing."
Just recently, Lithuanian intelligence raised another disturbing possibility: Russia using captured Ukrainian drones in a false flag operation against a Baltic country.
Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said that intelligence indicated Russia might employ captured Ukrainian UAVs in an operation intended to look as though Ukraine had attacked NATO territory.
The objective would be political rather than military, creating confusion inside the alliance and undermining support for Kyiv. Russia dismissed the allegation.
But that scenario becomes more plausible because something very similar happened in Latvia last spring.
Ukrainian strike drones have repeatedly wandered into NATO airspace, apparently in some cases because Russian electronic warfare has disrupted their navigation.
The incident in Latvia caused a political crisis that cost the defence minister his job, and eventually cost the prime minister her job.
Buck said there's a range of disturbing scenarios for Moscow to make mischief.
"It's in their interest to do it now," she said. "And I don't think NATO's quite ready to respond in a way, particularly because of the uncertainty about the U.S. response."

The story so far: The Union Health Ministry this past week tightened controls on all fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) containing chlorpheniramine maleate and phenylephrine hydrochloride, requiring manufacturers to carry a clear warning that they must not be used in children below four years of age.
What are these two drugs?
Chlorpheniramine is an antihistamine. It can reduce allergy symptoms such as a runny nose and sneezing. Phenylephrine is a decongestant, intended to relieve a blocked nose.
An FDC puts both ingredients into one medicine. Such combinations are commonly encountered in cold/allergy preparations.
The government’s action does not mean every medicine containing either ingredient individually has been banned. The specific regulatory action concerns FDCs containing the two ingredients together.
What has changed now is the rule where manufacturers must put the warning. “Fixed Dose Combination shall not be used in children below four years of age” — on the label, package insert and promotional literature. The restriction covers manufacture, sale and distribution of these FDCs.
This expands an earlier action. In 2023, India’s Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) had already directed manufacturers of a particular chlorpheniramine + phenylephrine formulation to warn against use below four.
In April 2025, restrictions were imposed on certain FDCs. The August 2026 notification extends the warning requirement to all such formulations.
Why are children under four the focus?
Young children are more vulnerable to medication-related adverse effects because their bodies process medicines differently from adults and because dosing errors can have proportionally larger consequences.
The government’s Expert Committee and Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) concluded that these combinations could pose risks to children below four and that safer alternatives are available.
There is also a broader international concern around giving young children multi-ingredient cough-and-cold medicines. The US FDA, for example, warns that decongestant- or antihistamine-containing cough/cold products can cause serious adverse effects in very young children and notes the risk of accidental overdose when several ingredients are combined.
Does this mean cold medicines don’t work?
Not necessarily. These drugs can relieve symptoms, but they don’t cure the underlying viral infection. Most childhood colds resolve on their own. What doctors have been saying is that while parents may understandably want to make a congested or coughing child comfortable, but more medication isn’t automatically better.
For nasal congestion, relatively simple measures such as saline nasal drops/spray, fluids and a cool-mist humidifiercan help.
The key message is don’t self-medicate a child under four with a chlorpheniramine + phenylephrine combination, even if the product is marketed as a children’s cold medicine.
Check the active ingredients, not just the brand name. Many cold preparations contain several ingredients, creating a risk of accidentally giving the same drug twice through different products.
For fever or discomfort, parents should use medicines such as paracetamol/acetaminophen or ibuprofen only according to age/weight-appropriate instructions and medical advice.

A suspected food packaging racket involving the alteration of expiry dates has been uncovered in Navi Mumbai under the leadership of Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe, with officials seizing products from brands including Maggi and Lay’s, the FDA said on Monday.
Following the operation, the FDA suspended the licence of Sadhana Enterprises, a firm operating in the TTC Industrial Area in Turbhe.
The seized stock included potato chips and snacks such as Lay’s, Kurkure variants and Fun Flips, along with Maggi Masala and Atta Noodles. Ready-to-eat and ready-to-cook food products were also among the items seized, according to the FDA.
The operation was conducted jointly by the FDA and the Navi Mumbai Police Crime Branch between August 24 and 29.
During inspections, officials discovered that the manufacturing and expiry or use-by dates printed on food packaging were being removed and replaced.
The FDA also found that the original labels displaying information about ingredients and nutritional content were being replaced with fresh stickers. The entire stock was subsequently being repackaged, the department said.
Meanwhile, the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration faced setbacks in two enforcement cases before the Bombay High Court, which criticised the regulator for acting with "undue haste" and taking a "pedantic instead of pragmatic view."
The court directed the FDA to withdraw its order suspending the operations of five restaurants at the Mumbai Cricket Association (MCA) premises in Bandra-Kurla Complex after a fresh inspection found the eateries 88% compliant with food safety rules. The bench of Acting Chief Justice Ravindra Ghuge and Justice Gautam Ankhad said the eateries could reopen, while asking the FDA to issue a fresh notice to MCA and provide it a hearing over its contract with M/s Shirke Infrastructure, which operated the restaurants.
The court warned of contempt action against officials, saying, "However, despite clearly saying this, the FDA has disobeyed our order and taken a pedantic view instead of a pragmatic view. We are tired of scolding the department and officers all the time. It is now time to pass stinging orders. We will issue contempt action against the concerned officers. Let them convince us or go to jail."
In a separate case, the FDA withdrew its order cancelling the drug sale licence of Cipla Pharma & Life Sciences Ltd's carrying and forwarding facility in Wadki, Pune. The licence had been cancelled from August 27 following violations linked to the packaging and recall of Reactin Plus tablets.
The court said the FDA had acted in a "high-handed" manner and that its order was "against the principles of natural justice", while questioning the regulator's procedure in the case.
(With inputs from news agency PTI)

I wasn't even born: Telangana voters question SIR notices seeking old documents
Voters at SIR hearings in Hyderabad said they were being asked for decades-old documents despite submitting Aadhaar, PAN and voter ID details. The complaints have prompted Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy and political parties to seek more time and safeguards against wrongful deletions.
‘I was not even born in 1987. Where am I supposed to get such a document from?’ That question from a Telangana voter captures the growing confusion around the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, with residents served SIR notices struggling to understand what documents they must produce to protect their names on the voter list.
The controversy has also reached the political level, with Telangana Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy seeking more time from the Election Commission and warning that eligible voters must not be removed during the revision exercise.
At hearings in Hyderabad, voters said they were being asked to produce documents dating back several decades to establish their identity, date of birth and address. Some questioned why government-issued documents such as Aadhaar and PAN cards, as well as existing voter records, were allegedly not sufficient for the verification process.
VOTER ASKS: ‘WHERE AM I SUPPOSED TO GET SUCH A DOCUMENT?’
One voter, Sai Kanmudraj, said he was asked to produce a document dating back to 1987, even though he was not born at the time.
“I was not even born in 1987. Where am I supposed to get such a document from?” he asked.
Kanmudraj said officials had initially indicated that different documents could be submitted, but later told him that Aadhaar and PAN cards were not being accepted for the particular verification requirement.
“The government issued me this Aadhaar card. The government issued me this PAN card. If neither of these is accepted, where am I supposed to get another document from?” he asked.
He also questioned why voter ID and bank-related documents could not be used, arguing that ordinary citizens should not be expected to produce records from decades ago if such documents were never issued to them.
“I have only one request to the government whether it is Aadhaar, PAN, a bank passbook or any other document, please accept it,” he said.
‘WHAT MORE DO THEY WANT FROM US?’
Another woman who received an SIR notice said she had repeatedly voted at the same polling booth but was now being asked to provide additional proof of her identity and address.
She said her father was no longer alive and that she had been asked to establish the address mentioned in the records. According to her, she had already submitted her Aadhaar card, but officials were allegedly seeking additional documents, including bank-related proof.
“My Aadhaar card has my number and all the details. It is complete proof. What more do I have to submit?” she questioned.
She said she had also submitted her voter ID but was told it could not be accepted for the requirement being raised.
The woman said she had passed her Class 10 examination decades ago, but the certificate did not carry her photograph, leaving her unsure about what additional document would satisfy the verification process.
“I have already submitted one proof. What more do they want from us?” she asked.
She was asked to return for further verification and photography, adding to the uncertainty over what documents she would ultimately need to submit.
OFFICIALS SAY NOTICES ARE PART OF VERIFICATION
An official involved in the exercise said notices were being issued and hearings conducted as part of the verification process.
G Vasanth Kumar, In-charge Assistant Municipal Commissioner and ARO, said around 360 notices had been issued for the day's proceedings.
According to the official, the exercise covers categories including ASDD entries, no-mapping cases and discrepancies. Figures cited during the hearing put the number of cases in the relevant categories at around 3,760 to 3,786, along with 2,856 discrepancies.
Voters receiving notices are being called for hearings and are required to submit documents prescribed by the Election Commission for verification.
REVANTH SEEKS MORE TIME FROM ECI
Chief Minister Revanth Reddy has raised concerns over the scale of the exercise and its possible impact on voters.
In a letter to Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, Revanth sought an extension of around four weeks for the claims and objections process. He also asked for additional time for voters to respond to notices, wider dissemination of the draft electoral rolls and helpdesks, particularly in urban areas.
According to the figures cited by the Chief Minister, Telangana had around 3.38 crore electors as of June 10, of whom nearly 73.39 lakh entries, or around 21.7 per cent, had been classified under the Absent, Shifted, Dead and Duplicate categories.
Revanth expressed concern that voters who had only temporarily moved could potentially be treated as permanently shifted.
At a public meeting in Hyderabad earlier this month, he had also urged Congress workers and leaders to visit households, verify voter details and ensure that eligible voters were not deleted.
The Chief Minister alleged that genuine voters could be removed in the name of SIR and said Telangana would not allow eligible voters to be excluded from the electoral rolls.
BRS: ‘NOT A SINGLE ELIGIBLE VOTER SHOULD BE DELETED’
The Bharat Rashtra Samithi has also raised concerns over the exercise, while supporting the removal of dead, duplicate and bogus entries.
BRS spokesperson Putta Vishnuvardhan Reddy said, “Our stand is very clear: we want to make sure that the votes of the people who are dead, people who are carrying duplicate votes, people with bogus votes they must be deleted from the electoral rolls.”
At the same time, he said the Election Commission must ensure that “not a single eligible voter should be deleted.”
Reddy cited an example from Banjara Hills, claiming that the number of voters registered at a commercial building increased from 19 before the revision to 44 afterwards.
“When we see these sort of anomalies that defy logic, there is definitely something wrong going on in the entire exercise, raising serious questions of collusion,” he said.
He also said large urban areas such as Hyderabad have voters whose forms may not yet have been collected because of various reasons.
“The focus of the Election Commission should be on migrants and tenants to guarantee that no legitimate citizen is robbed of their vote,” he said.
CONGRESS DEMANDS DEADLINE EXTENSION
Congress MP Anil Kumar Yadav also questioned the scale of the SIR exercise and called for more time and assistance for voters.
“Nearly one-third of Telangana’s population has come under scrutiny in the SIR exercise, with over 94 lakh voters flagged as ASDT. This raises serious concerns about the transparency of the process,” he said.
Yadav said many voters served notices belonged to economically weaker sections and slum communities and needed adequate time and assistance to respond.
“We demand an extension of the SIR deadline and insist that no eligible voter in Telangana should be deleted from the electoral rolls without proper verification and an opportunity to respond,” he said.
DOCUMENTS, DEADLINES AND VOTER DELETION IN FOCUS
The SIR debate in Telangana is now moving beyond political allegations, with voters appearing at hearings and seeking clarity over exactly what documents they need to establish their eligibility.
For voters such as Kanmudraj and the woman who appeared for a hearing, the central concern is straightforward: if documents such as Aadhaar, PAN or voter ID are not sufficient for a particular verification requirement, what can an ordinary voter realistically produce to prove their identity and eligibility?
With the Chief Minister seeking additional time and political parties demanding safeguards against wrongful deletions, the Election Commission's response to the concerns raised by voters and the state government will be closely watched as the electoral roll revision progresses.

Lionel Messi says he's retiring from playing internationally for Argentina
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina — Lionel Messi announced his retirement from international soccer on Monday after two decades representing Argentina.
"It was a decision that hurt — and still hurts deeply — but I understand that the time has come," the 39-year-old Messi said on his Instagram account.
"I swear to you that I always gave it my all — not just in these last few years when we won everything, but before that too; I always fought and left everything on the field for this jersey, to bring you joy and make you feel proud to be Argentine through football."
Messi played in a record-tying six World Cups, won it in 2022 in Qatar and led Argentina to this year's final, losing to Spain in extra time in New Jersey.
In the World Cup hosted in the U.S., Mexico and Canada, Messi played all eight matches and scored eight goals. He finished just one goal behind France's Kylian Mbappé, the tournament's top scorer. He concluded his international career as Argentina's all-time leading scorer with 125 goals, 21 of which were scored in World Cups.
He explained he wrote his retirement letter on July 21 — two days after the World Cup final — but waited to publish it because his father was facing health issues that eventually claimed his life.
Jorge Messi died on Aug. 8 in his native Rosario.
Messi will continue to play for Inter Miami. Over the weekend he scored four times in a 7-1 win over CF Montreal.
He made his Argentina debut in 2006 but his journey was fraught with frustration until he finally lifted the World Cup in 2022.
"Thank you for all the love these past 20 years," he said. "I'm going to miss hearing you all from the inside so much. Now I'm going to be one of you, cheering and supporting you from the outside (through thick and thin, even more so)."
In the letter, the Inter Miami captain did not say how long he intends to continue playing.
"I leave with the peace of mind and pride of having given you — along with my teammates — moments we once only dreamed of. Experiencing this with you was incredible. I love you all," he added.
The second retirement
Messi's stellar recent success with Argentina nearly didn't happen.
A decade ago, before the World Cup triumph and Copa América titles in 2021 and 2024, he retired from the national team. The decision followed Argentina's defeat in the 2016 Copa América final to Chile on penalty kicks, one of which he missed.
But Messi shook off the notion of not being able to win the big match. He continued starring for Barcelona, then Paris Saint-Germain, then Inter Miami.

For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

Story so far: The Supreme Court on August 20, 2026, has ruled that the police cannot independently investigate offences relating to illegal prenatal sex determination under the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994. The responsibility lies primarily with the Appropriate Authority, a specialised body constituted under the law. In a judgment authored by a Bench of Justice Sanjay Karol and Justice Nongmeikapam Kotiswar Singh, it settles a long-standing disagreement among High Courts over whether the police could register FIRs and investigate such offences because they are classified as “cognisable” and “non-bailable”.
What was the case about?
The case arose from an allegation of illegal sex determination of a foetus at a hospital in Bulandshahar, Uttar Pradesh.
The District Magistrate, who was the Appropriate Authority under the Act, received information about the alleged practice. A Tehsildar was authorised to conduct a decoy operation. Following the operation, a raid was conducted at the hospital, and an FIR was registered against the doctor and others.
The FIR included offences under the Indian Penal Code as well as the sex-determination law. The accused approached the Allahabad High Court seeking to quash the chargesheet.
The High Court noticed that courts had taken different views on the role of the police in such cases and referred the issue to the Supreme Court.
There were essentially three questions before the Supreme Court: Can the police register an FIR for an offence under the Act? Can they investigate it? And can a Magistrate take cognisance of the offence on the basis of a police chargesheet?
Who is the Appropriate Authority?
The Appropriate Authority is the specialised authority created under the law to enforce the ban on sex selection and regulate the use of prenatal diagnostic techniques.
Section 17 of the Act specifically gives it the responsibility of investigating complaints of violations and taking action.
According to the section, when appointed for the whole of the State or the Union territory, it should consist of the following three members i) an officer of or above the rank of the Joint Director of Health and Family Welfare Chairperson; ii) an eminent woman representing women’s organisation; and iii) an officer of Law Department of the State or the Union territory concerned.
The functions of the appropriate authority includes to grant, suspend or cancel registration of a Genetic Counselling Centre, Genetic Laboratory or Genetic Clinic; to enforce standards prescribed for the Genetic Counselling Centre, Genetic Laboratory and Genetic Clinic; to investigate complaints of breach of the provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder and take immediate action and to seek and consider the advice of the Advisory Committee.
The Supreme Court therefore held that the law has deliberately placed the investigation of such offences with this specialised authority.
So, can the police register an FIR?
Not for the purpose of independently investigating a violation of the Act.
The complication came from Section 27 of the law, which says that every offence under it is “cognisable, non-bailable and non-compoundable.” A cognisable offence ordinarily allows the police to investigate without first obtaining permission from a court.
But the Supreme Court said that Section 27 cannot be read on its own. It has to be read along with the provisions that specifically give the Appropriate Authority the power to investigate and Section 28, which lays down how a court can take up an offence under the Act.
The Court said, “The language of the statute, more particularly Sections 27 and 28 of the Act when read together, in light of the other provisions and the socially beneficial nature of the Act as also the requirement of sensitivity along with medical and technical know-how, indicates that the police are not meant to be the investigators for the purpose of this Act. This is further made clear by the fact that an FIR once registered cannot be taken to its logical conclusion as per the procedures of this Act. The restriction applies only to offences under this Act and does not restrict the police’s power to investigate or prosecute independent offences disclosed under substantive criminal law (IPC/BNS)”.
The Court held that allowing the police to independently investigate would undermine this specialised system.
It said, “the police are not meant to be the investigators for the purpose of this Act.”
The police can, however, assist the Appropriate Authority when their help is necessary. Rule 18A(3)(iv) says that police involvement should be avoided “as far as possible”. The Court held that this rule has statutory force.
The phrase does leave room for police assistance, but not for an independent police investigation. The Court said that, when involved, the police would have to act “strictly in a supplemental or aiding capacity.”
What happens if there is also another crime?
The Supreme Court has not said that the police have no role whenever a suspected sex-determination offence is involved. The police can investigate a separate offence under the IPC, BNS or another criminal law, even if it arises from the same incident.
For example, if the facts disclose both a violation of the sex-determination law and an independently constituted offence under general criminal law, the two investigations can proceed separately.
The Appropriate Authority would investigate the offence under the special law. The police would investigate the independent criminal offence.
But the police cannot use the existence of another offence as a way of taking over the sex-determination investigation. The Court’s concurring opinion makes the distinction clear: the police cannot use a general criminal offence “as a gateway to take over the PC & PNDT inquiry.”
Similarly, the special law cannot be used to prevent the police from investigating a genuinely separate criminal offence.
Can a Magistrate act on a police chargesheet?
No. This was the third question before the Supreme Court, and the Court’s answer was categorical.
Section 28 says that a court cannot take cognizance of an offence under the Act except through the complaint mechanism specified in the provision. A police chargesheet therefore cannot, by itself, give the Magistrate jurisdiction to take cognizance of a PC &PNDT offence.
The Appropriate Authority has to follow the procedure prescribed under the Act.
The Court concluded that there is a “complete statutory embargo” on taking cognizance except in the situations provided under Section 28.
What is the takeaway?
The immediate impact is on how a suspected illegal sex-determination case moves through the criminal justice system.
If information received by a police station discloses only a violation under the Act, the police should record the information and send it, along with the relevant material, to the Appropriate Authority. They should not independently investigate the offence.
If the information also reveals an independent cognizable offence under the IPC, BNS or another general criminal law, the police can investigate that offence while sending the sex-determination component to the Appropriate Authority.
The Supreme Court has also made clear that a police investigation cannot simply end with a chargesheet for the offence under the Act. Section 28 creates a separate route for bringing such a case before a court.
The ruling does not weaken the prohibition on prenatal sex determination. Instead, it clarifies who is responsible for enforcing it.

Messi announced his retirement from the Argentina national team through an emotional social media post. Enough new coalmining projects were proposed last year to increase global supplies by 2.5bn tonnes a year, an increase of 11% from the year before, even as demand for coal plateaus, according to a new report.
Global Energy Monitor, an NGO, found that India ignited a rise in new coalmine proposals in 2025 despite a global slowdown in the number of mine openings because of falling demand for the fossil fuel.
The increase was driven almost entirely by the states of Jharkhand and Odisha, which doubled their proposals for new coalmines in line with an ambitious plan from India’s ministry of coal to increase the country’s output.
India plans to increase its coal production by nearly 100m tonnes to 1.15bn tonnes in the 2025-26 fiscal year to help meet the country’s rising demand for electricity to support economic growth and contend with heatwaves, which have become more severe and more frequent because of the climate crisis.
The planned increases come despite signs that the world is beginning to turn its back on coal in favour of renewable electricity, Global Energy Monitor said.
Coalmine proposals slowed in the years after the Covid-19 pandemic but have begun to climb again, raising concerns that mining could increase in the future despite a slowdown in the number of new facilities.
The startup of new coalmining projects has fallen steadily in recent years, according to the Global Energy Monitor’s latest report.
It found that enough new coalmines to produce about 113m tonnes each year began operations last year, down by 40% from 2024, which was already the lowest annual total in a decade.
This was largely owing to a slowdown in new mines in China and Australia, which fell by 44% and 96% respectively.
Global Energy Monitor warned that India’s rise in new mine proposals was at odds with the slowdown in global coal demand predicted by the International Energy Agency for the end of the decade.
Wind and solar power surpassed coal generation in the global electricity mix for the first time last year, according to a separate report from energy thinktank Ember, in a “milestone moment” for climate action.
China and India were largely responsible for the rise in renewables, according to the Ember report, while the US and Europe continued to rely more heavily on fossil fuels.
Tiffany Means, a senior researcher at Global Energy Monitor and co-author of the report said: “The economic rationale for expanding coalmining becomes progressively weaker as low-cost clean energy continues to displace coal.
“Rather than locking in decades of additional coal production, governments have an opportunity to cancel projects that remain in the development pipeline before they advance to construction.”

For the past five years, security researcher Matt Burch has immersed himself in the esoteric and high-stakes world of ATM security, in which small software flaws can sometimes expose cold, hard cash. As Burch has bored deeper into the computers powering these digital lock boxes—and continued to find vulnerabilities in key digital security systems—he has started working to raise the alarm, not just about overlooked ATM flaws, but about how that same software used in other industries can introduce weaknesses in an array of critical systems.
At the Black Hat and Defcon security conferences in Las Vegas this month, Burch presented findings about nine vulnerabilities that have been fixed in disk encryption and pre-boot authentication software called CryptoPro Secure Disk. The flaws could have been exploited to bypass CryptoPro's integrity checks and gain full access to encrypted devices.
Made by the German software firm CryptWare, CryptoPro is marketed to ATM makers and is used in some ATMs, including as part of Diebold Nixdorf's Vynamic Security Suite. But CryptoPro is also sold as a security solution for other embedded-device makers, as well as big organizations using Microsoft Windows, underscoring the supply chain challenge of addressing bugs when software is widely implemented in numerous industries.
“ATMs are what brought me down this path, but I think there may be an even higher impact of these findings beyond that,” Burch says. “From the perspective of ATMs and the financial network, there are a lot of layers, and I think as a result of that, things just get implemented a certain way and then there’s limited technical insight—bugs can get overlooked or they don’t get addressed.”
CryptWare managing director Uwe Saame tells WIRED that the company patched the nine bugs in two phases with CryptoPro version 7.7.2 in early November and 7.7.3 in early December. Burch says the company was prompt and collaborative throughout his disclosure process and he validated that the patches actually fix the vulnerabilities he found. While CryptoPro does not seem to publicly release update notes, Burch says he believes that the company distributed information about the patches to its customers.
Diebold Nixdorf spokesperson Michael Jacobsen tells WIRED in a statement that only two of the nine vulnerabilities are relevant to Diebold Nixdorf's Vynamic Security Hard Disk Encryption, the system where the ATM maker uses CryptoPro software. Jacobsen says that Diebold Nixdorf issued fixes related to those two bugs in December, but that they could not have been exploited on their own to compromise a Diebold Nixdorf ATM.
In ATMs, embedded devices, and enterprise security more broadly, the challenge of the software supply chain comes from all of the steps to actually apply fixes in the world. As in this case, a developer has to release a patch, then companies that implement the product in their own software need to develop a tailored fix, and then customers need to actually hear about and install that patch—which can be difficult for systems that are running in the field or can't easily be paused and updated.
Speaking generally about this challenge, Jacobsen, the Diebold Nixdorf spokesperson, says that “when a security issue is identified, Diebold Nixdorf assesses the impact, identifies affected products and configurations, and develops any needed updates through our product security and engineering processes. We then notify impacted customers and provide updates through standard software distribution channels, including the Global Security Portal where applicable. For deployed ATMs, updates are coordinated with each customer based on their operating model, service agreements, and change-management processes.”
Security researchers have warned for decades about the danger of relying on “security through obscurity” by trying to hide software from view or keep it locked away. And, as a result of this work, internet-of-things manufacturers and those in critical industries like the financial sector and medical device manufacturing have made some progress on transparency and promoting patch adoption. But Burch points out that as AI systems make it easier to evaluate software and find vulnerabilities—even for researchers or attackers who don't have granular expertise in a given area—it is more pressing than ever to shed light on niche security products.
“AI really blows away the obscurity model,” Burch says. “You don’t need to fully understand how something works anymore to move forward and potentially have a big impact.”

Couple held in Manipur after body found on train
Police have arrested a couple in the Manipur’s Jiribam district in connection with the murder of a 38-year-old woman in Tamil Nadu’s Guduvanchery, officers said on Sunday, nearly a month after her dismembered body was found in a suitcase on a Delhi-bound train
Police have arrested a couple in the Manipur’s Jiribam district in connection with the murder of a 38-year-old woman in Tamil Nadu’s Guduvanchery, officers said on Sunday, nearly a month after her dismembered body was found in a suitcase on a Delhi-bound train.
Police identified the accused as Manik Uddin Laskar, 22, of Assam’s Cachar district, and his wife, Bhagabati Majhi, alias Ayesha Begum, 21, of Odisha’s Kendujhar district.
“A joint team of Tamil Nadu Police, assisted by Manipur Police, arrested Manik on the inter-village road between Lalpani and Rasidpur in Manipur’s Jiribam district on August 28. Co-accused Bhagabati was arrested the following day from Kashimpur village in the same district,” a Manipur Police statement said.
Manipur Police added that the couple were being handed over to the station house officer of the T8 Guduvanchery police station in Tamil Nadu for further formalities.
Chennai Government Railway Police superintendent of police P Rajan said on Sunday that the couple would be produced before a magistrate in Manipur before being brought to Chennai on transit warrants for further investigation.
A TN police officer, on the condition of anonymity, said the crime appeared to have stemmed from an alleged illicit relationship between Manik and the victim.
On August 5, passengers on a Delhi-bound express train from Tamil Nadu noticed a foul smell emanating from a red trolley suitcase in an unreserved compartment after the train reached Agra. The Government Railway Police were alerted, and they recovered the woman’s headless, dismembered body from the suitcase, police said.
Tamil Nadu railway police at Puratchi Thalaivar Dr M G Ramachandran Central Railway Station were informed of the incident and, along with Agra railway police, launched a detailed investigation, police said.
After reviewing more than 350 surveillance camera recordings, police identified a couple carrying the suitcase at Chennai Central railway station. Meanwhile, the victim’s son had filed a missing-person complaint at Guduvanchery police station.
A team led by Rajan from Guduvanchery police raided a rented house on Mosque Street in Guduvanchery, where police recovered additional body parts from a large cooking vessel. Forensic examination and DNA analysis identified the victim as Hayathun Nisha, a native of Odisha.
“The two suspects were staying at the victim’s residence and had known her for several years. Guduvanchery police later converted the missing-person case into a murder case and were on the lookout for those involved in the crime and the motive behind it,” Rajan said.
The investigation revealed that, after placing the red trolley suitcase on the Tamil Nadu Express on August 3, the couple fled to Manipur, officers said.

US PrSM missiles in Iran strike killed civilians up to 50 metres away: Report
The US-Israeli war against Iran began on February 28 with strikes across the country, including an attack on the southern Iranian city of Lamerd that killed at least 21 civilians, including seven children, according to Iranian officials.An investigation by conflict monitor Airwars, reviewed and independently verified by The Associated Press, suggests that three US-made Precision Strike Missiles (PrSMs) were used in the Lamerd strikes.Airwars found that civilians were killed as far as 50 metres (164 feet) from the missiles' apparent detonation points, while damage extended at least 170 metres (558 feet) in one case.The PrSM is designed to explode in midair and propel tens of thousands of dense tungsten pellets at high speed in all directions. £300m spent, bottom of the table... but Spurs boss De Zerbi 'not angry'
- Published
Tottenham manager Roberto de Zerbi said he was "not angry" and there was "no panic" after his side's second loss in two games left them bottom of the Premier League – but it was a depressingly familiar story for the club's fans.
Goals from Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa in a 10-minute second-half spell gave Newcastle a 2-0 victory, with thousands of Spurs supporters heading for the exits early.
They have every reason to be annoyed as they have now seen only three home league wins from their past 23 matches at their superb stadium.
Seventeenth in the Premier League in 2024-25, 17th in 2025-26, only avoiding relegation on the final day, but this season was meant to be different.
With more than £300m spent in the summer, Spurs fans were expecting a push to get back into Europe, having won the Europa League two seasons ago and been in the last 16 of the Champions League in March.
Instead, in the Premier League it is played two, lost two, scored none, 20th out of 20.
"We can improve in the defensive phases but today was an unfair result," said De Zerbi.
"Disappointed for the result because until the first goal we conceded, we played better than Newcastle.
"We are disappointed for the result and [for] our fans. We are working to be a great team. When we become a team, we can change the story of the last two seasons for Tottenham."
'I know where we are going and what the plan is'
After beating Everton on the final day of last season to stay up, Tottenham tried to ensure they were not in a relegation scrap this year.
In came midfielders Mateus Fernandes from West Ham and Sandro Tonali from Newcastle for £85m and £100m respectively, defender Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton for £52m and Manchester City winger Savio, formerly known as Savinho, for £75m, although he missed Saturday's match because of "muscle fatigue".
Defenders Marcos Senesi and Andy Robertson, plus goalkeeper Martin Dubravka, have arrived on free transfers and striker Omar Marmoush made his debut against Newcastle following his loan from Manchester City, with the deal becoming a permanent £60m transfer next summer.
After a 3-0 loss at Brentford last week, more home pain was inflicted on the Spurs support, although the Magpies scored with both of their attempts on target as Tottenham failed to convert any of their 17 attempts, six of which were on target.
"Forget the result," insisted De Zerbi. "I am not angry, we are working well and were unlucky today with the result.
"There is no panic. I know where we are going and what the plan is. I'm sorry for the fans for the result. We have to improve. We have to work hard on the pitch and find the connection between the players."
Old questions return early in season
Former Tottenham and England goalkeeper Joe Hart was not as positive about Spurs' performances and said: "The frustration in the stadium, and among the fans, will be they are looking at that Spurs team and wondering what they are trying to achieve.
"When you see a Newcastle side who have been through massive change over the summer - and a more difficult change than Spurs have - it's hard as in two games you can clearly see what [Newcastle boss] Matthias Jaissle is trying to do. The players are on board with it and they are flying.
"The concern for Tottenham is they can't say the same. But there's been a lot of change and it's not easy to bed in that many players under so much pressure.
"Hardly anyone has been able to find the remedy at the club so it's not like it's an easy fix. They've not just suddenly fallen off a cliff, they've been struggling in the league for a while.
"Roberto de Zerbi needs to get his new players to settle in quickly as the Premier League comes at you so fast, and it feels like his team are second-guessing everything at the moment."
Former England goalkeeper Rob Green, speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live, added: "Lukas Hornicek made some saves in the first half but Tottenham were short of invention, creation, goals.
"For Tottenham, the same questions last season are still here this season. Performances like this will indicate that they need a vast improvement from this set of players that have come into this club.
"They will need the characters as much as anything to turn this around. It doesn't take much for these Spurs fans to turn and the belief start to drain from the players."
One more signing to come?
The transfer window closes on Tuesday, and on Friday De Zerbi said he was still seeking "one player more in one specific position".
After the Newcastle match he was asked about the potential departures of Kevin Danso, Pape Matar Sarr and Richarlison, who have all been linked with moves away from Tottenham.
"I have very good relationships but if they want to leave, they have to bring the solution, the economic solution, to the club, and they can go," he said.
De Zerbi was only appointed at the end of March, earning 11 points in seven matches to keep Spurs up, and insists it will not be a quick fix to the club's problems.
"We have to improve and to change two seasons like the last two is impossible in 10 days and with people in the transfer market," said the Italian.
"We have to work hard on the pitch and find the connection with the players because last season before the end of the season we were in the Championship and we stayed up together.
"Now we have to keep calm and focus on improvement. We have a great squad and great players."

The Supreme Court cleared the way on Monday for President Donald Trump to continue building his White House ballroom, likely ending the administration’s legal battle with historic preservationists to block the project.
Key Facts
The court ruled 5-4 to allow the project to continue, with Chief Justice John Roberts joining the court’s three liberal-leaning justices in a dissenting opinion that said the project was "likely unlawful.”
The five judges determined the National Trust for Historic Preservation did not suffer the personal harm necessary from the construction to support their lawsuit.
The justices wrote that “mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury.”
The ruling upended lower court rulings that would have blocked construction from continuing on the grounds that the project required authorization from Congress to proceed.
The Supreme Court previously pushed back an Aug. 21 deadline imposed by a lower court to stop the project to consider the Trump administration’s appeal.
Crucial Quote
“We do not pass upon the legality of the government’s East Wing project,” the majority wrote. “We conclude only that, based on the submissions before us, the government is likely to prevail in showing that the Trust lacks . . . standing to challenge the project in federal court.”
Chief Critic
Roberts, writing for the justices in dissent, wrote that in ruling in Trump’s favor, “the court misconceives the plaintiff’s injury, allowing the Executive’s likely infringement of the Legislature’s power of the purse and authority to regulate federal property in the District of Columbia to continue.”
Key Background
The Trump administration has expanded the size of the project and its reasons for undertaking it since it demolished the East Wing shortly after Trump took office last year to make way for the 90,000 square-foot ballroom. The cost of the project has ballooned from the White House’s initial estimate of $200 million to at least $600 million, according to a June Washington Post analysis. The Trump administration has also argued the ballroom is necessary for security reasons, both to host events with world leaders and because it includes an underground bunker complex. It said in recent court filings that stopping construction now—when the ballroom is 65% complete—would be “dangerous” because it “would leave an unstable, unfinished 70-foot-tall structure on White House grounds.”

A video showing a man grabbing a young man by the collar, slapping him in a crowded area, and attacking him with a banana plant is being widely shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that a BJP MLA from Assam assaulted a man while attending a bridge inauguration ceremony. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video of a man being assaulted by an Assam BJP MLA during a bridge inauguration ceremony.
Fact: This video shows Samsul Huda, the All India United Democratic Front (AIUDF) MLA from Bilasipara East in Assam’s Dhubri district, allegedly assaulting an employee of a construction company during a bridge foundation stone-laying ceremony in March 2025. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to a video report published on Munsif TV’s YouTube channel on 20 March 2025. The video was captioned, “AIUDF MLA Samsul Huda Loses Temper During Foundation Stone Laying Ceremony in Bilasipara.”
A keyword search also led us to media reports about the same incident (here, here). According to these reports, Samsul Huda, the All India United Democratic Front (AIUDF) MLA from Bilasipara East in Assam’s Dhubri district, had attended a bridge foundation stone-laying ceremony, where he allegedly assaulted an employee of the construction company. The incident took place on 18 March 2025 and triggered widespread public outrage across Dhubri district.
To sum up, an old video of AIUDF MLA Samsul Huda assaulting a man is being falsely shared as a BJP MLA’s attack.

Soon after his appointment as the BJP’s national social media co-convenor, Arun Yadav made his X account private and then deleted more than 60,000 posts before making it public again. When the account was locked, it showed around 65,500 posts. By August 22, only 2,794 remained — a deletion exercise that wiped out virtually his entire publicly visible posting history.
At present, the oldest post that can be traced on Yadav’s timeline dates to August 19, 2026. All posts preceding it have been deleted. Many of those posts included abusive and racist remarks, attacks on women’s character, and content directly targeting Muslims in communally provocative terms.
On August 17, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) announced a new social media cell where Deepak Mhaskey replaced Amit Malviya a the party’s IT cell chief. One of the newly inducted members of the social media cell was Yadav, who had previously been removed from his position as head of the Haryana BJP IT Cell.
When attention turned to Yadav’s old social media record following his new appointment, he locked his X account, @BeingArun28. Yadav has now made his account public again, but not before deleting the posts on a massive scale. The sequence of events indicates that making the account private might have given him the opportunity to remove his old controversial posts and wipe his social media record clean.
A review of Arun Yadav’s social media activity over the past several years reveals a clear pattern: abusive and racist remarks against opposition leaders, attacks on women’s character, and several explicit instances of directly targeting Muslim minorities and making communally provocative statements.
The Post that Led to his Ouster in 2022
Arun Yadav’s history of controversial remarks goes back several years. In 2017, he shared an image of the Kaaba in Mecca alongside a glass of whisky and wrote in an objectionable post that he could see “the Prophet in a peg of alcohol”. Questions continued to be raised over the remark for years. Finally, amid mounting pressure, Haryana BJP removed Arun Yadav from his post as state IT Cell chief on July 8, 2022.
The timing of the action taken against him was particularly significant. It came just a month after then BJP spokesperson Nupur Sharma’s derogatory remarks about prophet Muhammad of Islam had sparked a massive controversy in India and abroad. During a television debate, the BJP spokesperson had made offensive remarks about the prophet, triggering an international backlash.
Amid intense international pressure, the BJP had termed its spokesperson a “fringe element” and expelled her from the party. The following month, a screenshot of Arun Yadav’s old objectionable post went viral on social media. In this sensitive environment, Yadav’s removal was, in a sense, a tacit acknowledgement that his post had crossed a line the party was not prepared to publicly defend at the time.
The significant new responsibility handed to Arun Yadav within the party sends a serious political message: the conduct for which his own party had once sacked him has not stood in the way of his appointment to a higher position with greater responsibility.
“The Digging will Continue until God leaves India, Keep Digging”
In May 2022, Arun Yadav made another objectionable remark about Islam, writing: “The digging will continue until God leaves India, keep digging.”
The post was made at a time when the Gyanvapi Mosque dispute was before the Supreme Court. The Hindu side had claimed that a “Shivling” was present within the mosque complex. Given the sensitivity of the case, the Supreme Court transferred the suit filed by the Hindu side from the trial court to a more senior and experienced district judge.
In this tense legal and social environment, Yadav’s statement was not merely an inflammatory post or an insult directed at a particular religion. It also sought to frame the “digging” of sites containing mosques across the country as a coordinated campaign.
Attack on Rahul Gandhi
Political opponents have also been among Arun Yadav’s targets. In a post from January 2023, he shared a video of Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s speech and used the phrase “the harvest of the brown aunty” for him.
The remark was not merely a deeply insulting personal attack but also reflected a clearly racist mindset. It was a direct reference to Rahul Gandhi’s mother, Sonia Gandhi, and her Italian origins. However, this is not an exception among BJP leaders. They have often been seen using such derogatory language targeting Sonia Gandhi’s foreign origins in the name of political opposition.
“…They Aren’t as Afraid Even when Their Wives Undergo Halala with other Men”
In a May 2022 post, Arun Yadav targeted Muslim women who were opposing surveys and excavations of mosques, making an obscene remark about them. Referring to the sensitive subject of “halala”, Yadav wrote: “As afraid as they are of the excavation of mosques, their wives aren’t even when they undergo halala with other men.”
In India, “halala” has long been the subject of an intense public debate. In Yadav’s post, the term was not merely used as part of a comment, but as a weapon to demean Muslim women.
More Islamophobia
In May 2022, Arun Yadav made another highly provocative post directly targeting Islam and the Muslim community. He wrote: “What kind of an ignorant community must those be whose Allah lives in temples stolen and looted from others?”
This was not simply a comment on the temple-mosque dispute. It was a direct attack on the Muslim community as a whole, using the dispute as a pretext. Yadav’s post was widely circulated.
“Who Got a Nine-month Recharge for Rs 500?”
One of the most shameful instances of Arun Yadav’s repeated targeting of Muslim women and making demeaning remarks about them emerged in May 2020. The case involved Jamia Millia Islamia student and activist Safoora Zargar.
Safoora was pregnant at the time and was imprisoned under the UAPA in connection with the 2020 Delhi riots case. While the detention of a pregnant woman was drawing criticism in India and abroad, Arun Yadav mocked Safoora’s pregnancy by comparing it to a mobile recharge plan.
Making a direct insinuation about her character, Yadav posted: “Who got a nine-month recharge for Rs 500?”
The matter did not end with the derogatory post. Yadav also actively endorsed other obscene and abusive comments posted under it. Arun Yadav was not the only BJP leader to make such remarks about Safoora’s pregnancy; several BJP leaders had also made demeaning comments about it.
The BJP’s IT Cell has long faced criticism over the spread of misinformation, targeting of minorities, promotion of regressive attitudes, circulation of controversial content and trolling. Its significance goes beyond the party’s own messaging: As one of the country’s most powerful political social media operations, it plays a significant role in shaping the information ecosystem — what millions of users see, discuss and believe online. Against that backdrop, Arun Yadav’s elevation is striking. A party that once disciplined him over communal posts has now entrusted him with a larger role in its national social media machinery. What was once grounds for his sacking has, years later, not come in the way of promotion.

The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on August 17 announced a new national social media team, replacing Amit Malviya with Deepak Mhaskey as its IT cell in-charge. The party also named four new social media co-convenors — Priti Gandhi, Shivanand Dwivedi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav.
Alt News had earlier reported that within minutes of BJP’s announcement, a search on X revealed that the accounts of the four social media co-convenors had either vanished or their posts had become inaccessible. However, screenshots and archived versions of their past tweets, often containing personal and contentious opinions, are available, raising concern over the sudden disappearance of their accounts. Yadav, for instance, deleted more than 60,000 posts before making her X handle accessible again. Mhaskey deleted at least 1,342.
Gandhi’s X account, which has over 500,000 followers, remains ‘protected’ or hidden from public view at the time of this article being published. A notice from the platform states “Only approved followers can see @MrsGandhi’s posts”.
An earlier screenshot of her profile captured by us shows her following 2,015 handles, which has now gone down to 1,875. In other words, she has recently unfollowed 140 X users.
Alt News spoke to Gandhi, and asked her why she had hidden her X posts, but she refused to comment. Her Facebook profile bio describes her as ‘IT & Social Media National In-charge for all 7 BJP Morchas’ and ‘Official Spokesperson, Maharashtra BJP’.
Recently, in November 2025, Gandhi courted controversy after targeting Indian cricketer Jemimah Rodrigues over her expression of faith during a post-match interview. After India’s semi-final victory against Australia, in which Rodrigues was named Player of the Match, she acknowledged her teammates’ support, said she had put her faith in God, and thanked Jesus in the post-match interview. Criticising this, Gandhi argued that while wearing the Indian jersey, Rodrigues represents Indians and “not her church”.
In her older tweets dating back to 2012-13, she expressed disdain for her surname, saying she would rather have ‘Modi’ or ‘Godse’ as a surname. She has repeatedly praised Nathuram Godse, the assassin of Mahatma Gandhi, in her tweets.
Declaring herself as a “huge fan and follower” of Godse, she has multiple tweets announcing that she “misses him” and that there is a need for “1000 more Godse’s” and that “India misses him.” Much of that record, however, is no longer readily accessible, but screenshots of her past tweets are shown below:
Long-time BJP Supporter
Her association with BJP, however, predates her formal organisational role. Gandhi has been a pro-BJP voice since around 2012. Initially, her X (then Twitter) handle was @pritirules. Aafter her anti-Congress posts were being shared by prominent BJP leaders, she changed her handle to @MrsGandhi. “I realised this name has a lot of potential, as there would be one Gandhi questioning the other. So I changed my handle,” she explained to the Telegraph.
In 2012, Modi started following Priti Gandhi on Twitter. According to her, she put forward her opinions aggressively — which caught Modi’s attention. Gandhi was even invited to Gandhinagar to meet Modi. “He [Modi] liked that I, as an independent person, defend him on social media”, Gandhi told The Telegraph.
In January 2014, Gandhi had falsely claimed that Julian Assange, the founder of WikiLeaks, had stated that “Modi is incorruptible”. Gandhi allegedly amplified a fake endorsement of Modi by Assange, featuring a poster of Assange alongside a quote that read, “America fears Modi because they know he is incorruptible.”
WikiLeaks responded:
