How Messi's decade of dominance almost never happened
- Published
"I've given it my all, I have nothing left to give."
Lionel Messi retired from international football on Monday as Argentina's all-time leading scorer and most-capped player. He captained them to World Cup glory at Qatar 2022 and to Copa America triumphs in 2021 and 2024.
But the world was almost denied his most successful period in the famous blue and white shirt.
On Sunday, 26 June 2016, at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, Messi broke the hearts of a nation.
Just two days after his 29th birthday and soon after missing a penalty in Argentina's Copa America final loss to Chile in a shootout, Messi decided he had seen enough.
After 113 appearances, he was adamant. In his mind, he would never pull on an Argentina shirt again.
"For me, the national team is over. I've done all I can. It hurts not to be a champion," he said.
The pain was understandable. Argentina had lost in the 2014 World Cup final, plus Copa America finals in 2007, 2015 and now 2016. The player many classed as the world's greatest had failed when it mattered most for him.
"It was the thing I wanted the most, but I couldn't get it, so I think it's over," Messi said, fighting back tears after another trophy chance slipped away. "I think this is best for everyone."
Fortunately for Argentina, Messi would have second thoughts.
Over the subsequent 10 years, he completed one of football's greatest ever stories. But it was a decade of dominance that almost never happened.
Since that retirement U-turn, Messi has played a further 94 times and scored another 70 goals for Argentina. He has lifted four major trophies.
The six-week period between his June 2016 retirement declaration and the 12 August announcement he would play on for the "love of the country" could be considered the most significant in Argentine football history - even in world football.
- Messi retires from Argentina duty with 'nothing left to give' 
  - Published3 hours ago
- Goals, records, tears ... Messi's most iconic moments 
  - Published1 hour ago
'He lacks the character to be a leader'
As Messi departs the international stage, words of criticism 10 years ago from the country's other legendary number 10 seem almost laughable.
"He's a really good person, but he has no personality," Diego Maradona said just weeks before Messi's first retirement. "He lacks the character to be a leader."
Back then it was the comparison with Maradona that was held against him. Yet Messi had already won eight La Liga titles and four Champions Leagues with Barcelona and was a five-time Ballon d'Or winner, and not yet 30.
Maradona's club career hadn't come close, but Messi's only major international honour had been Olympic gold at the 2008 Games. Maradona had almost single-handedly won the 1986 World Cup for Argentina.
It's hard to imagine it now, with Messi shirts dominating the last two World Cups, the Argentina team being built completely around him and the nation's fans worshipping him to an almost religious extent – but, back then, there was a lot of criticism.
"He's not as good as Diego", "he goes missing on the big occasion", "he is part of the country's failure". All accusations that were thrown in his direction.
This wasn't the first time Messi had considered walking away either.
Spanish football expert – and Messi biographer – Guillem Balague said: "Leo goes really down when he loses. He felt the pressure of being the captain of Argentina and the Maradona thing.
"Pecho Frio, people in Argentina called him, which means cold chest. It was an insult to say he had milk in his veins. So when he failed in 2016 at the Copa America, that was the third time – the first time in public – he had decided to leave the national side.
"The two previous ones was a matter of letting him lick his wounds, but this one he came out and said I've had enough. He sometimes cannot help himself as he says what he thinks."
The Maradona versus Messi debate is now surely over. Messi is Argentina's greatest, by most judgements. There are many who will say he is challenging Pele for the title of football's greatest ever.
A campaign, a statue and many apologies
Even people who criticised Messi eventually said sorry.
From the moment Messi quit his country, shockwaves reverberated around Argentina.
Yes, he had lost in four successive finals. But he was also the country's record goalscorer and the world's best player.
The 'Get Messi back' campaign started immediately as team-mates called for him to change his mind just minutes after his announcement.
"I can't imagine a national team without Messi," said goalkeeper Sergio Romero.
The social hashtag #NoTeVayasMessi (Don't go Messi) was used more than 20,000 times within 24 hours.
By that time, Argentina's President Mauricio Macri had already spoken with Messi over the phone to try to convince the Barcelona star to reconsider.
"I told him not to pay any attention to the comments being made because, in truth, we are very happy" with the job he has done," Macri told journalists at the time.
Less than a day later, the mayor of Buenos Aires, Horacio Rodriguez Larreta, had unveiled a statue in Messi's honour and called on the public to show him their love.
"As a football fan, Leo, I am asking you to please reconsider your decision," the mayor said.
Thousands of fans gathered in central Buenos Aires, while street signs throughout the capital displayed implored Messi to play on for Argentina.
Maradona stated Messi had to stay to take the team to the 2018 World Cup.
'It reminded us how much we loved him'
Edgardo Bauza became Argentina coach in August 2016, replacing Gerardo Martino after the Copa America failure. He lasted just eight months – but maybe his first few days were his most important.
The first thing he did was travel to Barcelona to persuade Messi to change his mind. The huge clamour for Messi to return proved irresistible.
"I love this country and this shirt too much," Messi said as he returned to the international fold.
"I'm grateful to all the people who wanted me to continue playing with Argentina. Hopefully we can give them something to cheer about soon."
Still, success didn't come instantly. In 2018, Argentina fell to France in the last 16 of the World Cup and many wrote off Messi's chances of ever lifting the trophy.
Quite incredibly, Messi did not win a senior international tournament until the age of 34 - and then he went on to win four in barely three years, including the 2022 Finalissima.
Questions about his international future were raised after each of those triumphs, but he played on to his sixth World Cup in 2026 where he scored eight goals and registered four assists en route to Argentina's defeat by Spain in the final.
He was strolling through games, lacking the speed of years gone by, but somehow proving every bit as effective.
The final took place in the same stadium where Messi 'retired' a decade earlier.
"When Messi retired [10 years ago] it reminded us all how much we loved him," said Argentina fan Benjamin who was in the Metlife for the 2016 showpiece final.
"When I heard him retire, I cried, the country cried. He did get criticism but only because everyone cared so much. Without Lionel Messi, Argentina would still be waiting for their next World Cup since 1986."
Messi's footballing future became a matter of fresh doubt after the death of his father Jorge just three weeks after this year's World Cup final.
This decision seems final and, at 39, another return to international football looks unlikely.
But South American football writer Tim Vickery said an official farewell in Argentina could be on the cards.
"Remember that, as a result of their behaviour at the World Cup, the next game Argentina play on home soil will only be in front of a crowd at 50% capacity," Vickery told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"But once those punishments are out of the way, I'm sure it will be in the mind of the Argentina FA: 'Why don't we hold a game back in Buenos Aires? River Plate, they have the biggest capacity in South America. Why don't we do an official farewell there? What do you think about it, Lionel? One last time?'."

Why are there so few African players in the WSL?
- Published
Plenty of talent was on show during the Women's Africa Cup of Nations this month - but why do so few players from the continent play for clubs in England?
The Women's Super League is widely regarded as one of the best leagues in the world and Europe's top talent is flooding in.
Two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas joined London City Lionesses this summer - the latest figure from Spain's World Cup-winning squad to move to the WSL.
It follows past high-profile moves from foreign players, including Australia captain Sam Kerr who made 158 appearances for Chelsea before joining Gotham.
Some of the United States' biggest stars are in the WSL too, including Chelsea duo Alyssa Thompson and Naomi Girma, Arsenal's Emily Fox and Manchester City's Sam Coffey.
There has also been an influx of Asian talent in recent seasons, with Japan captain Yui Hasegawa becoming one of the WSL's best players at Manchester City.
BBC Sport explores why the WSL has just four African players - Chiamaka Nnadozie (Brighton and Nigeria), Aisha Masaka (Brighton and Tanzania), Rofiat Imuran (London City Lionesses and Nigeria) and Ines Belloumou (West Ham and Algeria).
- Why Michaely Bihina is the keeper making waves at Wafcon 
  - Published5 days ago
- Cameroon claim first Wafcon title with victory over Malawi 
  - Published4 days ago
- African quartet secure Women's World Cup places 
  - Published9 August
Where are Africa's biggest stars?
The small representation in the WSL is not because of a lack of talent in Africa.
National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) clubs in America have shown huge interest, spending big money on some of the continent's best players.
Zambia forward Racheal Kundananji became the most expensive women's footballer at the time in 2024 when she joined Bay FC from Madrid CFF for £685,000.
Her compatriot Barbra Banda, who plays for Orlando Pride, was voted the BBC Women's Footballer of the Year in the same year.
Cameroon's Wafcon player of the tournament Monique Ngock is at Washington Spirit, where six African international players currently reside.
Temwa Chawinga won the NWSL Golden Boot and Most Valuable Player awards in her first two seasons with Kansas City Current.
Her sister, Malawi captain Tabitha Chawinga, plays for European giants Lyon and helped her country reach the final of Wafcon last week, where they lost to Cameroon.
Michaely Bihina, who was a standout performer in the tournament for Cameroon, plays for Benfica.
Nnadozie, who notably became the first African goalkeeper to be shortlisted for the Women's Ballon d'Or award, joined Brighton last year. The Seagulls goalkeeper ended her season with an FA Cup final appearance at Wembley against WSL champions Manchester City.
What are some of the barriers?
A major barrier for WSL clubs hoping to sign African talent is the Governing Body Endorsement (GBE) criteria set out in the league's registration rules.
Foreign players must earn a minimum number of points in five categories to be eligible for a GBE visa.
The number of caps they have for their national team, appearances in the Women's Champions League and the ranking of their former clubs play a part.
WSL sides also have to compete with the wages and transfer fees being offered by NWSL clubs, who are targeting the best African footballers.
They have to use resources for scouting which, at the moment, is prioritised across Europe.
Another major issue is the lack of coverage given to the domestic game in Africa, as well as issues around Wafcon.
There was confusion in this edition when the Confederation of African Football (CAF) named Channel 4 as the UK broadcast partner, but no matches were shown live in the opening round as an agreement had not been formally reached.
The tournament had also been postponed just 12 days before it was set to kick off in Morocco, eventually taking place three months later.
Switzerland captain Lia Walti, who signed for Brighton this summer, told BBC Sport that, globally, coverage of women's football has room for improvement.
"I think you have to bring the game to the people. You kind of have to force people to watch it. I felt that was how it maybe started in England," she said.
"In a lot of other countries I think they have bad coverage. It's not shown at all, or if it's shown, from where they film the game [makes it look] really poor.
"It affects the way you watch a game. You don't really see the speed, the tactics or anything and you don't enjoy watching the game."
- What we learned from Wafcon 2026 
  - Published3 days ago
'Africa shouldn't be left behind'
Malawi's magical route to the Wafcon final ensured they will play in the Women's World Cup for the first time next year, alongside champions Cameroon, and semi-finalists Algeria and Morocco.
Tabitha Chawinga believed the Malawi side put their nation on the map and showed their quality.
Speaking to BBC's World Service following their final defeat by Cameroon, the Malawi captain said: "It's really the best. No-one gave Malawi a chance to be in the finals, no-one gave Cameroon a chance to be in the finals.
"But as you can see, we watched fantastic football. There was amazing football from both sides."
Nigeria goalkeeper Nnadozie paved the way in the WSL last year with her move to Brighton.
She told BBC Sport in October her Ballon d'Or nomination made a "big impact" in Africa and put the spotlight on some of the continent's best talent.
"We have so many good players and they just need the opportunity to show what they can really do," she said.
"Very soon, we will have more numbers [in the Ballon d'Or nominations] from Africa. Trust me, there are so many good talents from Africa.
"Some players have had the opportunity to come to Europe but some have stayed back home. I hope in the future, bigger competitions will come to Africa.
"The Under-17s World Cup is in Morocco. This is big evidence that they are doing a lot of great jobs over there. It is just a matter of time.
"Women's football is rising and Africa shouldn't be left behind."

Trump’s new mass deportation target
The Trump administration is going after Haitian immigrants after ending deportation protections.
After ending legal protections for 350,000 Haitians living in the United States, the Trump administration is ramping up its efforts to deport them back to a country engulfed in violence — and bragging about it.
“Those with terminated TPS are in our nation Illegally,” the Department of Homeland Security X account posted on Thursday evening, alongside a video of chained Haitian immigrants set to cheery music. “They have two options: LEAVE IMMEDIATELY or be DEPORTED.”
Temporary protected status (TPS) is extended to immigrants for whom conflict, natural disaster, or another catastrophe means returning home would be unsafe, and Haiti certainly qualifies: The island nation has been in crisis since its president was assassinated in 2021, with armed gangs controlling most of the capital city; earlier this week, dozens were killed and kidnapped near the capital.
Despite all that, the administration first attempted to end TPS protections for Haitians living in the US last year, and succeeded after the Supreme Court gave its blessing in June.
Now, it’s sending them back to a country where the State Department warns Americans not to travel “for any reason” because of “crime, terrorism, kidnapping, unrest, and limited health care.” On Thursday, that effort included a deportation flight carrying families with young children born in the US.
Trump’s indiscriminate, record-breaking immigration crackdown
Haitian immigrants in the US aren’t the only people whom Immigrations and Customs Enforcement is targeting more aggressively. According to immigration data released this week by the Deportation Data Project at UC Berkeley and UCLA, ICE arrested a record number of people in two consecutive months this summer: first 43,000 in June, then nearly 50,000 last month.
As arrests surge, who’s being targeted is changing, too. More and more ICE arrestees don’t have a criminal record; in July, immigrants with only civil immigration violations made up a majority of arrests. Often, they also have active immigration cases pursuing asylum, a green card, or some other legal status, as the Seattle Times reported this week.
Overall, ICE detentions are also rising again, though they’re still lower than they were at the start of the year.
The pace of arrests reflects ICE’s growing size — 29,000 employees in June, according to the New York Times, compared to 21,000 in January 2025 — as well as its glut of cash after Trump’s reconciliation bill forked over $75 billion to the agency last year.
Nonetheless, the agency still wants more: As the New York Times reported in July, its internal target for arrests is 2,000 per day. That would mean a record of at least 60,000 people per month, the majority likely guilty of no crime at all.

As climate change intensifies, melting glaciers — such as those found in the Himalayas — can cause this scale of catastrophic flooding.

7 die, 5 injured as bus collides head-on with truck in Assam: Police
According to the investigating officer Dhiren Saika Sonowal, the bus carried 14 passengers including a driver and a helper
At least seven persons died and five others were injured on Sunday after a bus carrying them collided head-on with a goods truck on National Highway-27 in Assam’s Kamrup Metro district, police said.
According to the police, the incident happened in the Sonapur-Khetri area on the outskirts of Guwahati city on Sunday evening. Police said that three persons died on the spot while around nine injured people were shifted to Guwahati Medical College and Hospital (GMCH), four of them later succumbed during treatment.
The deceased have been identified as Prashanta Talukdar (34), Anima Deka Bordoli (32) and Gopal Das (46) of Morigaon, and Insan Ali Sheikh (54), Tafajul Ali (53), Jutika Ronghang (46) and Idris Ali (42) of Kamrup district, police said.
“The accident took place at Nalagedera-Tetelia under Khetri police station in Kamrup Metropolitan district and as per the preliminary investigation, the passenger-carrying bus was heading towards Guwahati from Nagaon when it hit a goods truck after losing control,” police said.
According to the investigating officer Dhiren Saika Sonowal, the bus carried 14 passengers including a driver and a helper, both of whom died on the spot. However, the police found 12 persons during the rescue operations. “We found 12 persons, seven of whom died and five are now undergoing treatment. We believe some people who were sitting at the back of the vehicle managed to leave the spot on their own,” the officer said.
As per the locals, the bus hit a large pothole on the highway before it crashed into the truck coming from the opposite side.
“It was so massive that the front part of the vehicle was completely mangled, and the rescue team had to cut open portions of the damaged vehicle to pull out the passengers,” a local resident said.
The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Traffic), Guwahati, Safiqul Hussain said the bus lost control and crossed the divider before hitting the truck. The truck driver also managed to flee the accident site, police are looking for him. Police are examining the reason behind this, including the claim that it happened because of a pothole.
Police said no occupant of the goods truck was injured in the collision.
Officers said that the bodies have been sent for postmortem and the family members of the identified persons have been contacted.
The incident triggered anger among locals and a group of protesters blocked NH-27 on Monday morning, alleging that accidents caused by potholes on the highway have become a regular occurrence and the local administration has been ignoring the matter.
Chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma on Monday visited the spot and said the state government would provide compensation of ₹5 lakh to the family of each deceased person.
He wrote on X, “The tragic accident at Khetri has left us anguished. My heartfelt condolences to the bereaved families.”
He said the issue concerning the condition of the road was being examined and the Chief Secretary of Assam will consult the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) on the matter.
“We have conveyed our concerns to NHAI and sought corrective action. If anyone is responsible, appropriate actions will be taken,” he said.
Kamrup Metropolitan deputy commissioner Swapneel Paul on Monday held a meeting at the Guwahati police commissioner’s office in Khanapara with representatives of the NHAI, police, district administration, elected representatives and local residents.
Following the meeting, NHAI agreed to repair all potholes along the Khanapara-Sonapur stretch within seven days. Paul said the administration had heard concerns from all sides before fixing the deadline.
“We have given NHAI a seven-day timeline to repair all potholes along the stretch from Khanapara through Sonapur to NH-37 in Kamrup (Metro) and they have agreed to comply,” Paul said.
NHAI official Abhishek Kumar said repair work will be completed within the stipulated period and that an investigation and legal action would be initiated against contractors connected with the stretch.
“We have also terminated our site engineer and have requested the administration to take legal action against the contractors and the respective agencies,” Kumar said.
A committee has been constituted to monitor the repair work and submit its report to the Deputy Commissioner by September 8.
Paul said that a special meeting of the District Road Safety Committee has also been scheduled at the Dimoria Co-District Commissioner’s office on September 3 to exclusively discuss safety concerns along the Sonapur highway stretch.

₹28.87 crore rice scam? CBI books 8 over diversion of subsidised grain
The CBI has booked eight people over an alleged Rs 28.87 crore subsidised rice diversion racket involving FCI and NERAMAC officials. The FIR alleges rice meant for vulnerable groups was routed through private traders in violation of OMSS rules.
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has booked eight people, including senior officials of the Food Corporation of India (FCI) and North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Ltd (NERAMAC), over an alleged Rs 28.87 crore rice diversion racket involving the distribution of subsidised grain.
According to an FIR registered on August 27, the agency has alleged a criminal conspiracy between public servants and private traders to obtain rice at concessional rates in violation of the government's Open Market Sale Scheme (Domestic), or OMSS(D). The alleged arrangement could have caused a potential loss of Rs 28.87 crore to the FCI, the agency said.
The case centres on the allocation of 62,000 metric tonnes (MT) of rice by the FCI's Delhi Region to NERAMAC between April 13 and May 15, 2026. Of this quantity, around 50,645 MT was actually released, according to the FIR. The CBI alleges that the rice was lifted from FCI depots by traders instead of reaching the vulnerable groups for whom the subsidised grain was purportedly intended. The traders allegedly sold the rice onwards to other traders for "huge profits".
Rs 28.87 CRORE ALLEGED LOSS TO FCI
The alleged financial loss forms a central part of the CBI's case. The agency estimates that the FCI could have earned an additional Rs 28.87 crore if approximately 50,645 MT of rice had been sold through e-auction at the applicable reserve price of Rs 28,900 per MT, instead of being released at the concessional rate of Rs 23,200 per MT.
The FIR also raises questions over NERAMAC's eligibility to receive rice without an e-auction under the OMSS(D) 2025-26 policy. According to the CBI, NERAMAC, despite being a Central government-owned enterprise, was not eligible for such an allocation. The agency said the policy permitted allocations without e-auction to state governments and their corporations.
Despite this, FCI's Delhi Region allegedly continued processing and approving NERAMAC's proposal. The FIR names then FCI Delhi Region General Manager Kunhiraman Padmini Asha, then AGM (Sales) Brahm Prakash and then Manager (Sales) Amarendra Vikram.
The CBI alleges that the officials handled the proposal with "undue haste" and failed to properly examine whether the allocation complied with the OMSS(D) policy. It further alleges that the General Manager continued approving the allocation and release of rice despite the alleged violation.
NERAMAC allegedly appointed three private entities -- Utapalakshi Agro Products Pvt Ltd, Dibesh Commercials Pvt Ltd and Super Grains -- as channel partners. The agency alleges that Rajesh Bajaj and Pankaj Saraf subsequently approached traders in the Delhi-NCR region and facilitated the lifting of rice from FCI depots.
According to the FIR, traders deposited Rs 23.25 per kg into NERAMAC's bank account, while the private entities allegedly received commissions ranging from 64 paise to Rs 2.50 per kg.
The CBI alleges that the rice was subsequently diverted from its stated beneficiaries, including daily wage earners, labourers and migrant workers. Instead, it was lifted from FCI depots at Ghevra, Mayapuri and Narela and sold to other traders for "huge profits". The agency further alleges that bogus date-wise charts were maintained in NERAMAC records to create the appearance that the rice had been distributed through retail outlets in Delhi and Noida. Antedated appointment letters were also allegedly prepared to show the appointment of 23 sub-distributors.
EIGHT PEOPLE NAMED IN FIR
The eight people named as accused in the FIR include senior officials of both FCI and NERAMAC, as well as representatives of the private entities involved in the alleged distribution chain.
They include Kunhiraman Padmini Asha, then General Manager of FCI Delhi Region; Brahm Prakash, then AGM (Sales) at the FCI Delhi Region; and Amarendra Vikram, then Manager (Sales) at the FCI Delhi Region. From NERAMAC, the accused include then Managing Director Bhaskar Barua, then Additional General Manager Anjal Kumar Dutta and then Deputy Manager (Agri-Business) Dilip Saha.
The FIR also names Rajesh Bajaj, Director of Utapalakshi Agro Products and Dibesh Commercials, and Pankaj Saraf, partner of Super Grains. The agency has also named unknown public servants and other unknown persons in connection with the alleged conspiracy.
HOW THE RACKET UNFOLDED
According to the CBI, NERAMAC Additional General Manager Anjal Kumar Dutta initially sought an allocation of 31,000 MT of rice per week from the Delhi government. The proposal reportedly said the rice would be sold at affordable rates to vulnerable sections of society. The Delhi government subsequently forwarded the proposal to the FCI.
The CBI alleges that NERAMAC then entered into memorandums of understanding with three private entities as channel partners. The MoUs allegedly claimed that NERAMAC had authority to procure and distribute rice under the OMSS(D).
However, the FIR says the FCI had not provided such authorisation.
The agency alleges that the arrangement ultimately resulted in thousands of tonnes of subsidised rice being routed through private traders instead of being distributed to the beneficiaries identified in the proposal. The allegations are part of the CBI's FIR and will be subject to investigation and further legal proceedings.

Milo Yiannopoulos, a British national known for his near-constant reinventions as a vizier within far-right American politics for more than a decade, has been detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Louisiana, according to the department’s records.
While it’s not clear which detention facility Yiannopoulos is currently being held in, the ICE directory instructs any family or legal representatives to contact the Enforcement and Removal Office in Alexandria, Louisiana, a processing center for the central part of the state, about 200 miles from New Orleans.
In an emailed statement, a spokesperson from the US Department of Homeland Security says that Yiannopoulos legally entered the country through New York City in May 2019. “He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” the statement says. “Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing.” The DHS spokesperson says Yiannopoulos was detained on Thursday, August 27 and that “he will remain in ICE custody pending removal.”
TMZ first broke the news of Yiannopoulos’ detention. He has previously lived and worked in the US, allegedly on an O-1 visa, which is for individuals with extraordinary abilities in the arts, sciences, and other areas, including journalism—but he has never been a US citizen.
Yiannopoulos got his start in US politics at the right-wing website Breitbart, where he worked from 2014 to 2017. He left the job after his remarks about sexual intercourse between adults and young adolescent boys, which he said could be “perfectly consensual,” resulted in a backlash. He has dipped in and out of right-wing circles for years, and in 2022 claimed to have arranged an infamous 2022 dinner with Kanye West, white nationalist Nick Fuentes, and Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago “to make Trump’s life miserable.”
Yiannopoulos married his long-term boyfriend in Hawaii in 2017 but in 2021 claimed he had become heterosexual and Roman Catholic, and announced plans to open a gay conversion therapy facility in Florida. He went on to work with Fuentes as well as former US representative Marjorie Taylor Greene.
Yiannopoulos also serves as spokesman for Kanye West, who is scheduled to perform at the Caesars Superdome in New Orleans on Friday night as part of his 2026 tour. The longtime provocateur joined West’s theoretical 2024 presidential campaign in late 2022, but walked away days after the rapper espoused Nazi beliefs and praised Adolf Hitler on conspiracist Alex Jones’ Infowars livestream. The two continually reunited and split over the following years, with Yiannopoulis claiming in a series of X posts in 2024 that West was addicted to nitrous oxide.
Throughout his evolution as a MAGA figure, Yiannopoulos has rarely shied away from highly public battles with enemies and rivals. Among the most outspoken is the Islamophobic conspiracy theorist Laura Loomer, who on Friday pinned a post on X announcing his detention by ICE—and appeared to take partial credit for it.
“I was the first person to report on the fact that Milo was in the US illegally where he incited violence against President Trump and worked for Marjorie Traitor Greene,” Loomer wrote. “Milo is going to be deported back to the UK where he can live among the Muslims he has recently chosen to embrace. Today is a great day for America.”
Last summer, Yiannopoulos endorsed a hardline anti-immigration stance on his own X account. “There is one concrete thing we must insist on this administration delivering,” he wrote. “We have got to deport millions and millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters.”

Good Good has seen major fallout from an ad with Callaway that critics say promoted violence against women — but creator economy insiders say there's a road to recovery.
Last week, Callaway cut ties with Good Good, Dick's Sporting Goods pulled its products from shelves, and the YouTube golf group stepped back from its title sponsorship of a fall PGA Tour event. A person close to Good Good said two people from marketing were fired.
So, just how bad is the situation?
"We're going to remember this for years," said Joe Perello, CEO of Props, a creator marketing company. "They have a long road ahead of them to establish relationships with big manufacturers like Callaway and retailers." He added that other up-and-coming golf brands are waiting to take Good Good's place.
The diversified business that had made Good Good a creator success story — and helped it raise $45 million last year — also exposed it to outside partners who didn't have the appetite to weather bad news.
There could be other shoes still to drop, said Chris Erwin, founder of RockWater, an M&A and strategy advisory firm for the creator economy. For example, Good Good has a partnership with Dude Perfect, aimed at gaining a foothold with younger viewers, that could be at risk.
Still, Erwin and others said all isn't lost for the brand. Good Good has a war chest, more than 2 million subscribers, and — ironically — a fresh wave of attention after the scandal. It also has a new president, who could help steady the ship.
The channel could double down on its core audience with paid subscriptions, direct-sold products, and live events while it recovers.
"It's a moment to show who they are," Erwin said. "If they do that, and advertising comes back, it could be a better business."
Good Good had a brand-friendly image and had rolled out a campaign, "There's More to Golf," earlier this year to promote inclusivity and reach new audiences. This ad scandal could severely hamper its efforts to grow its female viewership. Zappi, a consumer market research company, found a sharp gender divide in its ad scoring, with women at least twice as likely as men to feel negatively toward Good Good and Callaway after seeing the promo.
Good Good could shift its branding and adopt a more "outlaw" persona. Or, it could use humor to redeem itself, Perello said.
Self-deprecating humor is "the fastest pathway back to redemption," he said. "My advice would be, make hay of this and put yourself at the butt of the joke."
What about the rest of the creator economy?
Creator economy insiders said influencer marketing is too entrenched in the CMO playbook for companies to hit pause because of a single incident like the Good Good backlash.
That said, it could cause some marketers to ensure they have ad-approval systems in place to prevent a similar situation from happening to them.
"It could prompt some brands and their agencies to reassess where they draw the line between creative freedom and oversight, with greater scrutiny of creators and more checks around creative sign-off," said Ben Woods, head of creator economy at Enders Analysis.
There has been a push-and-pull for years between brands and creators over how much control each should have.
Ultimately, that could mean influencer marketing gets a bit more boring — at least temporarily — as some marketers tighten up the freedom they give creators.
"Creator content will become less authentic," Perello said. "There'll be an overcorrection."
No one who spoke with Business Insider expected it to have any lasting damage on the rise of influencer marketing, however. US advertisers are expected to spend $44 billion on creator marketing in 2026 — up about 18% from 2025, according to a report from the Interactive Advertising Bureau.

New South Wales police have appealed for information to find the mother of a newborn baby boy, whose body was discovered in a rubbish bin in Auburn in Sydney’s south-west on Monday morning.
Police said emergency services responded to reports of the body of a baby located in a rubbish bin at a unit block along Harrow Road in Auburn at 11.20am, with officers from the Auburn police area command finding the body of a newborn boy.
Acting superintendent of the Auburn area police command, Darren Sly, told reporters that the baby’s body was discovered by a local resident putting out the rubbish.
The baby was unclothed and was in a plastic rubbish bag, Sly said.
“It’s a sad set of circumstances,” Sly said.
“Our number one priority and our number one concern is that of the mother.”
A crime scene has been established and detectives have commenced an investigation into the incident.
Police said they hold “serious concerns” for the welfare of the baby’s mother, and have urged the mother to attend the nearest hospital to receive urgent care.
Sly told 2GB radio it was believed the baby was born in the past 36 hours, but the body will need to be examined more thoroughly.
Anyone with more information about the incident, or who was in the area at the time and may have dashcam or mobile footage relevant to the incident, are urged to contact Auburn police station or Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.
Sly said police were door-knocking in the area and looking for CCTV.
“All the small bits of information can obviously piece together to hopefully track down this mother,” he said.
“I appeal to the mother to come forward, to go immediately to your closest hospital and seek treatment.”

Lahore, Aug 30: Pakistan's human rights body has said the state resorted to “disproportionate use of force” against protesters in the PoK and raised serious questions about the credibility of the electoral process marred with violence and allegations of massive rigging.
A report by the fact finding mission of the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) released on Saturday attributed the unrest in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) to longstanding political and socio-economic grievances, institutional distrust and governance deficits.
“An increasingly confrontational state response, including the disproportionate use of force has further deepened polarisation and eroded public trust,” the HRCP said and added its mission received sharply conflicting accounts about the scale of violence and the conduct of security forces.
Elections to 45 seats to the so-called PoK legislative assembly were held in three phases from July 27 to August 10.
The banned Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), which had been holding a series of protests in PoK since June over the contentious 12 refugee seats, has alleged that the establishment manoeuvres these seats to install a prime minister, to lead the so-called government in PoK, of its choosing.
After negotiations between the government and JAAC failed on May 30, the Kashmir government proscribed the organisation on June 5 under an anti-terrorism act.
According to the JAAC, over 40 people were killed during the first phase of polls held on July 27. Besides, it claims that some 400 protesters have been killed since the first week of June, a claim refuted by the federal government.
The HRCP expressed particular concern at the allegations of “lethal and excessive” use of force against protesters and said it received multiple accounts from families, alleging that a number of protesters had been killed or seriously injured by the security forces. The Kashmir police chief had reported around 38 security personnel killed since June, it added.
“We could not independently establish the full scale or circumstances of civilian casualties, particularly because the team was unable to access Rawalakot, one of the main centres of violence,” the commission said and called for an independent and impartial investigation into all deaths and serious injuries since June, including “whether the use of force was lawful, necessary and proportionate.”
The report also raised concerns at the government’s use of anti-terrorism and preventive-detention provisions against political activists.
“Heavy deployment of security personnel, prolonged communications restrictions, boycott by major political actors, phased polling and postponement of seven constituencies raised wider questions about the credibility of the electoral process,” the HRCP report said about the polls in PoK.
India maintains that the entire Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh are its integral and inalienable parts. New Delhi also asserts that Pakistan has been in “illegal and forcible occupation” of parts of these Union Territories.
India on August 4 described the so-called local body elections in PoK a “complete farce,” asserting that such “hollow” exercises cannot hide the ground reality in the region.
The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) strongly criticised Pakistan's crackdown on protesters in PoK and said the international community should see through the “flimsy veneer” of Islamabad's “hypocritical lecturing” on human rights.
“This so-called local election in PoK is a complete farce. The real happening is that of public protests and wanton killings by Pakistani forces. Such hollow exercises cannot hide reality,” MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at a regular media briefing.
The HRCP report called for independent review of cases against protesters, activists, journalists and political workers, with cases withdrawn where individuals had been detained or prosecuted solely for peaceful political activity or lawful assembly.
It also chided restrictions on journalism and access to information, saying journalists had faced arrests, legal action, restrictions on access to affected areas and special security requirements while the prolonged communications shutdown severely constrained independent reporting and verification of deaths, injuries, arrests and alleged electoral irregularities.
“The communications shutdown went far beyond political activity, disrupting banking, education, commerce, transport, public administration and healthcare,” it said.
There are 53 seats in the so-called PoK legislative assembly - 45 are directly elected, while eight are reserved for women, technocrats and clerics.
Elections to seven of the 45 directly elected seats - five in Poonch district and two in Sudhnoti district - could not be held due to law and order situation.
The 38 members elected directly participated in the elections of eight reserved seats.
Prime Minister Shebaz Sharif led Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) now has 31 of the current 46 seats while its coalition partner at the federal level, the Pakistan People's Party (PPP) has 14 seats. A lone Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party winning member has also allied with the PML-N.
PML-N's Barrister Iftikhar Gillani, who was defeated by a PPP candidate in Muzaffarabad-III general election but later got elected on a technocrat seat, has been elected as the Prime Minister of PoK.
The PML-N, particularly its founding chair Nawaz Sharif, is facing immense criticism from all quarters, including his party members, for selecting a defeated candidate to head the government in PoK.

South Africa hold off All Blacks fightback to level series

'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series - second Test
South Africa (24) 33
Tries: Kriel, De Allende, Kolisi Cons: Kolbe 3 Pens: Kolbe 4

World champions South Africa delivered a powerful first-half performance as they edged past New Zealand and levelled 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series at 1-1 with two Tests to play.
The All Blacks travelled to Cape Town knowing a win would write them into the history books as the first New Zealand team to win back-to-back Tests in South Africa since the 'Incomparables' of 1996.
But South Africa dominated the basics and showed a more clinical edge this week, even though the lively All Blacks again outscored them on the try count by four to three.
New Zealand's fightback ultimately came too late, captain Ardie Savea barging over on 77 minutes to get the game within a score, but on the All Blacks' final attack Boks replacement Cameron Hanekom won a superb turnover that settled the nervy closing stages.
As he did last week, Springboks wing Cheslin Kolbe took on the kicking duties over fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, notching up 18 points in a player-of-the-match performance.
The first series in 30 years between these two mighty rugby nations is shaping into an epic, with the third Test back at altitude in Soweto, Johannesburg next Saturday.
Erasmus team tricks
The Springbok team that took the field at the Cape Town Stadium was markedly different to the one originally named by head coach Rassie Erasmus on Monday.
Fly-half Handre Pollard was fit and then injured and withdrawn in the week, while Kolbe was injured and then fit and eventually named on the wing.
On top of that, Erasmus switched around his whole front row in the hours before kick-off, with the starting trio dropping to the bench and vice-versa.
It meant there were five changes in all from the matchday squad announced on Monday and surely would have had the New Zealand management thumbing through the regulations of the tour agreement.
Boklash comes early
Despite producing a famous rearguard effort in the first-Test victory at Ellis Park, New Zealand boss Dave Rennie warned in the week his side would need to "go deeper" to cope with the inevitable Springbok backlash.
That South African onslaught came from the off.
Hooker Deon Fourie, at nearly 40 the oldest Springbok in history, found his target in the line-out, the South African maul powered into the 22, and lightning fast ball led to centre Jesse Kriel crashing over.
Kolbe added the extras as the world champions made the dream start.
But despite the fast start from the hosts, New Zealand grew into the contest, with referee Angus Gardner, himself a late call-up in place of Nika Amashukeli, presiding over a fast and fluent game.
Damian McKenzie made a clean break which almost put in Will Jordan, and while the Boks killed the ball from the ensuing breakdown, Eben Etzebeth got up to spoil New Zealand's five-metre line-out.
Despite their set-piece issues, the All Blacks came again. Intricate handling freed Jordan, who used his pace and strength to escape down the right and link with the outstanding Cam Roigard. Ruben Love levelled the scores from bang in front.
That score lit a fire in the Springboks, with Kolbe kicking a penalty and Damian de Allende barrelling over after another imposing maul as South Africa showed far more ruthlessness compared to a week ago.
With the Springboks dominating in the basics, the crowd in Cape Town smelt blood as the lead stretched to 17-7.
But with ball in hand, Rennie's crop are reminiscent of the great All Blacks side of old. Savea burst forward from a line-out, and perfect passing gave McKenzie a walk-in.
At 17-14 edging towards half-time the contest was in the balance, before a match-defining sequence just before the interval.
Kolbe forced a five-metre scrum, before which Erasmus brought on two of his strongest scrummagers in Malcolm Marx and Ox Nche, who immediately won a penalty.
From there, another scrum, another penalty advantage, and with the All Blacks back-pedalling captain Siya Kolisi crashed over for South Africa's third try and a 10-point lead after a pulsating first 40.
Boks withstand All Blacks fightback
New Zealand needed to score first in the second half, and they didn't, losing the ball when in Bok territory and then giving away a soft penalty which Kolbe kicked.
The All Blacks were on the ropes, Marx won a breakdown penalty, and Kolbe stretched the lead to 16 points with half an hour to go.
With the second half lacking the fireworks of the first, the All Blacks backs – led by Roigard - desperately tried to drag New Zealand back into the match.
After another McKenzie break led to nothing, some more beautiful handling resulted in Leroy Carter scampering into the left corner, a fabulous finish.
More excellent attacking play released Jordan down the right, and the recycled ball found skipper Savea, who crashed over to cut the gap to seven points with two minutes remaining.
But the Springboks held on, despite lock Lood de Jager being sent to the sin-bin for a high tackle.
Fittingly, it was a breakdown penalty that settled the game, with Hanekom winning the crucial turnover in an area South Africa dominated.
The All Blacks' impressive win in the first Test had temporarily shot them above South Africa in the world rankings, something Erasmus urged his side to rectify.
That they did, and with normal service resumed in the eyes of the Springboks supporters, South Africa travel back to the Highveld with the momentum.
But the All Blacks have played some wonderful rugby in the first two Tests, and will still believe they can join the legends of 1996.
The eyes of the rugby world now turn to Soweto.

Alpharetta, a prosperous suburb of Atlanta, Georgia, is home to about 67,000 people, served by about 120 local police officers. It also hosts several dozen cameras sold by Flock Safety, the increasingly controversial surveillance company that collects license plate data and other information and makes it searchable by police.
Data captured by those Flock cameras, WIRED has learned via public records requests, is accessible to more than 2,000 police departments, colleges, airports, and government agencies across the United States. These range from Morehouse College to Florida’s Fish and Wildlife Commission and include Medicare fraud investigators in Illinois, a drug task force focused on east-central Missouri, and the inspector general of a federal agency.
In return, Alpharetta receives Flock data from more than 1,300 entities, which span from the prosecutor’s office of Whitley County, Indiana, to the Metro Police Authority of Genesee County, Michigan.
The Alpharetta Police Department—which, as reported by WIRED, had an officer resign due to Flock misuse on August 5—also exchanges Flock data with several agencies that have been similarly rocked by recent incidents of officers misusing its technology, including Georgia’s Bibb County Sheriff’s Department, the Savannah Police Department, and the Dallas Police Department.
Alpharetta’s data-sharing network has expanded tremendously over the past year. Since June 2025, the number of entities receiving data from Alpharetta police has grown by about 42 percent, and the number of entities sending data to them has grown by about 125 percent. And, according to documents obtained via public records requests from several other cities around the country, Alpharetta is far from alone in having an expansive and complicated data-sharing system, providing a potent example of how pervasive Flock’s surveillance network has become.
One of Flock’s central selling points is its network of customers—mostly, though not entirely, law enforcement agencies. If a criminal suspect crosses city, county, or perhaps state lines, Flock tells its customers, a query can prevent them from falling through the cracks.
Data sharing across agencies is hardly novel. A police department can, for instance, share data from its automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) with state-run fusion centers, which centralize resources from law enforcement agencies in particular regions. They could also share it with a regional High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area (HIDTA) program. (Alpharetta police agreed to do just that in 2025, according to a memorandum of understanding that WIRED obtained.)
Whereas HIDTAs are federally funded public programs, Flock is a private company that manages a sprawling, interconnected ALPR network governed by rules and restrictions that vary wildly from city to city. And if police departments don’t closely supervise their settings for data requests and sharing within Flock’s interface, they can unwittingly become nodes in a much larger surveillance network than they necessarily know or understand.
This can lead to situations like that in Alpharetta, where citizens and visitors are embedded in a data-sharing network that has propagated to more than 2,300 nodes. So, how does it happen?
Setting Boundaries
To understand how cities like Alpharetta can build such expansive data-sharing networks with Flock, it’s important to understand how Flock’s interface actually works.
WIRED analyzed a cache of files on Flock’s website that are served by its login pages to anyone who loads them. Some of the code that WIRED analyzed illustrates what a Flock administrator might see in their own Flock interface—specifically, in their settings and sharing preferences.
An administrator can automatically share their agency’s Flock data with any organization within a custom radius, within their home state, or within one or more other states. Alternatively, they can individually choose organizations to share data with.
Administrators can also limit specific data that other organizations can receive, like live or archived videos. They can also limit which organizations can ask them for data. They could restrict this, for instance, to organizations based in the same state, or within a 50-mile radius.
Lieutenant Jason Hiott of the Alpharetta Police Department tells WIRED that per the city’s Flock settings, the department will “automatically approve” requests for its Flock data from law enforcement agencies within 500 miles. If they’re outside that radius, the police department has to individually request access to Alpharetta’s data.
Hiott was unable to say what the Alpharetta police department’s default settings were, whether it altered the default settings, or how long the radius has been set to 500 miles—though he did note that the department “does not share any live feeds, analytics, etc. with anyone.”
Flock spokesperson Jess Montejano claims that data sharing is turned off by default for new and onboarding customers—so no law enforcement agencies automatically get access to another agency’s data. Flock did not specify whether that has always been the case.
Paris Lewbel, another Flock spokesperson, adds that “historically,” its customers have been able to request data from other customers that are within the same state, or within 50 miles—the precursor to actually sharing data.
Coast-to-Coast
Flock’s network settings allow agencies to set specific limits on what Flock data it shares and receives, but in some cases, police departments have been caught off guard by how expansive the search settings were for their officers.
Often, the confusion has been tied to Flock’s Nationwide lookup tool, which the company introduced in 2021 and is available to customers that opt in, according to the company. It allows any Flock customer to query any other Flock customer in the country, as long as they have a specific license plate. (Flock disabled the tool for federal agencies following backlash to the company’s pilot program with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.) In several cases, Flock customers had no idea this tool was enabled.

|---|
| Are you a current or former police officer, government official, or Flock Safety employee who wants to talk about the company? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporters securely on Signal at carolinehaskins.61. | 
Chris Shook is the city attorney in Reynoldsburg, Ohio, where two officers recently resigned after the police department probed their alleged misuse of Flock’s technology. He tells WIRED that in June, the city’s police department made an unexpected discovery while attempting to complete a public records request: Per the department’s Flock settings, the Nationwide lookup tool was active. Police leadership, however, had been under the impression that officers could only search cameras within Ohio.
Shook says that the police department immediately changed the settings to enable only in-state camera searches. But they had no idea when, or why, nationwide searches may have been enabled. Lacking answers, Shook turned to Flock.
According to emails reviewed by WIRED, Flock customer success manager Caroline Bush could only say that Nationwide lookup “was enabled at some point before February 2025.” Due to an “event-log limitation” prior to that month, she could not say exactly when. But she added that, upon checking the police department’s audit, she “found nationwide searches as early as 03/2023.”
This came as a surprise to Shook. If nationwide search was enabled, he said, there must have been an error, “but we are unsure of how that error could have occurred.”
“The most likely explanation is that the setting was enabled during initial account setup or onboarding,” Bush replied. She said Nationwide lookup “was a common default configuration for agencies at that time, before Flock introduced stronger in-product disclosures and tighter controls around this feature.”
In California, the Palo Alto Police Department had a similar experience. In a city council “study session” led by city manager Ed Shikada on June 1, he claimed that Flock activated Nationwide lookup “for all customers” in mid-2023. Flock says this is a “false claim,” based on research that found “agencies across the country that have never been in the Nationwide Network including in the state of California.”
Notably, California law forbids sharing ALPR data with federal or out-of-state law enforcement. Shikada said that Flock quietly “disabled” Nationwide lookup for Palo Alto police in October 2024, and for all California law enforcement by March 2025.
However, Shikada said Palo Alto police didn't know Nationwide lookup had ever been active until December 2025.
Meanwhile, Commander David Hart of Minnesota’s Beltrami County Sheriff’s Office tells WIRED that while his office didn’t have a debacle with the Nationwide lookup tool, he had to reel in the permissions that were set up when the county started using Flock in early 2024.
For the first few months, his officers could send and receive data requests to any Flock customer in the country. But toward the end of 2024, Hart says, he limited outgoing and incoming data requests to in-state agencies. No data requests are approved automatically. (Minnesota’s ALPR statute sets specific standards that agencies must meet before capturing or receiving ALPR data.) Hart tells WIRED that on principle, he doesn’t believe in using Flock casually for wide-ranging searches.
“It’s gotten to the point where people want to search more agencies just to be able to search more agencies, without a real reason behind it,” Hart says.
When examining Flock audit logs, it’s not always obvious why an officer would want or need to expand the scope of their search.
WIRED filed a public records request to the Reynoldsburg Police Department and received 549 pages that log every Flock query its officers made from January 2024 through April 2026. The records show that even from query to query, the number of probed Flock networks can vary significantly.
On January 1, 2025, for instance, a Reynoldsburg police officer queried 53 Flock networks. The officer’s “reason” for the search, according to the log, was a potential criminal offense coded “30.” Just 40 minutes later, the same officer cited the same criminal offense code but, for reasons the log does not specify, instead queried 5,392 Flock networks. Similar examples appear regularly throughout the log, though most of the searches WIRED reviewed had probed fewer than 100 networks.
Flock users, as illustrated in a recent video on the company’s YouTube channel, can customize the number of networks they want to probe in a single query. A police officer can probe every single camera network their department has access to—or they can limit their search to their state, or simply their own jurisdiction. That decision is left up to the officer.
“The particular officer can narrow the networks they want to search, but typically they don't,” Shook tells WIRED. “Typically, they search every network they have access to.”
Mixed Company
Alpharetta’s Flock data-sharing network shows that it sends data to and receives it from agencies that, along with being geographically distant, are a far cry from the local police departments and county sheriff offices that represent Flock’s prototypical customers.
It’s often unclear, outside of a fluke circumstance, what the agencies would gain from exchanging data.
For instance, it’s not obvious why the Office of Inspector General for the federal General Services Administration, Region G of the Alabama Drug Enforcement Task Force, or the University of North Texas’ Denton campus police would need to have a mutual exchange of Flock data with the police department of Alpharetta, Georgia. (None of these agencies responded to requests for comment.)
WIRED contacted more than a dozen agencies sending or receiving data with the Alpharetta Police that are neither a police department nor a sheriff’s office, and most did not respond to requests for comment. Just one answered specific questions about its use of Flock: Kentucky’s Louisville Regional Airport Authority, a nearly seven-hour drive from Alpharetta.
Natalie Ciresi Chaudoin, the airport authority’s director of public relations, tells WIRED that the Louisville Regional Airport Authority has 13 Flock cameras across its properties. She says that the airport shares data from its cameras with 2,240 federal, state, and local agencies across the country and receives data from 1,124 agencies.
Chaudoin adds that the airport’s Flock settings are configured to “automatically accept a request for data-sharing with in-state law enforcement agencies, while out-of-state agencies’ requests are manually accepted or declined following their review.”
When asked about Alpharetta, Chaudoin says that the airport was “aware that it received data from an agency” in the city. The airport has not shared its data in return.
Limiting Factors
Twenty-four states, as well as Washington, DC, have statutes covering ALPR use. The regulations they impose differ widely from state to state, with some being quite specific: Since 2023, it’s been illegal for law enforcement in Illinois to use ALPR data in criminal cases related to immigration or abortion.
The effects of California’s restrictions are visible in records obtained via public records request from the Northern California Regional Intelligence Center (NCRIC), which are published publicly on Muckrock, a public records request facilitator. According to the records, the fusion center shares and receives data from fewer than 400 agencies—a fraction of the agencies in Alpharetta’s network—and they’re all based in California. However, that fact alone doesn’t paint the whole picture.
According to an audit of searches run on the NCRIC’s Flock network, NCRIC member agencies ran more than 57,000 Flock queries in the single month between November 26 and December 26, 2025. Many of the queries probed thousands of Flock networks, and more than 96 percent of them probed at least 100.
In other words, the scope of the NCRIC queries tended to be significantly larger than those of the Reynoldsburg Police Department—the police department in a state with no ALPR statute, where officers had access to the Nationwide lookup tool until June and from which two officers recently resigned due to allegedly misusing Flock.
On August 13, Flock announced a set of changes to how its software works, seemingly in response to a surge in news coverage about police officers misusing the technology. The company said that it is now “recommending a 7-day ALPR data retention period,” a reduction from 30 days. But Flock customers can pay for extended data retention, according to documents obtained via a public records request from St. Petersburg, Florida.
Flock also says that law enforcement can’t run a Flock search without entering a criminal case code and that by the end of the year, all customers must activate its Audit Assistance tool, which scans for “defined criteria for abnormal behavior” and “automatically” suspends Flock access if detected.
In Alpharetta, according to Lieutenant Hiott, police chief Trent Lindgren learned about the Audit Assistance tool in July and promptly activated it. By July 20, the department had opened an investigation into one of its officers. On August 5, the officer resigned.

Jury hears closing arguments in Tupac Shakur murder trial
Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis, 63, faces life in prison without parole if he is convicted of involvement in the 1996 murder
A jury heard closing arguments on Monday in the trial of a former Los Angeles gang leader accused of involvement in the sensational murder three decades ago of chart-topping rapper Tupac Shakur.
Duane “Keffe D” Davis, 63, a one-time leader of the South Side Compton Crips, is accused of ordering the September 7, 1996 killing after his nephew had been beaten by members of Shakur’s entourage in Las Vegas.
“Duane Davis, in the culture of gangs, could not let that stand,” prosecutor Binu Palal said. “So what did he do? He acquired a firearm, got his group together, and went hunting for Mr Shakur.”
Palal was the first to address his closing arguments to the jury in a Las Vegas courtroom and will be followed by Michael Sanft, the defence lawyer for Davis.
Shakur, who was in Las Vegas for a Mike Tyson fight, was shot about two hours after the confrontation by a gunman in a white Cadillac that pulled up at a red light alongside the BMW in which the rapper was travelling in the front passenger seat.
According to prosecutors, Davis handed the gun to someone sitting in the back seat of the Cadillac and ordered that person to shoot Shakur, who died six days later.
The driver of the BMW, Death Row Records co-founder Marion “Suge” Knight, was wounded.

Google updates maps to show Lake America in the U.S. — but Canadians are now seeing it, too Google says website developers must set their region to Canada for 'Lake Ontario' to appear on map Some Canadian websites, including for the federal government, displayed maps with Lake Ontario renamed as Lake America on Sunday, a day after Google Maps announced the change to align with an executive order by U.S. President Donald Trump. The search giant said in a Saturday post on its corporate website that it made the change because the U.S. government's geographic names database has formally renamed the lake. Google said the change would only affect U.S. users, but a number of websites for Ontario and Canadian entities appeared to display Lake America on maps. Among them were Hydro One's outage map, the Liquor Control Board of Ontario's (LCBO's) store locator, GO Transit's station finder and the federal government's housing and infrastructure map. "We are aware that Lake Ontario is being incorrectly labeled on our outage map," a spokesperson told CBC News in an email, adding that Hydro One regrets the "error." "The issue originates from a third-party mapping service," the utility said. "We are working with our vendor to correct the issue as quickly as possible and restore the proper geographic reference." Metrolinx, an Ontario government agency that owns GO Transit, said in a separate email to CBC News that it is aware of the issue. "We are actively reviewing our websites to make sure they all identify Lake Ontario by its correct name: Lake Ontario," Metrolinx said. "We are in the process of disabling the map function on the GO stations' page where this occurred." By late afternoon on Sunday, the GO Transit map in question had been disabled, and the LCBO map had been changed to again show Lake Ontario. MapQuest, a U.S. online mapping service, has posted on social media that it would not change the lake's name, while Apple has not publicly commented on the matter. In a statement Sunday night, Google said website developers who embed Google Maps on their sites can select a region to localize the map. That determines how place names are displayed on sites, the company said. "'Lake Ontario' will show when developers have set their region to Canada," the statement said. APIs behind the confusion: tech expert Tech analyst and journalist Carmi Levy said although websites like Hydro One's and the LCBO's are Canadian, their maps are likely powered by Google's application programming interface (API). APIs are not location-aware, so all maps powered by Google API have switched to Lake America. "Even if it's a government website or a government app or government digital service, it will show as Lake America in Canada because we're stuck using an American technology to power it under the surface," Levy told CBC News. Companies and government organizations use third-party APIs rather than developing their own mapping software. Google Maps itself provides results based on a user's location, so people within Canada's borders should still see Lake Ontario — even if they type Lake America. Levy said Google has updated its search index globally, "so that Lake America is now searchable no matter where you live." On Sunday evening, Google's pin — a red, teardrop-shaped marker — was showing up as Lake America in at least some Canadian searches when either name was typed in the search bar. Zoomed in closer, however, the map still said Lake Ontario. The name change highlights the cost of Canada not having its own Google Maps equivalent or mapping APIs, Levy said, leaving a huge portion of online activity powered and collected by American companies. "In many cases, that data is sitting on an American server. I'm screwed if the government decides to put limits on that or starts to scrape that data for whatever purpose, wants to use it against me the next time I decide to cross the border," Levy said. "The fact that we aren't more digitally sovereign, we are today seeing a very high-profile example of what that costs us as Canadians." Stephen Crawford, Ontario's minister of public and business service delivery and procurement, acknowledged the issue on social media and said the provincial government is "actively reviewing our websites" to make sure they identify Lake Ontario as such. Some Ontario government agency websites pull map data directly from Google Maps. Following recent changes by Google, we're actively reviewing our websites to make sure they all identify Lake Ontario by its correct name: Lake Ontario

Delhi Police tells SC it ‘no longer wishes to pursue’ 13 FIRs from NEET protests in July
Earlier in the day, the Centre had filed an application before the top court to quash the FIRs against the NEET protesters.
Delhi Police on Monday evening told the Supreme Court that it "no longer wishes to pursue" 13 FIRs from the Cockroach Janta Party-led NEET protests in July, invoking Article 142 over the matter.
Delhi Police stated that the Centre, on July 25, 2026, decided to move away from prosecuting the broader protest FIRs, which cover rioting, attempt to murder, and property damage, and instead decided to narrow its focus.
In its application, filed on behalf of the Union government, the police said that they would not register any further FIRs in connection with the protests between July 20 and July 25. The plea is likely to come up before a bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Tuesday.

The move comes days before the proposed September 5 protest march announced by the CJP from India Gate to the Delhi Police headquarters, with withdrawal of FIRs against student protesters being one of the principal demands of the group.
The Supreme Court earlier on Monday declined to interfere with the proposed march, leaving the question of law-and-order arrangements to the Centre and Delhi government. The court, however, expressed confidence that all stakeholders would act peacefully and within the legal framework.
Single fresh FIR against those with 'serious criminal antecedents: Police
The Delhi Police told Supreme Court that a single fresh FIR would be filed against against 2,873 persons who were prima facie found to have “serious criminal antecedents.”
The application said the new FIR would be in conformity with the court’s clarification on “criminal antecedents” in its previous order. “The investigation is required to ascertain their role, if any, in the commission of offences relating to bodily harm or destruction of property at the said protests,” it stated.
The Delhi Police said that their probe will focus only on people's role in violence and damage, informing the top court that remaining protesters booked across the 13 FIRs are “effectively let off.”
Its affidavit also states that no further FIRs will be filed for these incidents hereafter. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta mentioned the application before the CJI and sought an early hearing, saying the Centre was seeking to resolve the issue concerning the FIRs.
