New Delhi, Aug 31: The All India Muslim Personal Law Board on Monday announced a nationwide "people's movement" to protect the "Constitution and Sharia (Islamic law)", under which it would organise public meetings and protest programmes in major cities across the country.
The All India Muslim Personal Law Board (AIMPLB) said it will prepare and disseminate a comprehensive white paper documenting incidents of discrimination against Muslims, constitutional violations, and human rights abuses to the media, human rights organisations, intellectuals, elected representatives, and relevant institutions.
It said the "Movement for the Protection of the Constitution and Sharia" is not a movement of any particular community or section but a shared national struggle to safeguard the Constitution of India, the supremacy of democracy, the rule of law, religious freedom, human dignity, national unity, peace and fraternity.
"We firmly believe that justice, love, dialogue, mutual respect and constitutional struggle are the true guarantees of India's peaceful future. With this conviction, we invite every justice-loving, democratic and peace-loving citizen of the country, every social and religious organisation, and every responsible member of civil society to join this movement," the Board members said at a press conference.
The Board said over the past several years, conditions have continuously emerged in the country in which vulnerable and marginalised sections, particularly Muslims, have been subjected to severe pressure, insecurity and discriminatory treatment at religious, social, political and economic levels.
"Mob violence, extra-legal bulldozer demolitions, targeting of mosques, madrasas and shrines, illegal occupation of Waqf properties and graveyards, arbitrary arrests of Muslim youth under baseless cases, interference with religious freedom, attempts to undermine Muslim Personal Law through the Uniform Civil Code (UCC), and attempts to undermine the beliefs of minorities by making the singing of Vande Mataram compulsory, have deepened a sense of insecurity among a large section of the population," the AIMPLB said.
Eminent scholars, religious leaders of different faiths, intellectuals and social and political personalities will address these gatherings, and a protest will be organised in New Delhi, it said.
The Board said it will submit a comprehensive Charter of Demands to the President of India through the Governors in each state and the district administrations in every district.

Meta is testing robots that can plug in cables, reset servers, and handle other tasks inside its data centers, according to several current and former workers familiar with the projects. The ongoing effort, which has not been previously reported, may eventually allow Meta to operate its rapidly expanding data center footprint with fewer humans, keeping labor costs in check as its spending on AI infrastructure soars.
Meta is using robots and related hardware from several different vendors, including Watney Robotics, Kinova, and ABB, according to the same workers, who asked to remain anonymous because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media. Kinova and ABB declined to comment. Watney didn’t respond to requests for comment.
In one experiment, Meta is evaluating whether a Kinova Gen3 robotic arm could be used for power cycling or cutting off electricity to servers. The company is also testing a different robot to swap networking cables. One Meta data center worker estimates that if it’s successful, the bot could replace up to 80 percent of some people’s workloads. “We thought those of us performing the physical tasks were safe for a while, but not anymore,” says the worker. “It’s coming for us all, unfortunately.”
At some facilities, Meta quietly adopted another, relatively simple robot. It looks like a finger—or perhaps a pointy stick—that can press the power button on a Mac Mini or other device to restart it when remotely prompted by a human.
Meta declined to comment on the testing described in this story. Company spokesperson Francis Brennan said in a statement that Meta is investing heavily in training and hiring workers to build and operate its data centers. “America is in the middle of its biggest infrastructure boom since World War II, and there’s a major shortage of skilled workers to fill the roles; we need more workers, not fewer,” he said.
But at a conference last year, Eric Xu, senior manager for robotics at Meta, said the company’s “long-term goals” are to put robots in data centers, arguing they could speed up incident response, monitor the environment, and handle preventative maintenance. “We believe more collaboration and research will be needed, but we have to start, otherwise we don’t have a chance to do this,” he said.
Until recently, robots largely weren’t well suited for the delicate work happening in data centers. They were expensive, and in earlier trials in the industry they sometimes crushed servers while attempting simple tasks, a person briefed on the experimentation says. But the hardware has gotten cheaper, and the AI models powering robots are now far more capable than they were a few years ago. Several startups are currently working to build commercial robots capable of assembling servers, swapping parts, and replacing wires.
Robots could offer more consistent output at a lower cost than human labor, especially in less populous regions where data centers are plentiful but qualified workers are scarce. Proponents also rally behind a pro-worker message: Like AI agents promise to do for knowledge workers, they argue robots could take on data center technicians’ most repetitive and dangerous tasks while freeing them to focus on more complex challenges. Longer term, getting workers out of the picture could make it more feasible to run data centers underwater, in space, or in other environments potentially inhospitable to living, breathing species.
“More and more of our customers are telling us ‘we want to run our data centers using humanoid [robots]’ because you can run them at higher temperatures, in the dark, and all these things,” says Paul Golding, who oversees so-called physical intelligence at the chipmaker Analog Devices.
The growing use of robots has received little attention from the activists driving a powerful nationwide movement against data centers. Tech companies often tout jobs for humans as an upside to the developments that can be used to justify tax breaks for them. In Altoona, Iowa, Meta operates what is now its largest data center campus, which employs hundreds of workers. The company opened the facility in 2014 and has several years left of a property tax break that allows it to save tens of millions of dollars annually, which the city has viewed as a worthwhile trade-off for having its cachet upped by having Meta jobs.
In Altoona, Meta worker group chats have taken on a demoralized tone, “saying we’re all going to be gone in a few years anyway because of the robots,” a person familiar with the discussions says. Even if adoption of robots proves slower than anticipated, some worry the quality of jobs available is trending downward. Two of the workers say that Meta is developing AI software and other technologies that they believe will allow it to hire lower-skilled—and thus, lower-paid—workers and centralize some roles in areas such as Denver, Colorado, that are more financially advantageous to the company.
“They no longer want people who can think independently, come up with creative solutions, or perform complex troubleshooting,” one Meta data center worker says. “They want ‘smart hands,’ people who are just capable enough to follow AI instructions and not mess anything up.”
Meta contends its need for skilled workers remains robust. This year, the company launched a long-term program to train thousands of people annually from any background in electrical, mechanical, and plumbing work at no cost to them. Meta is even guaranteeing employment in states such as Louisiana, Ohio, Indiana, and Texas for those who complete the training. It also partnered with building trade unions to fund apprenticeship programs.
But as communities rethink data center tax breaks and weigh putting new rules on the industry, the prospect of robots replacing at least some jobs may need to become a bigger concern. Altoona Mayor Dean O’Connor tells WIRED he hasn’t given much thought to robots taking jobs at Meta’s data center, though he frames automation as inevitable. “We will deal with it as it comes,” he says.
Tripping Cables
In a 2023 YouTube video, Meta touted that it was using a self-driving tugger robot to transport heavy server racks within its data centers as well as a wheeled, barcode-reading robot developed in-house to track inventory. The next year, Microsoft and Google unveiled separate investments in robots for their data center operations, and Amazon last year discussed using robots to help recycle parts at its facilities.
Pursuing robotics for “economically valuable tasks,” like “replacing a faulty server rack,” is “absolutely something we’re looking into at Microsoft,” Ashley Llorens, a managing director for the company’s research accelerator, tells WIRED.
Meta’s tugger and inventory robots are now operating in a number of the company’s data centers, including in Iowa and Virginia, according to the people familiar with the projects. They say the robots generally work well, though there are limitations.
The inventory bot is now also being used for failure inspections, but it can’t differentiate between green and red indicator lights on equipment because its camera only detects grayscale, meaning human checks are still required to assess some breakdowns. The device also struggles with corners and traversing the cables that are often in the path of its wheels. Because there aren’t that many of them, the robots need to be moved between buildings, which requires a door-opening human who maneuvers the robot with a remote control.
Two sources also describe the inventory bot as too slow. One says Meta previously explored using drones as a faster alternative, but ultimately didn’t pursue the idea.
Inside the Testbed
The Altoona data center campus is often where Meta prototypes new technologies. “What they do here in Altoona, they take to their other sites and put that in place there,” says O’Connor.
Since last June, Meta has been trying out a pair of dual-armed Watney robots for some cabling work at one of its Altoona buildings, according to one of the people familiar with the company’s efforts. The robots are supervised by humans and can’t work as fast as people yet, but they show promise.
After Watney launched in 2023, it put out a demo of a laundry-folding robot that it claimed could also handle janitorial work inside businesses. The San Francisco startup quietly pivoted to data center robots early last year, according to archived copies of its website.
Meta is testing additional robots in New Albany, Ohio, at the company’s newest data center campus known as Prometheus. Four-wheel robots “with a scissor-lift-style riser and a six-axis arm on top” made by the automation giant ABB are being used there to reseat parts and, eventually, they may take on other tasks with diminishing human oversight, a person familiar with the product says.
But the idea that robots will prevail over humans isn’t guaranteed. “There’s been a lot of pilots and demos, but no provable working solution,” says Helen Oleynikova, CEO of Exclaim Robotics, which is developing prototypes to replace broken parts and reset cables in data centers.
At Meta’s data centers, some workers have complained about the amount of downtime the robots need to recharge their batteries, according to the people familiar with the matter. Meta has also acknowledged internally that robots aren’t equipped for certain tasks, such as the intense cabling work required to run an Nvidia GB300 supercomputer. “Things have been designed for human hands forever to make everything a five-minute repair,” says one former Meta employee. “Redesigning everything will take time.” But the robots are getting prepared.

A devastating flash flood on Wednesday, August 26, near the Nepal-Tibet border, resulted in massive destruction in several districts of Nepal, including Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Gorkha, with over 700 dead and over 2,500 people still missing. Reportedly, a glacial landslide of ice and rock caused the flash floods, which destroyed homes roads, bridges and power plants.
In the days following the catastrophe, social media was rife with video clips showing the extent of devastation — from gigantic waves of floodwater gushing through entire villages, to buildings collapsing, and people being swept away under the debris.
However, Alt News found that a large number of these videos circulating on social media were not authentic. Several of these videos were not from Nepal at all, but drawn from various other calamities which occurred across the world in the last few years.
Clip From 2025 Uttarakhand Floods
An X user, Said Ercan (@saidercan), posted a compilation clip on August 27 showing the havoc wreaked by large flood waves. The first clip shows a torrential river flowing through a mountainous area, and eventually sweeping through the houses on the banks, destroying them in an instant. The post has garnered over 5.8 million views and been reshared over 5,000 times at the time of publishing. (Archive)
To verify whether the video is of the Nepal floods, we broke it down into keyframes and ran a reverse image search. This led us to an Instagram post uploaded by The Times of India, on August 5, 2025, featuring the same footage.
View this post on Instagram
The caption states that the footage is of the Uttarakhand cloudburst havoc. “At least four people have died and many are feared missing after a devastating flash flood triggered by a cloudburst in the upper catchment area of the Kheer Ganga river caused large-scale destruction in Dharali village in Uttarkashi district…,” read the caption.
A Dainik Bhaskar report also features the same video to show the scale of damage caused by the cloudburst in Uttarkashi. We ran relevant keyword searches, and found news reports from sources like Reuters, BBC, Al Jazeera, The Hindu, and others, that corroborated this finding. Thus, the video footage shared by the X user is actually of the 2025 Uttarakhand flash floods, and not of the recent Nepal havoc.
AI-generated Clip
In another instance, X user Ayesha Khan (@Ayesha0Khaan) posted a video clip, of huge waves sweeping away cars, building structures, and people. The clip received over 1 million views. (Archive)
X user Ravi Shankar Singh (@Ravishanka34381) also posted the clip with the same claim. However, we noticed some discrepancies in the video — for instance, around the 0:05 timestamp, a tree log appears out of nowhere in the debris flowing through the floodwater, indicating that the clip could be AI-generated.
We ran the video through Hive’s AI detection tool, which confirmed our suspicion, showing a 99.9% possibility of the video containing AI-generated content.
Clip From 2024 China Incident
News outlet Medya Post (@medya_post) uploaded a clip on X, which showed around 15 people getting swept away by powerful flood waves. The caption stated: “Tourists who wanted to take videos and photos during the flood disaster that occurred in Nepal were swept away by the current and disappeared.” The post had seen massive traction on social media, with over 1.5 million views. (Archive)
Two other X users with the handles (@JMNewsNetwork_) and (@redpillmd) had uploaded the same video, with the former having deleted it after it had been viewed over 45,000 times.
To verify the clip’s authencity, we ran a reverse image search, which led us to an X post, originally uploaded by an user with the handle (@Arab_Storms) on September 8, 2024.
التصوير اصبح اهم من الحياة #شاهد ❗️#الصين جرف المد القوي لنهر تشيانتانج العديد من الزوار الذين كانوا يحاولون التقاط صورة ،،،#Yagi pic.twitter.com/bdiEj7fk9b
— طقس_العالم ⚡️ (@Arab_Storms) September 8, 2024
According to the caption, the video had been taken in China, showing the powerful waves of the Qiantang River overpowering tourists on the shore who were clicking photos. The incident, which occured in the days following Asia’s most powerful storm in 2024, the Super Typhoon Yagi, had also been reported on by The Indian Express, and Newsflare.
Video From West Bengal Landslide
A news outlet TNT Media (@TNT_Media1) posted a clip which showed a mudslide from a vantage point. It also features the narrow escape of some vehicles and people gathered at the spot. The caption, written in Arabic, claims that horrifying scenes correspond to the recent Nepal flash floods. (Archive)
مشاهد مروعة من نيبال.. 😯😯 pic.twitter.com/N7f5jBl4i6
— 𝐓𝐍𝐓 (@TNT_Media1) August 26, 2026
We noticed that the car, visible in parts of the video, bears a number plate whose state code (WB) corresponds with that of West Bengal. Moreover, the recorder of the video, while shooting the clip, speaks in Bengali to warn people to get away from the waves.
A reverse image search on several keyframes of the video led us to this X post, uploaded by The Daily Jagran on August 17.
A biker had a narrow escape after a massive landslide struck the Bindu area of West Bengal’s Kalimpong district. Huge rocks, soil and debris suddenly came crashing onto the road as vehicles passed through.#Kalimpong #Landslide #WestBengal #Biker #ViralVideo #Monsoon pic.twitter.com/HgFLY7Dhjy
— The Daily Jagran (@TheDailyJagran) August 17, 2026
The caption states that the video shows a landslide in the Bindu area of West Bengal’s Kalimpong district, thereby proving that this video clip is not related to the Nepal flash floods.
Compilation Clip From Various Calamities
An X user named “Leonard Sardua $TOR” (@lsardua) posted a compilation of clips showing structures collapsing under the deluge, claiming they showed the devastation caused by the flash flood in Nepal. The clip garnered over 3.3 million views and 3,700 reshares. (Archive)
Two more users, “HadY Azmy” (@HadYAzmy1) and Ahmad Ansari (@Ahmadansari2233), amplified the same clip on August 27. The former video, which has now been deleted, had garnered over than 2.5 million views and over 3,000 reshares.
On running a reverse image search on one keyframe from the viral clip, we were led to an article published by The Times of India on July 21. The report shows the same building structure collapse under the force of floodwater, and states that the video was from the Budgam district of Jammu and Kashmir.
Another segment of the compilation shows a red building being engulfed by the gushing floodwater, sweeping away cars and other structures amid the debris.
Running a reverse image search on this keyframe, we found that the clip could be traced back to a mudslide in Japan’s Atami city from July 2021. An X user with the handle @d_t_dcg_sdh had uploaded several clips showing the mudslide sweeping away houses and vehicles. We also found news reports from Al Jazeera and Spanish news outlet La Nacion, corroborating that the clip was recorded during a mudslide in Japan in 2021.
The same compilation video also included a segment which showed a bridge being torn down by the raging floodwater.
This, we found, was in fact from an incident in Indonesia, showing the collapse of the wooden Molintogupo Bridge, owing to the overflowing of the Bone River. A video uploaded by Newsflare on Dailymotion, notes that the incident occurred on June 11, 2020. It was also reported on by VGTV.
Another segment of the same clip shows two men watching a bridge being dismantled and swept away by floodwater.
We found that this video was from Argentina. A reverse image search on a keyframe led us to this X post by AccuWeather on December 25, 2023, which shows a bridge in Argentina’s Catamarca being blown away by the turbulent floodwater.
A bridge was swept away in Catamarca, Argentina, on Christmas Day, leaving a city completely isolated.  pic.twitter.com/hVdwxmQ7QU
— AccuWeather (@accuweather) December 27, 2023
Another video, showing a white car being dragged along by the torrential flow of mud water, was also part of this compilation.
This, Alt News found, was originally from Islamabad, in Pakistan, dating back to a devastating flood that took place in July 2025.
Similarly, a segment showing a woman overlooking a building structure being swept away by flood water, was also part of this compilation, alleging that it was from Nepal.
A reverse image search proved that the image has existed on X since at least September 2024. On further investigation, we found that it showed the damage caused by Hurricane Helene in North Carolina, United States.
Don’t worry guys, weather modification isn’t real! It’s just a coincidence that Hurricane Helene is one of the most devastating “inland damage storms” in history and that hundreds of pro-Trump counties are being massively impacted during the most important election of our… pic.twitter.com/lyi8YZXB8A
— Matt Wallace (@MattWallace888) September 28, 2024
Another clip showing a submerged bus making its way through the floodwater was also featured in the compilation.
We found that this video was shot during a downpour in Pakistan’s Karachi, which left the city flooded and resulted in at least 16 deaths. Pakistani news media outlet 24 News HD, in their report on the flood dated March 19, used the same clip of the submerged bus.
Thus, the compilation clip uploaded by users “Leonard Sardua $TOR”, “HadY Azmy”, and Ahmad Ansari, with the claim that the footage depicts the havoc in Nepal is fake and misleading. The entire compilation stitches together footage from real calamities, occuring in various other parts of the world in the past few years, to wrongly claim that they are visuals from the Nepal flash floods on August 26.

Novak Djokovic is set to leave the Top 10 in the ATP rankings after eight years following his shocking first-round loss to Mariano Navone at the US Open in New York on Sunday.
The 39-year-old Djokovic, a 24-time Major winner, lost 7-6(5), 5-7, 4-6, 6-2, 6-1 to Argentina’s Navone, ranked 48th in the world, in a match that lasted four hours 36 minutes. This was his first defeat in the opening round of a Grand Slam since the Australian Open in 2006.
Last year, the Serbian, a four-time US Open winner, had made it to the semifinals at Flushing Meadows before losing to Spain’s Carlos Alcaraz, the eventual champion. Following the failure to defend those ranking points this time, he will exit the ATP Top 10 for the first time since 2018.
READ | Novak Djokovic’s US Open exit ends 23-year Grand Slam streak involving Big Three
Djokovic made his top 10 debut in 2007. Ten years later, during the quarterfinals at Wimbledon, he was forced to retire due to an elbow issue. He missed the rest of the season and was pushed out of the top 10 in November. But in 2018, he returned to the top 10 following his fourth title at the grass Major.
Djokovic holds the all-time record for the most weeks (428) spent as world No. 1 in ATP rankings history.
But as per the live rankings, the Serbian has slipped from fifth to 11th spot.
It also means that for the first time since October 2002, none of The Big Three members - Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Djokovic - are in the top 10 of the ATP rankings. Federer, who won 20 Majors, retired in 2022 while Nadal, a 22-time Grand Slam champion, bid farewell to the sport in 2024.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed amendments to the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, to promote ease of doing business. The amendments seek to simplify regulatory requirements, standardise testing fees and facilitate faster market access for eligible medical devices.
The Centre has eased regulatory requirements for medical device manufacturers by removing the need for a separate licence for outsourced sterilisation and expanding the list of countries and regulatory jurisdictions whose approvals can facilitate waiver of clinical investigation requirements in India, a release issued by the Ministry said on Monday (August 24, 2026).
Under the proposed amendment to Rule 44, manufacturers that outsource sterilisation of their medical devices to a facility holding a valid licence under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, will no longer have to obtain a separate loan licence for the sterilisation activity.
Earlier, manufacturers had to secure a separate loan licence even when the outsourced sterilisation facility itself held a valid licence. The government said removing the duplication would reduce paperwork, administrative burden and compliance costs, particularly for manufacturers without their own sterilisation facilities.
However, a traceability requirement has been retained. Manufacturers will have to mention the licence number of the sterilisation facility on the medical device label. A six-month transition period has been provided to allow companies to modify labels, packaging and related processes.
The government said the change was intended to balance regulatory oversight with ease of doing business by retaining traceability while simplifying the licensing framework.
In another change, the amendment to Rule 63 includes the European Union (EU) among the stringent regulatory jurisdictions recognised for waiving clinical investigation requirements for medical devices that do not have predicate devices in India.
The provision already recognises the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada and Japan. With the EU now included, medical devices approved in the EU that meet the eligibility conditions can benefit from the waiver provisions in India.
The move is expected to reduce regulatory timelines for eligible importers and manufacturers and facilitate quicker availability of newer medical technologies to Indian patients.
The amendments follow stakeholder consultations and are part of the government’s broader effort to streamline the regulatory framework for medical devices while maintaining standards for their quality, safety and performance.
The changes are also expected to promote greater international regulatory convergence and improve the competitiveness of India’s medical device industry, the government said.

Thea Frodin once played a young Serena Williams on the big screen. Now, the teenager is ready to follow in the American great's footsteps at the US Open.
Five years ago, Frodin was chosen as a tennis-playing body double for the actress cast as her childhood idol in the Oscar-nominated film 'King Richard'.
That involved the then 12-year-old working alongside actor Will Smith as he portrayed Richard Williams, the father of sisters Serena and Venus.

Now, Frodin will make her main-draw singles debut at her home Grand Slam, where Serena and Venus will this year team up in the doubles.
To make the occasion even more special, she has been drawn against world number two Elena Rybakina, a two-time major winner and the reigning Australian Open champion.
"I'm trying to stay in the moment as much as possible," said Frodin.

Trump pushes Apple to change 'Lake Ontario' to 'Lake America' on its maps

US President Donald Trump has asked tech firm Apple to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America on its Maps platform to comply with his executive order changing the name of the Great Lake, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has said.
Burgum told Fox News on Monday that "the president has reached out to Apple directly", adding: "I'm sure we may be seeing that change coming up soon."
Google made the switch for its US-based users over the weekend, though users in Canada still see the lake, which borders the province of Ontario and the state of New York, as Lake Ontario.
The BBC has contacted Apple for comment.

The renaming has faced pushback in Canada, where one electrical utility company apologised on Sunday for its map displaying the Lake America name.
Hydro One, a utility company based in Toronto, said in a post on X that the name appeared due to their use of a third-party mapping service.
"We are working with our vendor to correct the issue as quickly as possible and restore the proper geographic reference," the company said in its statement. "We regret the error and apologise for any confusion it has caused."
Maps by other Ontario-based agencies also appeared to briefly display the name Lake America, including Hydro Ottawa and the Liquor Board of Ontario.
Trump signed the executive order on Thursday seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, following the collapse of trade negotiations between Canada and the US.
The order directs Burgum to "take all appropriate actions" to rename the lake, including updating the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the official US government map database.
Google said in a statement on Saturday that its maps will display the Lake America name for US users to comply with the GNIS.
It added that those in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario displayed. In the rest of the world, users will see the name displayed as: Lake Ontario (Lake America).
Not all map providers are changing the name. MapQuest, an American free web mapping service launched in 1996, said "we're not changing it" in a short Facebook post on Friday.
The platform also unveiled a tool that allows users to change the lake to any name they choose and share their creations.
After its announcement that it will not be changing the name of Lake Ontario, MapQuest rose to the top of the most-downloaded free applications as of Monday morning on the Apple App Store in Canada.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a large sign by the lakeshore on Saturday that read "Lake Ontario Now and Always" in both English and French, Canada's official languages.
"No one's going to call it Lake of America," Ford told American TV host George Stephanopoulos on Sunday. "It's been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It's going to continue being Lake Ontario."
The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words.

A federal judge on Thursday barred the Trump administration from designating Anthropic a national security risk over a dispute about the use of its AI models, ruling that the designation amounted to unconstitutional retaliation.
The decision handed down by US district judge Rita Lin in California vacated the February 27 decision by defense secretary Pete Hegseth to label Anthropic a “supply-chain risk” and make the company ineligible for federal contracts. The ruling also lifted an additional punitive measure by Hegseth that prevented contractors or suppliers to the US military from doing business with Anthropic, a position Lin called “arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, and otherwise not in accordance with law.”
“Though the Department of War is undisputedly free to select the AI vendor of its choice, the evidence demonstrates that the broad measures imposed on Anthropic were illegal and baseless,” Lin wrote in a 59-page ruling.
The judge also ruled that nine agencies—including the Pentagon, the Treasury Department, the State Department, the Department of Homeland Security—had improperly imposed sanctions on Anthropic. The ruling removes those penalties.
However, Lin affirmed that the Pentagon is not required to use Anthropic’s models, and the ruling does not prevent the Pentagon from electing to simply use other models. A Pentagon spokesperson could not immediately be reached for comment, but the department is expected to appeal.
In a statement, Anthropic spokesperson Danielle Cohen said: “We welcome the court’s ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful. We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security.”
The case stems from a bitter dispute earlier this year between the Pentagon and Anthropic over a $200 million deal to use the AI lab’s Claude models military applications.
The rift began after reports that the US had used Claude in the operation to capture Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro. After the operation, a Palantir employee relayed concerns from an Anthropic staffer to US officials about how its models had been used.

In negotiations, Anthropic insisted on certain limits on how its models could be deployed, including support of lethal autonomous weapons and mass surveillance systems. But Hegseth rejected any curbs, contending that a contractor could not dictate how the technology could be used once deployed and insisted the contract allowed “all lawful use.”
After negotiations broke down in February, Hegseth was widely seen as punishing Anthropic by designating it a “supply chain risk,” a national security tool that blacklisted the company from doing business with the federal government.
The Pentagon said at the time that the supply chain risk label was appropriate because giving Anthropic access to any classified systems would “introduce unacceptable risk” if the AI lab could disable or alter its technology, for instance, at a time of war.
Anthropic filed two lawsuits in response—one in federal district court in California and one at the US court of appeals for the District of Columbia—accusing the Pentagon of violating its First and Fifth Amendment protections on ideological grounds. The DC case is ongoing.
Anthropic’s top AI models are considered some of the best in the world. Separate from the supply chain risk designation, Anthropic's models recently became subject to the Trump administration’s AI oversight framework due to their powerful capabilities.
Lin cited the administration’s involvement in reviewing advanced Anthropic models as part of her ruling. “Even now, the government is discussing collaboration with Anthropic on its new model, Mythos, in an array of sensitive contexts,” she wrote. “None of that is consistent with a genuine fear that Anthropic is a saboteur who would poison its software to harm national security.”

The World Is Telling the Wrong Story About China
The country’s ‘stability’ hides a host of problems.
Compared with Donald Trump’s chaotic, divided, and violent America, China is a bastion of steady progress and serene order. This, at least, is the story that Beijing’s propagandists have been eager to spread. The Global Times, a Communist Party–run news outlet, proclaimed earlier this year that “the world’s peace and development increasingly rely on China’s stability.” The state news agency Xinhua chimed in that “in today’s uncertain world, China’s stability and predictability provide a rare and valuable anchor, which is set to benefit other countries.”
This message appears to be resonating around the world. A Pew Research Center survey of three dozen countries recently found that China is now seen more positively than the United States. Respondents expressed more confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping to “do the right thing” in world affairs than Trump.
China’s stability may appear desirable to a world in turmoil. But inside China, this “stability” looks a lot like policy paralysis, economic stagnation, and intensified political repression. What all the handwringing over China’s growing influence and surging exports fails to recognize is that the country is flatlining politically and economically. The evidence is in plain sight.
Policy makers around the world are understandably fixating on China’s abundant and cheap electric cars and competitive AI models, which present a serious threat to national industries. But these advances are one small part of a broader economy with pernicious and deep-rooted problems. The country’s property-market downturn, triggered by the 2021 meltdown of the real-estate developer Evergrande, has not hit bottom. Home prices continue to fall, eating away at the wealth of many middle-class households.
Trump’s war with Iran has pushed up oil prices, raising the cost of production for Chinese companies and ending three years of deflation. But the underlying problems of oversupply and weak demand remain entrenched. Youth unemployment, which emerged as a major social issue in 2023, has become chronic. The jobless rate among workers aged 16 to 24 stood at 18 percent last month.
These pressures have left Chinese consumers reluctant to spend. Retail sales grew a paltry 0.6 percent in July. Domestic sales of EVs have been falling. China’s economic problems have become so dire that some economists suspect that the official government statistics are overstating the country’s true performance. Although China’s economy has been growing a respectable 5 percent annually for the past three years, the research firm Rhodium Group estimates that China’s actual growth rate was probably near 2 percent in 2023 and closer to 3 percent over the past two years.
Any hope that China’s leaders will tackle these problems is almost certainly misplaced. Xi has stubbornly resisted the difficult and politically sensitive reforms necessary to fix the country’s economic model during his nearly 14 years in charge, and he is unlikely to change his approach anytime soon. He remains as myopically focused as ever on state-led programs to advance Chinese technology and industry, and particularly AI, and is apparently convinced that they will boost the entire economy. Perhaps this strategy will one day pay off, but the signs aren’t good. China’s debt has exploded on Xi’s watch—at three times the size of the economy, it surpasses even America’s debt burden. Growth in the second quarter of 2026 was the slowest since 2022, when China was still battling the coronavirus pandemic.
The Communist Party could theoretically change its leadership team at a major congress next year, but in the absence of any clear alternatives or successors, Xi is likely to secure yet another five-year term as general secretary. Xi’s ruthlessness in office has been marked by regular purges of possible rivals, generals, and members of other party factions. His latest victim appears to be Fang Xinghai, a former top securities regulator well-respected by international business leaders, against whom the party recently launched an investigation for unnamed disciplinary violations. With Fang’s fall, the government is sidelining yet another economic reformer with valuable expertise who might have helped fix the economy’s woes but whose market-oriented philosophy has fallen out of favor with a regime that prefers a top-down approach to national development.
Xi maintains social order through this never-ending malaise by controlling information and repressing alternative views. A sweeping new law took effect last month that mandates Mandarin as the primary language in education and orders parents to guide children to “love the Chinese Communist Party.” In prizing national unity over ethnic autonomy, this policy seems designed to force the country’s various ethnic minorities, including Uyghurs, Tibetans, and Mongolians, to assimilate into the majority Han Chinese culture. Even humor must follow the party line. Local authorities are reportedly investigating Guo Degang, a popular comedian who made the mistake of altering the lyrics of a patriotic song cherished by Communist cadres during a performance in the city of Wuhan last month.
Despite global surveys that report a growing fondness for China, the country’s “stability” comes at a steep cost to other countries. China may not be dropping bombs, but Beijing is arguably helping other countries drop theirs. By economically supporting Iran and Russia, Xi is essentially fighting proxy wars in both Europe and the Middle East.
In the absence of domestic demand, China’s subsidized and bloated manufacturing industries are exporting their problems and threatening the survival of competitors around the world. Given weak sales at home, Chinese automakers are shipping twice as much of their production overseas as they had a year ago. European Union officials are seeking greater powers and enhanced cooperation among its members to protect the continent’s industries from an onslaught of cheap Chinese imports, which have not only cost the region jobs but have run up a trade deficit with China topping $1 billion a day.
As Trump’s unpredictable and self-obsessed decision making saps America’s economic competitiveness and military might, China’s rise on the world stage is destined to continue, if only by default. But Xi’s insistence on preserving stability instead of addressing China’s serious structural problems threatens this ascent. Perhaps, then, the competition between China and the U.S. is less a contest for supremacy than a race to see which country hits bottom first.

Robinson's rhythmical action reminiscent of McGrath - Agnew
- Published
After Ollie Robinson's England debut five years ago I said he was the most natural bowler I have seen.
A lot has gone under the bridge since – he was dropped, recalled, dropped again and is now back - but nothing has changed my mind on that.
Using the word robotic to describe him may give the wrong impression. It is a compliment.
Australia's great bowler Glenn McGrath was like that. Everything was utterly rhythmical, repetitive and perfectly grooved.
Robinson is the same.
As a former bowler I watch and see he has inherent rhythm and such a beautiful action. His wrist is just perfect.
Yes, the conditions this summer, in which he has now taken 23 wickets in three matches after England's win in the second Test at Lord's, have been perfect. Robinson would carry them around in his cricket bag if he could.
But the 32-year-old has performed magnificently in them.
Whatever he has wanted the ball to do – to swing in or out or to wobble off the seam – it has done.
He has not needed to go searching for wickets, instead just letting the ball flow naturally from his fingertips.
He will feel like he could take wickets running in blindfolded. There is no better feeling.

Another thing I admire in Robinson is that he is a really good reader of the game.
Tactically, he is extremely sharp. He can spot a batsman's weakness and interpret that into what it means for his own plans very quickly.
A coach told me when he first came into the side that he was a bowler who would give talks to his team-mates about how to get batsmen out even then.
It all adds to what makes him such a good bowler.
Many people will say Robinson's performances this summer show Ben Stokes, Brendon McCullum and managing director Rob Key were wrong to leave him out of their Ashes squad last winter.
Amid talk of a breakdown in trust between Robinson and the Stokes-McCullum regime, they prioritised bowlers with greater pace.
He probably has lost his way with his fitness at different times but I also think back to bowling coach Jon Lewis calling out his fitness in 2022.
There are times Robinson has not been handled as kindly as he might have been.
Perhaps last winter's omission focused his mind, allowing Joe Root to now reap the rewards.
Robinson can also thank Australia for bringing back into the fashion the age-old tactic of the wicketkeeper standing up to the stumps to pace bowlers.
Alex Carey did it so effectively during the Ashes and England are now copying with Robinson.
It may seem obvious but that tweak is really playing into Robinson's strengths.
If the wicketkeeper was stood back the modern batsman would be walking down the pitch to Robinson. With Jamie Smith up they can't because of the risk of being stumped.
It means Robinson can bowl a yard fuller, giving his deliveries more time to swing through the air and means more of Robinson's deliveries would hit the stumps rather than bouncing over from a shorter length.
Of course, you cannot do any of this without a good wicketkeeper. Praise must also go to Jamie Smith.
After we saw Smith struggle badly through the Ashes, he has clearly improved his glovework. Wicketkeeping coach Sarah Taylor has been working him hard before play with a drill where she whacks tennis balls towards him with a racket.
The ball skids through and, with a batsman stood in front edging, missing and hitting the ball, Smith has to stay low and take them.
The results speaks for themselves.
Now the next question for Robinson is whether he can repeat this success on harder, flatter pitches, or in hot conditions which will test those fitness levels. England will face them in their three-Test series in South Africa this winter.
They have often left Robinson out for Test on more batter-friendly pitches but it is time for them to throw him in. He has earned that right.
England are working behind the scenes to get Robinson into the position where he maintains his pace around 82mph, rather than his current place of starting there before dropping to 77 or 78mph.
If he does that, the extra bounce he will get as a result should negate the loss of movement.
And before then I desperately hope England do not rest Robinson, Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson or Josh Tongue for the third Test in Edgbaston.
England's new quartet has shown real promise. They may not have a frontline spinner but Robinson, who conceded runs at just 1.29 per over across the Lord's Test, can effectively do the holding job of a slow bowler if needed.
Do not break things up now.
After their poor run England just need to keep on winning matches and, just as importantly, this group needs to get used to bowling together as an attack.
Joe Root must also learn how to use each of them best.
This, with Robinson as the leader, is England's best attack. Stick with it in Birmingham and beyond.
Jonathan Agnew was speaking to BBC Sport's Matthew Henry

Conspiracy theories surrounding singer and philanthropist Dolly Parton’s recent death have flooded the internet, referencing everything from satanic rituals to cloning. But one conspiracy theory has dominated all the others: the claim that Parton’s death was caused by “turbo cancer” brought on by the Covid vaccine.
There is no evidence to support the claim that Parton’s death had anything to do with the vaccine. Parton, 80, died after “a short battle with cancer,” her family said in a statement. In May, Parton shared that she was responding well to treatment related to her immune system and digestive system.
In 2020, the singer donated $1 million to fund research in support of the vaccine. The following year, she filmed herself getting the vaccine, singing an adapted version of her hit song Jolene before receiving the shot. “Vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, I'm begging of you, please don't hesitate," Parton sang in a video.
Now, a number of influential right-wing conspiracy theorists and MAGA-aligned pundits have spent the past few days claiming—or, in many cases, suggesting—that the vaccine killed Parton.
“Was Dolly Parton yet another Covid vaccine victim?” far-right radio host Wayne Allyn Root, who recently interviewed President Donald Trump on his show, wrote on X. "She took the vaxx on TV. She changed the name of her hit song 'Jolene Jolene' to 'Vaccine, Vaccine.' She encouraged fans to get it. Now she's dead of cancer. This sounds like another case of 'turbo cancer. RIP Dolly.” (Earlier this month, Root urged Trump to declare a national emergency during the midterms when he had the president on his show. “Let me just say, stranger things have happened, OK?” Trump responded.)
“Dolly Parton thought she was doing the right thing by backing the Moderna mRNA Covid shot,” Toby Rogers, who works with the Brownstone Institute, a think tank founded to oppose Covid restrictions and which has deep ties to the Trump administration, wrote on X. “But it very well may have killed her.” The Brownstone Institute was founded by Jeffrey Tucker, a close ally of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has long undermined trust in a variety of vaccines.
While Kennedy has not commented publicly on Parton’s death, he has spent recent days blaming the Covid lockdowns for measles-related deaths, after the measles-related deaths of two unvaccinated people in Pennsylvania this week.
Valerie Anne Smith, a health influencer with 273,000 followers on X, shared multiple posts about Parton’s death, all of them suggesting that the Covid-19 vaccine was the cause of her death.
“Soon after being injected she developed severe autoimmune, liver and kidney issues,” Smith wrote. “Cause of death ... CANCER.”
“Dolly Parton was as universally beloved as a person can be,” Travis View, cohost of the QAnon Anonymous podcast, tells WIRED. “That’s exactly what made her a target for conspiracists online. Many anti-vaccine conspiracy theorists despised Parton because she not only encouraged others to get the vaccine, she even helped fund vaccine development.”
The conspiracy theories were not limited to X. Facebook was also flooded with wild allegations about Parton’s death, none of which provided any evidence to back up their claims.
One of the most popular themes focused on a video Parton made just weeks before her death in which she thanked pop star Taylor Swift and her husband, NFL star Travis Kelce, for their $2 million donation to Imagination Library, Parton’s childhood literacy charity. She jokingly also asked the couple if she could have their “firstborn” child.
The conspiracy theories focused on a brief moment in the video when Parton was moving her hands. Some social media users claimed that if paused, the video showed her making a “devil horns,” sign. The still image has been posted dozens of times on Facebook in recent days, garnering tens of thousands of likes and shares.
“Nothing to see here, folks, just Dolly Parton—the same woman who dropped $1 million to help fund the Moderna Covid vaccine—flashing devil horns while casually demanding Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s firstborn child,” an anonymous X account named Red Pill USA wrote, adding: “It’s a big Satanic club … and you ain’t in it.” The post has been viewed almost 1 million times.
On YouTube, conspiracy theorist David Nino Rodriguez, who has 613,000 followers, also referenced the Taylor Swift video and dedicated his show on Wednesday to claims that Parton’s death had been prophesied, and that it was a “marker for what comes next.”
“Some of these theories came specifically from her advocacy for the Covid vaccine and gay rights, and they're pretty rare when balanced with the outpouring of love,” Mike Rothschild, an author who writes about conspiracy theories, tells WIRED. “But a lot of what was said about Dolly was just standard-issue brain rot. There is a small part of the internet that now believes nobody dies without some involvement from the Covid vaccine, trafficking, or Satanism.”

It's no exaggeration to say the large language models that power AI bots like ChatGPT and Gemini are changing the world. Many of us are now relying on them for coding, writing, summarizing, and searching the web. Whatever directions AI goes in over the next few years, LLMs will be part of that future.
If you use ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, or any of the other AI platforms, then you're using an LLM. What's less commonly known is that these LLMs can be run locally, on your own computer. The key benefits are offline access and greater privacy, because you're not sending anything to the cloud for anyone else to analyze or review.
You're also not paying any AI companies a monthly subscription or hitting any usage rates. Numerous LLMs are available to download for free, including from big names like Meta and Google. Though they tend not to be as advanced or as speedy as the LLMs inside the apps you have to pay for, they're capable enough for everyday use, and you can pick and choose between them as needed.
There is more maintenance involved here, and you lose some of the convenience that comes with just loading up the ChatGPT app. (You'll need to handle updates yourself, for example.) However, you get a more personalized and private AI system all to yourself, and it's not difficult to get started.
What You Need to Get Started
You can run local LLMs on Windows, macOS, and Linux, though macOS tends to be the preferred platform for most AI enthusiasts. Everything is more unified and consistent on Macs—unlike Windows PCs, only one company makes them—and Apple Silicon chips combine the CPU, GPU, and RAM together, which AI models like.
Whichever platform you go for, having plenty of RAM helps. The bare minimum is 8 GB, though if that’s all you’ve got, you'll be somewhat limited in terms of the size of the LLMs you can run and how fast they'll go. Sixteen gigs is better, and 32 or more is required if you want to use the biggest and fastest models. For the best results, you need plenty of VRAM on a dedicated GPU (anything above 8 GB will make a difference), as this type of memory is optimized for the kind of tasks AI models do.
If you're on Windows, a dedicated Nvidia GPU helps a lot: Graphics chips are better for running AI processes than standard processors, which is partly why Nvidia and the AI boom are so closely interlinked. These dedicated graphics cards will also have their own RAM, which gives AI models extra thinking space.
So while there's no “minimum spec” for running a local LLM, as much RAM as possible and a discrete graphics card will certainly help. You then need a piece of software to run the model (to act as the outer interface), plus the model itself. There are plenty of choices for both, so you can pick and choose as required.
For those getting started, LM Studio Bionic is generally considered to be the best AI app choice on Windows and macOS, and it’s free to use. Other popular and trusted options include vLLM, Llama.cpp, Ollama, and GPT4All, which are again available for multiple operating systems. These pieces of software are a little more technical and involved, though.
With an AI app chosen, the other decision is to settle on an LLM. The software programs we've mentioned will guide you toward some options, and there are also online repositories of models, the most well-known being Hugging Face (which has more than 3 million models available—quite the selection).
An Example Local LLM Setup
A whole host of setups are possible when it comes to local LLMs, but we'll take you step by step through the process of setting up LM Studio Bionic on Windows, to give you an idea of how it works. Once you've downloaded the installation file from the website and have LM Studio Bionic up and running, click Create Project to get started, and give your first project a name.
A blank conversation window opens: If you click Choose a model in the prompt box, then Get local models, you'll be taken to the main model picker for LM Studio Bionic. Each of the available models is listed together with its size, its popularity, and a few details about it—keep an eye out for the staff picks if you want some recommendations to get started with. Smaller models won't be quite as capable, but they will download faster and take up less room on your system.
Back in the chat interface, everything works similar to a standard AI chatbot app. In the prompt box at the bottom you can choose between your AI models (if you have more than one LLM installed), and on the left of the prompt box you've got a + (plus) icon for submitting images and files (if this is supported by the current model).
On the left of the interface is the navigation pane, where you can switch between your projects. Via the Settings link (lower left) on the navigation pane you've got the preferences screen for LM Studio Bionic. There are a bunch of ways to customize the software here, from how deleted chats are handled to the interface elements onscreen.
Click Library in Settings to manage your existing models or the Explore menu entry to find new ones. If you need support for images and documents, look for multimodal models. (Technically, these build on top of the capabilities of an LLM, though they often get called LLMs anyway.)
The final part of the LM Studio interface that is important to know about is the right-hand sidebar, which can be shown or hidden via the button on the very top-right corner. These give you further options for managing files across projects and giving the program access to the file system on your computer, if needed.

The China Masters 2026 gets underway on September 1 in Shenzhen, but India’s contingent at the Super 750 event has been thinned out by a string of withdrawals, with several players pulling out just days after competing at the BWF World Championships in New Delhi.
Ayush Shetty, who produced one of the standout moments of India’s home Worlds campaign, has withdrawn from the men’s singles. The 21-year-old stunned former world champion Shi Yuqi in the opening round, winning a dramatic three-game contest (21-14, 13-21, 21-19) before advancing to the Round of 16. He eventually lost there in straight games to Indonesia’s Alwi Farhan.
P.V. Sindhu has also pulled out of the women’s singles draw. The two-time Olympic medallist opened her home World Championships campaign with a comfortable win over Ireland’s Sophia Noble before beating Canada’s Wen Yu Zhang to reach the pre-quarterfinals. She was then edged out in three games by China’s Wang Zhi Yi.
Malvika Bansod and Aakarshi Kashyap have also withdrawn from the women’s singles field.
With Sindhu and Ayush out, Lakshya Sen and Kidambi Srikanth will lead India’s men’s singles challenge, while Unnati Hooda, Devika Sihag and Tanvi Sharma carry the women’s singles hopes. India’s doubles pairings remain largely intact, with Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty leading the men’s doubles contingent alongside Hariharan Amsakarunan and Arjun MR. India will have no representation in women’s doubles after Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand’s historic bronze medal-winning Worlds campaign.
The withdrawals mean India will have a reduced presence at the Super 750 event. Coming shortly before the Asian Games, the tournament remains an important checkpoint for the remaining Indian players looking to build momentum.

Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets. The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership. Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. “Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership. Building on the momentum, ten new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Of these, Klassroom, SEDEMAC, Kissht, LEAP India and Shiprocket made a bumper debut on the bourses. Nevertheless, the IPO pipeline remains strong. Thirty two startups have already filed their DRHPs with SEBI, while over 24 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO, Razorpay and Zetwerk alone could raise over ₹34,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs. However, recalibration is likely to define 2026 as investors are expected to prioritise strong fundamentals, profitability and low cash burn when backing new-age tech companies. “IPO-bound startups in 2026 will be increasingly defined by their ability to demonstrate predictable cash flows, sustainable unit economics, and operational discipline rather than headline growth alone. Public market investors will place greater emphasis on governance, capital efficiency and long-term value creation, favouring companies that balance scale with financial prudence,” Orios Venture Partners’ managing partner Rehan Yar Khan told Inc42. There are other challenges as well. Average retail subscription levels are moderating, while foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are pulling back in droves, reflecting caution amid geopolitical tensions and muted secondary market performance. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has further complicated the situation. Yet, the overall outlook remains bullish for new-age tech IPOs. Maturing business models, deeper domestic capital pools and an evolving regulatory framework favouring transparency position India as a leading startup IPO hub.
