In mid-2026, some people on social media celebrated a story from the Faroe Islands, a self-governing archipelago north of Scotland.
Apparently, 2026 marked the 10-year anniversary of the time a Faroese woman allegedly strapped cameras on sheep to map the country when Google wouldn't, according to a post on X (archived). The opening of the post read:
Google would not send a Street View car to the Faroe Islands, so in 2016 a Faroese woman strapped a camera to a sheep and mapped the country herself.
The grievance was legitimate. Eighteen islands in the North Atlantic, some of the most spectacular road in Europe, causeways and tunnels and single track cut along the edge of a cliff face, and none of it on Street View. Google had been up Mont Blanc. Google had been to Greenland. Google had been above the Arctic Circle in half a dozen countries. The Faroes had about fifty thousand people and a coastline, and they were simply not on the list.
Durita Dahl Andreassen worked for the tourist board in Tórshavn. Her reasoning was straightforward and, in its way, unanswerable. There are more sheep on the islands than people. They walk freely. They go everywhere. They have no schedule and no other commitments.
So a fellow islander built a harness. Onto it went a 360 degree camera, a mobile phone and a lightweight solar panel to keep the batteries up, the whole rig weighing under a kilo. The camera was set to fire every minute. Five sheep in five locations were fitted out and released to do what they were going to do anyway, which was walk about eating grass on the edge of some of the most photogenic drops in the North Atlantic.
The images came back tagged with GPS coordinates, over a mobile signal, from a sheep. Andreassen uploaded them to Google Maps.
They called it Sheep View 360. Her job title, for a period, was Sheep View 360 Project Manager, which remains one of the finest lines ever printed on a business card.
The one technical hitch, reported by the tourist board with total sincerity, was motivation. The sheep had to be encouraged to go to the interesting bits, which meant somebody standing behind them doing the thing you do to move sheep. The technology worked perfectly. The talent needed direction.
The claim also spread on social media websites such as Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived).
The claim is true. Visit Faroe Islands (archived), the island territory's official tourism board, celebrated the 10-year anniversary of its "Sheep View 360" campaign on July 12, 2016.
Leading the campaign for Visit Faroe Islands was Durita Andreassen, who explained the project in a video on the Visit Faroe Islands Sheep View 360 webpage. The day Visit Faroe Islands launched the campaign, it released a video showing the sheep walking around with the cameras on their backs.
A map from the campaign shows Andreassen's sheep captured images of the Hosvik area. There are three spots near Hosvik on Google Street View in which the Sheep View 360 can still be seen today.
The campaign worked. On Aug. 11, 2016, Google announced it had started working with the Faroe Islands to bring Google Street View coverage to the area.
Just over a year later, Visit Faroe Islands proudly announced that the territory now had Google Street View coverage.
For further reading, Snopes has previously fact-checked claims about sheep, including a miscaptioned photo that incorrectly asserted sheep went through a fence gate that wasn't there.

Noah Wyle and fellow cast members of The Pitt took time out Sunday from depicting the trials of working in a Pittsburgh trauma center for the highs of cruising space in the 23rd century.
Wyle, along with Katherine LaNasa, Taylor Dearden, Fiona Dourif, Shabana Azeez and Ayesha Harris performed a live read of the 1966 pilot script for Star Trek at Retro Reads, the Writers Guild Foundation‘s nifty series that benefits the organization’s writing and mentorship programs.
Attendees at the sold-out event at Highland Park’s The Lodge got to watch Wyle channel Capt. James T. Kirk, while LaNasa took over as Dr. Leonard McCoy and Dearden interpreted Spock in an entertaining read of “The Man Trap.”
“I am nervous to be here because this is such an unbelievably large set of black boots to fill and a lot of people have a lot of reverence for this show and for this character,” Wyle told Deadline before the table read got underway. “So I’m just looking not to offend and hopefully enhance if possible.”
Watch on Deadline
He and his cast members did more than that. Wyle and LaNasa brought down the house with the dated dialogue from the George Clayton Johnson-penned script, which chronicles how the USS Enterprise touched down on a planet where McCoy’s ex Nancy and her husband Robert have been maintaining an archeological research station. Dourif was a hit as the amorous Nancy, who’s really just a shape-shifting creature that craves salt for her survival. Clark Gregg (The Avengers) was a surprise guest who took over as Nancy’s professor husband.
The night kicked off with a read of the “Mudd’s Passion” script from a 1973 episode of Star Trek: The Animated Series. Nathan Fillion (The Rookie) took over as Kirk while D’Arcy Carden (The Good Place) assumed the role of Spock and Adam Arkin played the mad creator of a love potion. Other participants from the night included Iman Vellani (The Marvels), and Paul Scheer and Paul F. Tompkins, both from Star Trek: Lower Decks.
Rod Roddenberry was there to remember his dad, series creator Gene Roddenberry, and pay tribute to both the foundation’s 60th anniversary as well as the 60th anniversary of Star Trek.
“This is a good episode of Star Trek. I don’t think many people claim it as their favorite,” admitted Roddenberry about “The Man Trap.” “But it got the show on the air. I hope these guys go up there and just have fun with it. I like to be serious about Star Trek, but tonight’s not a serious night. Tonight’s a night to celebrate.”
Before the read, Star Trek: Strange New Worlds co-showrunner Henry Alonzo Meyers gifted Wyle with a stuffed Tribble, a replica of the fictional alien species that appeared several times over the course of the series. Wyle immediately recognized the furry critter since he grew up watching Star Trek with his dad.
Wyle also copped to owning a few action figures back in the day. “I had Spock and maybe Bones, but I didn’t have Kirk,” he recalled. “And pretty soon, they lost their clothes and their feet came off, but I did play with them for a while.”
The Retro Reads event was a fundraiser for WGF that was co-sponsored by CBS/Paramount+, and Deadline was the media partner. To purchase a ticket to stream the event, click here.

The Taliban in Afghanistan have launched a diplomatic effort to end their isolation as major regional and international powers show a readiness to engage more closely with the repressive regime despite its systematic human rights abuses.
Five years after the Taliban took power, an increasing number of countries are renewing ties or scaling up diplomatic contacts with the hardline Islamists, who seized power in Kabul in 2021 after 20 years of brutal insurgent warfare.
Campaigners fear that the individual contacts by different countries risk undermining “coherent, consistent” demands for an improvement in human rights in return for any diplomatic concessions.
The United Nations described a recent “cascade of [Taliban] edicts and laws” that have banned women from universities and most employment, denied teenage girls education and imposed strict dress codes. Minorities have been persecuted, while activists and journalists face repression. Afghanistan has become a “graveyard for human rights,” the UN said in March.
India, Qatar, China, Iran and several central Asian states all recently welcomed Taliban officials or opened new channels of communication. Russia, which recognised the Taliban government in Kabul just over a year ago, signed a military cooperation agreement last month. In June, the European Union held talks with Taliban officials in Brussels about returning failed asylum-seekers to Afghanistan. Individual European countries have also deepened their own contacts with Kabul.
“There is no doubt there has been an evolution. The Islamic emirate is now in a confident position. They have realised they are indispensable for regional countries right now and even with Europe and the US they have identified how to engage,” said Shivam Shekhawat, at the Observer Research Foundation in Delhi.
“The Taliban see any kind of contact as a diplomatic win and they have been able to capitalise on that as a sign granting legitimacy to the regime.”
A strict policy of isolation imposed after the Taliban seized power in 2021 towards informal or “de facto” recognition is now fragmenting. Some western commentators have suggested more countries recognise the regime. Others want intensified “back channel” engagement.
“We are not against any engagement … There is a need for engagement even if just for aid agencies to mitigate the ongoing humanitarian crisis but we are worried about the end goal of these contacts and the discussions that are taking place,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.
“There should be a consistent and coherent message from the international community to the Taliban that they will not have any friends if they do not show real progress in terms of the women’s rights and human rights situation … and that is not happening.”
The new contacts stem from a combination of regional security concerns, pressure in the west to reduce illegal immigration and a general recognition that the Taliban are unlikely to be forced from power in the foreseeable future.
The European Commission downplayed its discussions in Brussels with a Taliban delegation, the first such formal encounter since 2021, as merely “technical” and focused on returns, but a Taliban spokesperson claimed it was a historic visit that was a step towards regularising consular relations with EU countries.
The meeting prompted outrage.
“You cannot condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and then announce talks on immigration in the next … The Taliban are telling their constituency back home that they are now accepted by the international community,” said Abbasi.
This year officials from Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan have all visited Kabul or other Afghan cities, seeking trade routes and pipeline deals that would allow their landlocked countries access to seaports or third countries beyond.
India too has moved to reinforce relationships that were frosty after the fall of Kabul to the Taliban in 2021, in part to exploit new tensions between the movement and the Islamist movement’s historic sponsors, Pakistan.
New Delhi secured a sanctions waiver last year so that Amir Khan Muttaqi, the Taliban foreign minister and a veteran official who has spent decades at the heart of the movement, could travel there.
In June, India’s UN envoy suggested a rethink was necessary on sanctions, such as travel bans, asset freezes and arms embargoes, that target dozens of Taliban members.
“The political reality of Afghanistan has changed in the last five years, and the current UN sanctions regime must take that into account,” said Harish Parvathaneni.
Afghan authorities’ diplomatic strategy has involved hosting envoys in Kabul, including those from China, Japan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Last year, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, made the first visit by an Iranian foreign minister to Kabul for almost a decade.
The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan “seeks relations with all countries”, Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said, though “the countries of the region and our neighbouring states have particular importance, because our economic ties and interests are closely linked”.
Anna Borshchevskaya, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute focusing on Russia’s policy towards the Middle East, said Moscow had multiple reasons for recognising the Taliban regime and seeking closer relations.
“One likely objective is simply having allies … Afghanistan is also very significant for Russia geographically and Russia just wants influence in that part of the world. There was an opening and they were able to take it,” Borshchevskaya said.
“It’s a very cold, cynical calculation. It’s part of a very simple zero-sum view that for Russia to win the US has to lose. From the Kremlin perspective, this is a global battle and whether you are looking at Europe or Afghanistan or wherever, it’s one geopolitical chessboard.”
Britain has said it pursues a policy of “limited and pragmatic” engagement with Taliban officials, largely through the UK Mission to Afghanistan based at the British embassy in Qatar. Discreet meetings with the Taliban have also repeatedly been held by other western countries in Qatar. In Germany and at least four other western European capitals, key consulates are now controlled by the Taliban, not representatives of the former Afghan government.
Taliban officials have also sought cross-border infrastructure projects to boost the country’s fragile economy and diplomacy. Natural resources are another lure for overseas powers. Kabul has expanded the mining sector, attracting firms from neighbouring China and elsewhere.
China, which is worried about Islamic militancy on and around its south-western borders, has welcomed Taliban officials in recent years, and hosted talks when Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war earlier this year.
The Taliban are split, with deep disagreements on the ban on women’s education among other issues, but remain dominated by the most conservative factions. Recent laws have further reinforced repression, designating many religious minorities, including Shia Muslims, as heretics and imposing strict punishments to silence dissent.
Other new laws recognise only “excessive” beating as domestic violence against women and facilitate the marriage of girls without their consent. 
Analysts do not believe the Taliban are likely to moderate their position in the near future and point to the continuing authority of Hibatullah Akhundzada, the reclusive and authoritarian cleric leader.
Ramin Mansoori, a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Endowment who studies Afghan politics, said the Taliban’s priority was its domestic agenda.
“They are not going to make any significant concessions. Most of them don’t have an international perspective,” Mansoori said.

Cole Hosack vanished from Dawson Creek, B.C. in 2023. Does this man know what happened to him?
Man tied to local drug trade heard discussing what happened the night Hosack went missing
New evidence, including a potential confession, has been uncovered in an investigation by the CBC's the fifth estate into the suspicious disappearance of a man in northern British Columbia.
Cole Hosack vanished on New Year's Eve in 2023 after leaving a bar in the town of Dawson Creek, 1,200 kilometres north of Vancouver.
The investigation is part of a CBC podcast. The Mile Zero Murders, released as part of the CBC's Uncover series, is the result of a two-year investigation into a cluster of disappearances and killings in the community with a population of 13,000.
Fifteen people have been killed or gone missing over the last five years, nine of them in 2023 alone, including Hosack. The RCMP have said they believe Hosack is no longer alive.
Episode 5 of the podcast, which is available Monday, includes an interview with a confidential source who describes overhearing a conversation with a man admitting to a role in Hosack's disappearance on the night he went missing.
"He openly admitted in front of a bunch of people that he had a big part in Cole Hosack's disappearance and that it was an accident," the source told the fifth estate. We are protecting the identity of the source over fears for his safety.
The man the source overheard confessing is 29-year-old local resident Matt Lawton, who other sources say is connected to the drug trade in Dawson Creek.
"[Lawton] openly kind of admitted that they had picked [Hosack] up and the fact that he owed them for drugs," the source said.
When approached by the fifth estate, Lawton denied any involvement in Hosack's disappearance, saying he wasn't familiar with the name Cole Hosack.
"I don't know who that is," he told podcast host and fifth estate producer Timothy Sawa, who explained Hosack went missing while visiting Dawson Creek in 2023.
"I have no clue," Lawton said.
Hosack's story made national headlines in 2024.
At the time, he was the fourth person to disappear from the small town in the same year. All four cases are being treated as homicides by the RCMP. There were also five other killings that year.
A grieving dad
Hosack was a grieving dad who was passing through Dawson Creek in December 2023, on his way to a new job.
He and his fiancée had recently lost an infant son after the baby was diagnosed with a rare heart condition.
The baby was "pure frickin' magic, that boy," said Morgan Crawford, Hosack's partner.
"He looked just like his dad.… Just trauma. Absolute trauma. Cole and I were both in really bad places."
Hosack was living in Prince George at the time. He was offered a job operating heavy equipment in Alberta, which was meant to be a fresh start for the couple, Crawford said. Hosack got a ride from a friend, who needed to stop in Dawson Creek along the way.
Their plan was to celebrate the new year in the northern B.C. community.
On the evening of Dec. 31, according to two people who were with Hosack, he and three others were moving from bar to bar as the night progressed.
A series of Snapchat videos obtained by the fifth estate show Hosack appearing to have a good time.
"Happy New Year's, goofs," he said in one, with cheers and music in the background. "Y'all need to come out here bro and flip this town upside down.
"I'm sure we won't remember tonight, not even a little bit."

- THE FIFTH ESTATEBehind the fear: The unsolved killings in Dawson Creek, B.C.
Hosack and his friends ended the night at a local bar called The LoneStar. According to several witnesses, the only thing that stood out was a short altercation between Hosack and two other men over whose turn it was to use the pool table.
"We're just sitting there having drinks and stuff, and those people that were there came by the pool table and started saying stuff to him," said Dawson Creek resident Laura Lambert, one of the people partying with Hosack that evening.
"I couldn't hear what they're saying, but nit-picking at him and stuff when he's shooting pool."
Lambert said eventually they left him alone and the festivities continued.
Down a dark alley
Throughout the evening, Hosack was in touch with his fiancée, who was back in Prince George, four hundred kilometres south of Dawson Creek.
"He would call me and he'd be outside smoking or he'd be drinking," Crawford said.
"He was drunk, but he was not wasted.… He was happy-drunk that whole night. He kept it to a very chill medium."
The final call from Hosack came shortly before midnight.
"The phone call ended, ‘I love you. I'll see you tomorrow or the next day,'" Crawford said.
Shortly after that, the fifth estate learned, Hosack was captured on the security camera of a local business, hurrying down a dark back alley, followed by a truck.
That was the last time anybody has seen Hosack alive.
Hosack's mother, Julie, declined to comment for this story.
On Facebook, she has been adamant that she believes her son's disappearance is not connected to the drug trade in Dawson Creek.
3 local suspects
More than two years later, following an investigation by the fifth estate, a clearer picture is emerging about what happened that evening.
The fifth estate spoke to six sources who confirmed different aspects of this story. Two of those sources indicated Lawton is heavily involved in the drug trade in Dawson Creek.
Lawton didn't respond to attempts from the fifth estate seeking comment on this fact.
Lawton has never been charged or convicted of a drug-related offence, but the fifth estate has confirmed he was arrested, questioned and released by the RCMP early in 2024 in connection with Hosack's disappearance.
Cellphone records obtained by the fifth estate show the last person Hosack phoned the night he disappeared was Lawton. Lawton never answered the call.
According to multiple sources, three local men were considered suspects in Hosack's disappearance, including Lawton.
According to the source who overheard the potential confession, Hosack owed someone money for drugs and that's why he was being followed down that alley.
"Matt … apparently chased him from LoneStar is what I had heard," he said.
"I overheard Matt kind of like crying and shit, being like: ‘Oh, it wasn't our fault. It was an accident. We didn't mean to [kill him]. We were just trying to threaten him for money.'"
According to the source, Lawton said he didn't cause the death, but he was there when it happened.

- RCMP identify remains in suspicious death investigation near Dawson Creek, B.C.
The RCMP won't comment on the new information, but say they are still working on the case.
"I can tell you it's an active investigation," said B.C. RCMP Supt. Sanjaya Wijayakoon.
Wijayakoon said investigators are still open to all possibilities, but they believe Hosack is no longer alive.
"I believe foul play is at work here."
Lawton needs to come forward: Hosack's fiancée
The new information about the potential confession came as a surprise to Crawford, Hosack's fiancée, but she says it lines up at least partly with something she heard.
She was told by someone in town that Hosack was just supposed to be scared and possibly beaten that night. He wasn't supposed to be killed.
The fact that he might have owed someone money for drugs was new to her.
"My brain is going a million miles a minute right now. What I make of it is that he was struggling with a lot of things and trying to numb all the pain that he had.… We lost a child," she said.
"He struggled, we both did."

Crawford said Lawton needs to come forward and tell the police what he knows. She said Hosack's other young son deserves answers about what happened to his father.
"It's frustrating that Matt [Lawton] is still just doing what he wants to do. He's still just living his life," she said.
"[Cole's son] is getting older. And it would just be nice to be able to tell him [what happened to his dad]. To have his dad home with him in a way. That would bring him some sort of comfort."

SC refuses to restrict CJP's September 5 march in Delhi, says authorities expected to maintain law
The Supreme Court observed that there were no “compelling circumstances” to presume that anything untoward will happen during the CJP march.
The Supreme Court on Monday refused to impose restrictions on the Cockroach Janta Party's march planned for September 5 in Delhi. Chief Justice of India Surya Kant observed that there were no “compelling circumstances” to presume that anything untoward will happen.
The apex court was hearing a plea seeking restrictions on CJP’s proposed march till after the BRICS Summit, which is scheduled to be held in the national capital on September 12-13.
CJI Surya Kant said the authorities were expected to maintain law and order. They must ensure that all sides act peacefully, responsibly and in accordance with the law, he said.
Earlier in the day, CJP co-convener Saurav Das said that it was "unfortunate" that the Supreme Court was being "dragged" into major issues concerning a mass movement. "It will do well for such petitioners to not derail," he wrote on X.
CJP announces September 5 march
Last week, the Cockroach Janta Party announced that it will hold a peaceful march from India Gate to Delhi Police Headquarters on September 5 over the government’s failure to honour its July 25 commitments.
In a statement released after a key press meet, the party said the march will be led by families of deceased NEET victims and victims of alleged police brutality during the July 20 ‘Sansad Chalao’ march.

Welp, the Supreme Court has decided that President Donald Trump gets to build his ballroom. The decision in National Park Service v. National Trust for Historic Preservation is 5-4, with Republican Chief Justice John Roberts joining the three Democratic justices in dissent.
The Supreme Court just gave Trump his illegal ballroom
And the justices didn’t even bother to explain why…
Notably, no member of the Court argued that Trump’s ballroom, an enormous structure that the president plans to build on the former site of the White House’s East Wing, is legal. As Roberts points out in dissent, a federal law prohibits the construction of any “building or structure … on any reservation, park, or public grounds of the Federal Government in the District of Columbia without express authority of Congress.” And, as Roberts writes, “Congress has not passed any law resembling ‘express authority’ for the Executive’s construction of” Trump’s ballroom.
Nevertheless, the five Republicans in the majority manage to rule in favor of Trump by effectively immunizing his ballroom from federal lawsuits.
Their opinion highlights two of the most troubling things about the current Supreme Court: its reluctance to impose limits on Trump’s imperial-style presidency, and the frequent incoherence of its reasoning, especially in Trump cases.
Their opinion suggests that no one is allowed to sue to challenge Trump’s decision to destroy and replace much of the White House. But it is short, does not explain key points of its argument, and relies on several distinctions that do not make any sense.
As a general rule, no one is allowed to file a federal lawsuit unless they can show that they were injured in some way by the defendant they are suing — a requirement known as “standing.” But the Court has long held that plaintiffs suing under conservationist laws that seek to preserve a pristine, sacred, historical, or otherwise beautiful site have standing to bring a suit enforcing such laws against defendants who would damage or destroy such a site’s beauty.
In Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife (1992), for example, the Court said that “the desire to use or observe an animal species, even for purely esthetic purposes, is undeniably a cognizable interest” that can be asserted in federal court. Similarly, the Court held in Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw Environmental Services (2000) that “environmental plaintiffs adequately allege injury in fact when they aver that they use the affected area and are persons ‘for whom the aesthetic and recreational values of the area will be lessened’ by the challenged activity.’”
So that’s how standing worked right up until Monday afternoon, when the Court handed down its latest opinion. The new rule is…well, it is difficult to parse.
The plaintiff in National Park Service is a conservationist organization whose members include a retired professor who would frequently walk by the White House and who admired its beauty. Under decisions like Lujan and Friends of the Earth, that was enough to give her standing to sue in order to challenge the ballroom.
The five Republicans in the majority, however, falsely claim that this individual merely argued that she is offended by Trump’s construction project, and that past decisions have involved “more than mere offense.” The Republicans note that, in Friends of the Earth, the plaintiffs not only wanted to view a river, but also to fish and swim in it and to camp nearby. But they don’t really even attempt to distinguish Lujan beyond a vague statement that Lujan requires a plaintiff’s injury to be “concrete and particularized.”
Thus, because the majority opinion is so poorly explained, it is hard to tell what its implications will be. If the Court had explicitly overruled its past decisions holding that a plaintiff may often sue to challenge the destruction of something beautiful, that would be an existential threat to countless environmental, conservationist, and historical preservation laws that all exist to preserve natural or historic beauty.
But the Court’s failure to explain why Lujan does not require them to rule against Trump leaves lawyers and judges to guess at what the Court just did to the rules governing standing. Perhaps this is a one-off decision intended solely to do a favor for Trump. Or maybe it’s the harbinger of a future decision setting much of America’s environmental protection regime on fire. The five justices in the majority barely explain themselves, so we cannot yet know what National Park Service means.
But one thing that is clear is that the decision makes no sense. As Roberts writes in dissent, “it now is the case that ‘I want to look at a crocodile’ can adequately answer the ever-critical ‘what’s it to you?’ question of Article III standing, while ‘I want to look at the White House’ cannot.” But the justices in the majority couldn’t even be bothered to explain why.

Investigators reported a dose-dependent drop in biomarker levels on certain measures, meaning higher doses led to greater reductions, a sign the drug is having an effect.
Pacibekitug is an antibody that targets IL-6, or interleukin-6, a protein involved in regulating immune responses.

4 ways to cope with constant thoughts about your body image
In the age of weight loss drugs, Instagram face and an endless scroll of Facetuned bodies, it can be difficult to love how your body looks.
But what if you could change the way you think about your body?
Life Kit
How to stop fixating on your body in the era of GLP-1s
Psychologist Diana Hill, a specialist in acceptance and commitment therapy, helps her clients practice mental exercises rooted in "body image flexibility." It's a term from the field of psychology that describes the ability to cope with uncomfortable feelings about your looks.
Body image flexibility doesn't require you to love how your body looks, or even feel neutral about it. It's more about what you do when you have negative thoughts about it.
"How much energy and time are you putting into obsessing about [your looks] in the mirror versus engaging in your life and the things you care about?" Hill says.
Hill, co-author of ACT Daily Journal: Get Unstuck and Live Fully with Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, shares exercises to help you stay present — and deal with the very real pressures we face to obsess about and alter our appearance.
Focus your attention inward
When you look in the mirror and all you can see is your nose, belly, acne or wrinkles, practice flexible attention. That means being mindful of negative thoughts about body image — and redirecting them.
One way to do this, Hill suggests, is to turn your attention to what's happening inside your body instead. Think about all the things your internal organs are doing right now. Are you hungry or full? Does your stomach feel tense or relaxed? Are you feeling nervous? Excited? Happy? Calm?
"It's what we call 'interoceptive awareness,'" Hill says. "It's associated with benefits like better ability to pay attention to hunger and fullness, and better empathy and interpersonal awareness."
Appreciate what your body can do
You can also turn your attention outward by focusing on your body's functionality, Hill says. Ask yourself: How are you using your body at this moment?
You might say, "Right now, I'm sitting on the floor. My eyes are seeing a tree," Hill says. Then take a moment to appreciate those physical abilities. "My eyes may not always be able to see a tree the way I can see a tree now. My ears are receiving sounds. My body is breathing in air. These are ways in which my body is connecting me to this world."
Interrogate your intentions
If you're uncomfortable with a body part, say, your stomach, and are in the habit of sucking it in to make it appear smaller, take a moment to notice that behavior, Hill says. Then, ask yourself some questions.
- Are there times when you're sucking your stomach in more — or less? "There may be times when you let it go a little bit because you feel safer. Maybe you're alone on a hike or in bed," Hill says.
- Is how you feel about your stomach based on a message you've received from culture and society? "Is that messaging [what] you want to believe and let guide your life?" Hill says.
- How do your feelings about your stomach affect your daily life? "Are you less comfortable in your clothes? Are you distracted? Are you not standing up and speaking in front of a group?" Hill says.
This exercise may help you see that "there's a whole slew of things that are happening at the biological level, the psychological level and the social level," Hill says, that leads us to "just automatically shut off a part of our body."
Do an energy audit
"Get honest about how much time and effort is going into your body and where it's taking energy from your life," says Hill. Maybe you're spending a lot of time posting selfies for likes on Instagram, or buying beauty products.
Then ask yourself: What fuels your energy in relationship with your body? "Maybe it's being outside, doing movement you enjoy or playing with your dog," Hill says.
Swap some of the time you spend focusing on your image with another activity that helps you enjoy your body.
"Every little bit of energy you're putting into sucking in your stomach or [feeling] distracted by your shiny face pulls away energy from you," Hill says — your creative force, your ability to connect and your talents. "And what people want is you."

Climate breakdown is happening on one Earth, but two different worlds. In one, its impacts increasingly encroach on everyday life; longer periods of discomfort and shorter periods of sharp pain. Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice in Nepal that so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.
The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. Responses to this summer of wildfires in Europe included a rapid scrambling by the French government to provide everything from tax breaks for businesses affected by the fires to relocation costs and aid to rebuild homes. The UK government had deployed almost £100m before the summer to strengthen wildfire resilience.
Entire industries exist to absorb the impact, undergirded by sophisticated technology, disposable income and evolved sectors. Wildfire insurance in the US is being powered by AI, which spits out numbers to estimate risk based on location and construction material. Outside North America and Europe, there is little of that buffer. The result is asymmetry. While developed countries will still be stressed as events triggered by climate breakdown become more regular and chronic, and they are still not immune to globalised outcomes – rising food costs, droughts, water shortages – what they experience and how disruptive that will be are far removed from other parts of the world.
The difference in scale and resources is colossal. What is needed to rebuild Nepal’s flood damage may constitute up to a 10th of its entire economy – something like $5bn, and that’s not even factoring in all the technical foreign assistance, equipment, expertise and labour required. Also colossal is the difference in exposure to the obliterative effects of events.
Take the death of coral reefs, and how that disproportionately affects coastal populations. Across the Caribbean, coral bleaching caused by rising ocean acidification and temperatures not only dramatically reduces marine life, which is a source of food and income for entire populations – 90% of Jamaica’s economic income is generated alongside its coasts – but also increases the scale and intensity of storms. Coral reefs are a sort of natural storm barrier, absorbing the force of sea waves and buffering coastal areas from flooding. The intersection between these geographical and economic features means countries in the Caribbean are being pummelled on the weather front (climate breakdown also increases the power of hurricanes through warming ocean water), as well as having their incomes drastically reduced and therefore their ability to bounce back.
Then there is the heat. Temperatures are not just jumping far above the average in Europe but also in warmer areas where the base temperatures are already high. Last week, a Harper’s Index summary of estimated heat-related mortality in India showed some staggering numbers: 3,400 excess deaths “caused by a single day of extreme heat”; 30,000 deaths “caused by five consecutive days of extreme heat”. In April of this year, all 50 of the world’s hottest cities were in a single country, India, something which according to the air-quality monitoring platform AQI “has no modern precedent across global weather data”.
This is another double whammy for poor communities without access to shelter or cooling systems of unlimited fresh water. These are the so-called climate breakdown hotspots, identified as “areas where strong physical and ecological effects of climate change come together with large numbers of vulnerable and poor people and communities”. Few places on Earth demonstrate this category more vividly than Sudan. A country already in the grip of war and food insecurity is now succumbing to the delayed rains caused by the El Niño climate pattern, cracking the dry earth and draining the Nile. The risk of famine stalks populations that are already acutely hungry.
And what is felt asymmetrically has been caused in that way too. These poorer, more vulnerable countries are paying the price for the emissions caused by wealthy countries, and not even being extended the full, remedial support from the coffers of those nations that accumulated the wealth generated by industries that contributed to climate breakdown and global heating. We are not just battling complacency, or indifference to the importance of climate justice, but a political climate that has in recent years, led by Donald Trump’s second term, seen its own collapse.
Look closer and the problem isn’t only historical failure but a casual disregard, an adventurism that launches wars and stresses economies with buffers already damaged by the climate crisis. The Iran war in combination with El Niño is a weather and politics collaboration that has hiked fertiliser costs on the one hand and choked rain on the other. More broadly, what was a generously named albeit tenuously implemented “rules-based order”, which at least had some bedrock of global cooperation and aid, has been cancelled altogether. Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris agreement set the tone, while the dismantling of USAID cut the funds that diverted billions of dollars from the rich to the developing world to help with the fallout of extreme weather and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Here is another cascade. As the US withdraws from its commitments, sending the signal that there are no rules or duties, and indeed no problem with climate breakdown at all, pressure will rise on other countries to contribute more. They will need to figure out a way to hold together a coordinated response in the shadow of a destabilising hegemon, as well as try to foster that sense of social obligation in a time of political sociopathy.
The foolish shortsightedness of it all is that even though there is a large gap between experiences, and so a sense that glaciers and floods and famines are happening all the way over there, their knock-on effects and food supply challenges, and political and refugee crises, will affect us all. Things will get dramatically worse for the hotspots, but there is still no outrunning it all in the long term. It seems that at precisely the moment when this realisation should yoke us together in all the ways life is rapidly changing, we are all being untethered. But ultimately, whatever different spheres we inhabit, we are all still trapped on the same planet.

Good morning. Liz Cooney here filling in for Theresa. Our colleague, Europe correspondent Andrew Joseph, has been covering the European Society of Cardiology meeting in Munich this past weekend (more below). I typically pick up American Heart Association meetings stateside.
Which group has the better venues, assuming one ever escapes the giant conference halls long enough to find out? ESC was in Madrid last year and will land in Milan in 2027. AHA has recently toggled between Chicago and New Orleans, but Boston (STAT’s HQ, btw) gets the nod next year. Tell me your preferences as a conference-goer, or a global traveler.
Maybe ‘mRNA’ is no longer a four-letter word
Maybe, just maybe, using mRNA technology to beat back cancer will mean “mRNA” and “vaccine” are no longer taboo. That hope comes after Moderna and Merck’s stunning success with an mRNA vaccine that lowered the odds of surgically removed melanoma spreading or coming back. Reports on top-line results released last week for the neoantigen cancer immunotherapy seemed to dance around calling it an mRNA vaccine.
“There’s a possibility that people will say, ‘Oh, if we can vaccinate against cancer, that’s good,’” Ryan Sullivan, a Mass General Brigham melanoma physician and immunologist who has worked with Moderna, told STAT’s Angus Chen. “Maybe that will thaw some of the stigma around vaccines. I don’t think it’ll fix all of it, but maybe just a little bit helps us think of ‘vaccine’ not as a dirty word, ‘mRNA’ as not a four-letter word.”
The caution makes sense, given the post-pandemic backlash against all vaccines and Moderna in particular. The same agency that funded Operation Warp Speed’s swift success with Moderna’s Covid-19 vaccine later stripped the company of more than half a billion dollars in grants supporting mRNA vaccine development projects.
Read more about the whiplash — not the first for mRNA therapies.
At ESC, a winner, a loser, and a mid-stage signal
The European Society of Cardiology Congress is wrapping up later today. Here are some highlights from STAT’s Andrew Joseph in Munich:
- A newly acquired Novartis drug successfully lowered signs of inflammation in a mid-stage study attracting attention for targeting interleukin-6, a protein involved in regulating immune responses. Pacibekitug is an antibody that targets the IL-6 pathway, although some experts maintain skepticism about the approach. The hope is that targeting inflammation can reduce people’s risk of heart disease or emergencies like heart attack or stroke.
- If “autopsy” is in the headline, the news can’t be good. And it wasn’t for AstraZeneca. The company disclosed details on the surprise failure of its experimental “silencer” drug to offer additional benefits for patients with the progressive condition ATTR-CM who were largely already on another type of medicine, called a “stabilizer”— the latest twist in a multibillion-dollar market.
- It took Cytokinetics 27 years to win its first regulatory approval. The second one could happen much faster than that. The company unveiled the full pivotal study data of its drug aficamten in an inherited heart condition called non-obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, showing that the medicine helped patients feel better and exercise more. Already approved for the obstructive form of HCM, if it wins approval for what’s known as nHCM, it would be the first treatment specifically cleared for the non-obstructive kind.
What could be worse after the Lindsay Clancy case
In the Lindsay Clancy case, it sometimes looks like the mental health system is also on trial. While few would say that system is perfect, there could be a dangerous, unintended consequence, two forensic psychiatrists write in a STAT First Opinion. The legal and public scrutiny around the deaths of Clancy’s three young children could make psychiatrists more reluctant to treat mothers with mental illness.
There are too few reproductive psychiatrists to meet the need, leaving general psychiatrists and OB-GYNs to care for mothers with mental illnesses before and after childbirth. Fears of liability could make these doctors wary of treating mothers who need psychiatric help.
“The many psychiatrists and trainees following this case may be more likely to err on the side of caution by overtreating these symptoms with unneeded hospitalization (and possible separation from their infant), and potentially inappropriate referrals to child protective services,” say Renee Sorrentino, a forensic psychiatrist in Boston, and Susan Hatters Friedman, a forensic and reproductive psychiatrist at Case Western Reserve University. “This then would paradoxically make mothers less likely to report their symptoms, to get the treatment that reduces their risk.”
A solution starts with awareness. Read more about what they suggest.
Pushing boundaries for new radiopharmaceuticals
Radiopharmaceuticals are all the rage in some biotech circles, but some voices of caution are saying slow down. That doesn’t sit well with Louise Emmett, a leader in the field who works with such global drugmakers as AstraZeneca and Novartis. She told STAT’s Allison DeAngelis the time to speed up is now, despite safety concerns in some studies about adverse effects on patients’ kidneys, liver, or bone marrow from the targeted treatment. Radiopharmaceuticals work by directing toxic radiation specifically to cancer cells, decimating them on site.
“I’m interested in how we actually improve survival in our patients, not the toxicities,” said Emmett, who is the director of nuclear medicine at St. Vincent’s Hospital in Sydney.
Her study, called OPTIMAL-PSMA, front-loads doses of radiopharmaceuticals, giving more frequent infusions in the first few weeks of treatment than is the industry standard. The one approved drug in this class, Novartis’ Pluvicto, is administered once every six weeks, adhering to dosing guidelines used for external beam radiation.
So far, results have looked promising in Emmett’s trial. Full data will be reported early next year, potentially at the ASCO Genitourinary Cancers Symposium in February.
Read more about who else is trying this approach.
2.7 million
That’s how many more people around the world will be living with type 1 diabetes by 2049. In the U.S., that means an increase of more than half a million cases, topping out at 2,055,235. The global estimate, presented Friday at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes in Milan, reflects a 29% jump from 9.4 million in 2025 to 12.1 million near the mid-century mark. New cases per year, projected to grow by 14%, are rising more sharply in low-income countries, but absolute numbers remain higher in high-income countries. The researchers say those differences likely stem from a combination of genetics, environmental triggers, and higher case-detection rates in high-income countries.
Who left the dog out?
We all know service animals, often dogs that help humans better navigate the world. Some of us may have seen therapy dogs in the hospital, offering comfort and bringing smiles to patients young and old. But the bond between animals and humans can sometimes get in the way of health, rather than promoting it, if having to care for a dog, for example, means the human says no to a recommended hospital admission.
In their perspective published Saturday in the New England Journal of Medicine, a veterinarian and an oncologist quickly point out the social determinants of health at play in this scenario. What if pet care costs too much? What if the patient is unhoused?
They offer a simple way to solve the problem: talk to the patient.
“Asking about a patient’s pets can improve clinical encounters and strengthen the clinician-patient relationship,” Rustin Moore of the College of Veterinary Medicine at Ohio State University and Reshma Jagsi in the department of radiation oncology at Emory University School of Medicine write. “Physicians who initiate such conversations report improved communication, greater patient openness, and disclosure of information relevant to care, such as responsibilities and routines that shape how patients’ decisions are made.”
No word from the dogs.

French high schools are rushing to put in place a ban on mobile phones this week as Emmanuel Macron pushes for children to spend less time in front of screens.
Education unions warned that banning mobile phone use in lycées – where children are aged 15 to 18 – would be hard to implement quickly.
Macron approved the high school phone ban this month after another measure he had hoped would be a key legacy, his proposed social media ban for under-15s, was knocked back as unconstitutional.
The text of the social media ban is being rewritten in the hope it can be pushed it through before Macron leaves office in May.
France has already banned children from using mobile phones in primary schools and in middle schools, or collèges, which are attended between the ages of 11 and 15.
The government’s focus is now on banning mobile phone use among older teenagers at school from September, as it argues that too much screen time is harming children’s development.
In order to enforce the hurriedly signed-off ban, high schools must amend their rules – a lengthy process – and many schools have said they will struggle to implement the measure swiftly.
“It’s impossible to put this in place from scratch from 1 September,” said Jérôme Fournier, the national secretary of the SE-Unsa trade union. “Schools will need to change their internal regulations and that requires a full consultation process and a vote, and for high school students to be consulted. So we need time for everyone to meet and work on this.”
Fournier said a key challenge was that high school students were often obliged to rely on school smartphone apps to find out even the most basic information for the school day, such as timetables, room changes and homework. “Some even have to use apps on their phones as a badge to enter the canteen to eat lunch or to borrow books from the school library,” he said.
Fournier said high schools often hosted students for higher education courses or apprenticeships, some of whom were aged 20 and needed to use their phones for their work.
He said the key issue for each high school was to decide where exactly to enforce the ban, whether across the whole school, including corridors, or with exceptions such as in the playground. He said teenagers could be tempted to leave the school grounds in order to use their phones on the street outside, which could have implications for security and road safety.
Fournier said students should be consulted on the process rather than being treated as children. “These older teenagers are pre-adults – some in their final school year are going to vote in the upcoming presidential election,” he said.
Macron’s office has said he has no plans to give up on his push to bar under-15s from social media platforms such as TikTok and Snapchat, and the government is working redraft the law.
France’s constitutional council recently struck down the first version of the law after concerns that its definition of social media was not specific enough. This meant a host of sites not generally considered social media but that allowed commentary or communication could be banned, amounting to a “disproportionate restriction” on freedom of expression.
The constitutional council also raised concerns about the privacy implications of putting in place an age-verification system for all users.
Valère Ndior, a law professor at the University of Western Brittany, said it was no surprise to legal experts that the law in its current form had been knocked back, and it would be a challenge to rewrite it. “For the moment, as a legal practitioner, I can’t see how it’s possible to strike a balance between European law and French constitutional law,” he said.

Quick Answer
PowerShell commands such as Get-Help, Get-Command, Get-Process, Start-Process, Stop-Process, Get-Service, Stop-Service, Get-Content, Get-ChildItem, Copy-Item, Move-Item, Remove-Item, and Set-Location help you manage apps, services, files, folders, and system tasks faster on Windows.
PowerShell is a Windows program that simplifies system administration. You can use it to perform many system tasks efficiently and automate repetitive ones. However, to do either, you must know the right commands, or cmdlets (command-lets), as PowerShell calls them.
A typical PowerShell cmdlet follows the verb-noun structure, where the noun is the object you want to act on, and the verb is the action you want to perform on it. This makes them predictable and easy to remember.
Here’s a quick reference guide covering all the essential Windows PowerShell commands to help you get started with PowerShell.
Table of Contents
Essential PowerShell Commands for Windows
Get-Help
Get-Help is a handy cmdlet you can use any time you want to learn about a PowerShell concept or command. It shows information for everything from cmdlets and functions to aliases and scripts. Plus, it shows the exact syntax along with all the available parameters to eliminate the need for guesswork.
Syntax:
Get-Help
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Help cmdlet:
- Get-Help Get-Process : Find out what the Get-Process command does
- Get-Help Get-Process -Detailed : Get a detailed description for the Get-Process cmdlet
- Get-Help Get-Process -Online : View a detailed explanation of the command with examples on Microsoft’s official documentation online
If Get-Help doesn’t return any result, try updating it by running:
Update-Help
Get-Command
Get-Command lists all executable commands installed on your computer, including cmdlets, aliases (or shortcuts that point to other commands), and functions (snippets or scripts that perform specific actions). It’s useful when you want to make sure the command you’re trying to use is supported by PowerShell and available on your system.
Syntax:
Get-Command
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Command cmdlet:
- Get-Command -ListImported : Get a list of all commands in the current session
- Get-Command Get-AppLockerPolicy : View information about the Get-AppLockerPolicy cmdlet
- Get-Command -CommandType Alias : List all alias-type executables
- Get-Command *Service* : Get all the service-related executable elements on your system
Get-Process
Get-Process returns a table of all operating system processes (apps or executables) running on your computer locally. For each item in the table, you see the process name, ID, CPU consumption, and a few other details. This makes it really easy to identify which process is consuming significantly more resources, so you can act on it accordingly and free up system resources.
Syntax:
Get-Process
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Process cmdlet:
- Get-Process -Name notepad : Get details about the Notepad process
- Get-Process explorer | Format-List * : Display detailed information about the explorer processes, including all its properties and their values
Stop-Process
Stop-Process allows you to stop one or more running processes on your computer right from the PowerShell window. To use it, you need the process name or the process ID (or PID), which you can identify by running the Get-Process command.
Syntax:
Stop-Process
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Stop-Process cmdlet:
- Stop-Process -Name notepad : Close the Notepad app
- Stop-Process -Name notepad -F : Force close Notepad
- Stop-Process -Id 3380 : Close the app with a PID of 3380
Start-Process
Start-Process is a PowerShell command that lets you launch one or more processes (or apps) on your computer. You can even open an executable file using it. Start-Process also gives you the ability to choose how you want to start a process. For instance, you may start a program as an administrator or open specific files with their default apps.
Syntax:
Start-Process
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Start-Process cmdlet:
- Start-Process notepad.exe : Launch the Notepad app
- Start-Process -FilePath “notepad” -Wait -WindowStyle Maximized : Open Notepad in a maximized window
- Start-Process -FilePath “sort.exe” : Start a process that uses the sort.exe file
- Start-Process -FilePath “powershell” -Verb RunAs : Open PowerShell as an administrator
Get-Service
Get-Service retrieves and gives you the status of all Windows services running on your computer. It’s useful when you want to identify the status of background services.
Syntax:
Get-Service
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Command cmdlet:
- Get-Service -Name wuauserv : Check the status of the Windows Update service
- Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq "Running"} : Filter services to only view the ones that are currently running
Stop-Service
The Stop-Service PowerShell cmdlet lets you stop a system service. You’d typically use it after you’ve run the Get-Service command and identified the problematic service running in the background.
Syntax:
Stop-Service -Name
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Stop-Service cmdlet:
- Stop-Service -Name wuauserv : Stop the Windows Update service
- Stop-Service -DisplayName “telnet” | Stop-Service : Stop a service using its display name
- Stop-Service -Name Spooler -Force : Stop the Spooler service along with other dependent services
Get-Content
Get-Content helps you read the contents of an item within the PowerShell window. You’d mostly use it to get the contents of a file. All you need to do is specify the file and its location. You can even mention the number of lines in the file you want to read, among other things.
Syntax:
Get-Content -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Content cmdlet:
- Get-Content -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -TotalCount 10 : Read only the first ten lines of the file
- Get-Content -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -Wait : Monitor a file and display new lines as they’re added and the file is saved
Get-ChildItem
The Get-ChildItem cmdlet allows you to view all the items (files and folders) at your specified location. Running it without any parameters returns items in your current location, but you can force it to find items at other locations, too.
Syntax:
Get-ChildItem -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-ChildItem cmdlet:
- Get-ChildItem -Path D:\Test : Find files and folders in the Test folder in the D: directory
- Get-ChildItem -Path D:\Test -Name : Get the names of files and folders at a specified location
- Get-ChildItem -Path D:\Test -Filter *.txt -Recurse : Scan a directory and its folders for all text files
Copy-Item
Copy-Item lets you copy items (files and folders) from one location to another. You just need to specify the path of the file or folder you want to move along with the path of the location where you want to move it. The copied file continues to live at the original location.
Syntax:
Copy-Item -Destination
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Copy-Item cmdlet:
- Copy-Item D:\Test\sample.txt -Destination D:\Test2\sample2.txt : Copy sample.txt file to another location with sample2.txt name
- Copy-Item D:\Test\ -Destination D:\Test2\ -Recurse : Duplicate the Test folder along with all its subfolders and files to Test2
Move-Item
Move-Item is a handy cmdlet for when you want to move an item (file or folder) from one location to another. Unlike the copy command, it doesn’t keep the item at its original location after the operation. Instead, it moves it to the new location.
Syntax:
Move-Item -Path -Destination
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Move-Item cmdlet:
- Move-Item -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -Destination D:\Test2\ : Move the sample.txt file from the Test folder to the Test2 folder
- Move-Item -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -Destination D:\Test2\sample2.txt : Move the sample.txt file to the Test2 folder and rename it to sample2.txt
- Move-Item -Path .\*.txt -Destination D:\Test2 : Move all files with the .txt extension in the current directory to Test2
Remove-Item
Remove-Item allows you to remove or delete one or more items (files and folders) from a location. Remember that this cmdlet permanently deletes the item instead of moving it to the Recycle Bin for restoration.
Syntax:
Remove-Item -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Remove-Item cmdlet:
- Remove-Item -Path D:\Test*.* : Delete all files with a dot (.) in their name
- Remove-Item -Path D:\Test*.* : Delete all files with a .doc file extension in the Test folder
Set-Location
Set-Location lets you change the current working location to your specified location. It’s quite handy when you’ve to perform multiple operations on different directories.
Syntax:
Set-Location -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Set-Location cmdlet:
- Set-Location -Path D: : Set the working location to the D: drive
- Set-Location -Path D: -PassThru : Set the working location to the D: drive and display that location
You Should Also Learn Command Prompt
PowerShell is just one of the many powerful tools Microsoft bundles with Windows. You also have Command Prompt (CMD) — a command-line interpreter that lets you perform various system operations using commands. If you haven’t already, be sure to check out our essential Command Prompt commands cheatsheet, as that can help you use your Windows PC more efficiently as well.

Some people take a coffee before a big meeting. VC Doug Leone said he once took a Novocaine-less tooth removal.
During an interview on the "David Senra" podcast, released on Sunday, Leone, one of Sequoia Capital's best-known partners, said he skipped the numbing agent during a dental drilling procedure.
"I told the dentist, 'Drill without any Novocaine,' and he says, 'You're out of your mind,'" he said. "My whole life, I wanted to see if I was a badass or not."
In an email with Business Insider, Leone clarified that his decision had a practical motive: He had a meeting after, and the dentist told him Novocaine might make him sound or look funny. "That's when I thought, 'Now I will find out whether I am a badass or not,'" he wrote.
It's the kind of story Leone tells often, he said on the podcast, because it's an example of how some of his most consequential moves have been motivated by fear rather than ambition. Each career shift, he said, wasn't inspired by a "vision of greatness," but a "deep and secure need to remain relevant."
"I love fear," he said. "It does wonders for me. It gives me the challenge to overcome that gives me then a sense of security."
Now, clips of his description of the pain-embracing dental trip have made the rounds on the internet. People are giving him the Chuck Norris treatment:
During the interview, Leone also said that when he became a partner at the firm in 1993, he was homeless after a divorce left him with only an allowance for a monthly car note.
"I slept in my car for a week. I showered at 3000 Sand Hill Road. I was down to no money," he said, before adding that he wasn't particularly scared: "My future earnings were going to be terrific. So, I wasn't panicked — I just knew it was only an inconvenience."
That mindset has defined a career that's now in what could be a final act. Leone worked at Sequoia Capital from 1988 to 2022, rising through the ranks to eventually become managing partner. Toward the end of that tenure, he partnered with the first Trump administration on a task force to reopen the US economy following the COVID-19 lockdowns. He stepped down in 2022 at age 65 — but rejoined this past March, amid renewed excitement over AI investing.
Back at the firm, Leone says the fast-paced AI frontier still motivates him through fear — and he's leaning into that, too. He calls himself a "low-level analyst" who must "prove myself" to stay relevant.
"If nine months from now, which is one year since I returned, I feel just as irrelevant, I'm going to take myself," he said. "I don't know if I can do it again. And so, therein lies the fun."

There is much to be said for the extraordinary women living ordinary lives, who nonetheless shaped India. Women have changed public life in the country far more than their presence in formal politics would suggest.
And so, as India marked its 79th birthday over the weekend, I found myself reflecting on the multitude of people’s movements, big and small – as well as the women who helped shape them. During India’s struggle for freedom from British rule, women organised boycotts of British goods, made contraband salt and marched to confront the police, taking on roles usually dominated by men. In the 1970s Chipko movement, protesting deforestation, women put their bodies on the line, wrapping them around trees to stop them being felled, turning a local struggle into a national reckoning over environment and development. More recently, grandmothers in Shaheen Bagh sat to protest the citizenship law, which critics have denounced as discriminatory, creating space for dissent when many thought none existed.
Today, routes into public life for women have multiplied, with social media enabling people without political links to be in the public eye. But not all barriers have disappeared. Electoral politics remains notoriously hard to break into, especially for women. Almost half of all female parliamentarians and state legislators come from political families, while for men it is 18%, a 2025 analysis by Association for Democratic Reforms showed.
What makes a woman leading an ordinary life suddenly want to put her head above the parapet to change things for everyone? I spoke to women thrust into the spotlight in the recent student movement, who have stepped in front of vans, starved themselves and had abuse hurled at them in the process – to find out why they do it.
‘Politics is not just slogans and protests’: Neha Bora, 29
The president of the leftwing All India Students’ Association, Bora fasted for 23 days, demanding accountability over exam paper leaks and the resignation of the Education Minister during the Cockroach Protests. Now, she is touring the country as part of a Gen Z Rising outreach campaign on education reforms.
“I am a PhD student at Jawaharlal Nehru University in theatre and performance studies. My family’s political understanding is very different from mine. I ended up joining politics because that was the only way I could make sense of the times that I was living in – to not be … completely helpless in the decisions that are made for me, that should be made by me. To have a say in what I do, how I do it and what gets done around me. What is tolerable, what is good, what is injustice – all these definitions made sense to me through politics. Theatre was the first thing that taught me that politics is not just slogans and protests. Politics is the very language in which you talk to yourselves, the thoughts you formulate in your head, the relationships you have with your friends, family and peers. Student politics reaffirmed this idea.
Freedom as a student means the ability to study in a university where the model of education has not been turned into an opportunity for profit. Where education is something that helps societies move forward from dogmatism, conservatism and orthodoxy.”
‘Freedom for me is to have a voice – and not be ashamed’: Rhiya Ahir, 27
A model, actor and theatre artist from Mumbai, Ahir made the split-second decision to physically block a police van holding detained protesters – an act that exposed her to an organised hate campaign.
“I started doing theatre when I was four and a half. It taught me empathy and understanding other people’s pain, even people I don’t know. I’ve always been raised with the belief that if you see something wrong you have to step in.
Freedom for me is to have a voice, to put it across confidently and to not be ashamed. I was trolled for a photo in a swimsuit. But what about the uncles who wear chaddis at the Ganga ghat? My clothes are not my character. My clothes cannot overshadow the point or the fact that I was there, and I helped 20 students get back home safely that day. So, my clothes are just my clothes.
The hate did make me second-guess myself. The first two days [after the Mumbai protest] were very difficult because I was still trying to wrap my head around what had happened. They couldn’t find fault with my argument, so they started questioning my character. They went through my Instagram and found that I was a model. They talked about what I wear. They said she’s doing it for the camera.
When the hate started pouring in I was like, ‘What did I do to offend someone? Did I do something wrong?’ Then I realised this doesn’t change my reality. This doesn’t change who I am as a person. I don’t have to prove myself to anyone.”
‘The police have visited my ancestral village asking for information on me’: Danish Ali, 24
Ali was among the student activists on hunger strike at Jantar Mantar. A member of the Jawaharlal Nehru University student union, she faces a year-long suspension for dismantling a facial recognition system at the campus library. For her, freedom is deeply personal and rooted in her identity as a Muslim woman.
“I come from a very small town in Madhya Pradesh. No one in my family had even visited the city, so going to Delhi for higher education was almost like going abroad for education. Since the protest, the police have visited my ancestral village asking for information on me. They called my father, asking him to tell me to focus on my studies.
As a student activist, freedom means to be able to critique the government openly and say that we don’t like their policies. Freedom is being assertive about your individuality and not caring what the society would says, what your parents might say or what the state might do to you.
Freedom also means being an equal citizen in this country. Muslims in this country are being made to feel as if they are secondary and that they don’t have any right to express their religious or cultural identities. I am an equal citizen and I don’t want anyone to tell me otherwise.”
‘What used to work … won’t work with the youth’: Ratna Singh, 31
She traded a career in the law and journalism to join the Cockroach Janata party, where she now serves as the legal head. She felt drawn to the protests, seeing her work reflected in the students’ demand for accountability. Initially hesitant to become its public face, she stepped forward as spokesperson when they needed female voices.
“When I was in law school, most of my classmates would go to law chambers for internships but I would spend the summers teaching children at NGOs. Education has been something I have been very sensitive towards, and I believe every child should have access to it.
A lot of people were criticising us [and calling us] an impatient generation. We are impatient because we want to see change. We can’t be protesting and be OK with not getting answers from the government. We are also just done with divide and rule politics on the basis of religion. Political parties need to understand that what used to work for a certain mindset of people – it won’t work with the youth.
There are so many protests which have begun in different parts of the country. The fear of speaking up is gone. We are seeing a lot of leaders coming up in their own districts. They are starting their own initiatives. I think that’s giving us all hope to keep going.”

A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other measures to address the enduring legacy of racial discrimination.
Guidance published on Monday by the committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) said the obligations arose from a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.
The committee described the approach as a “paradigm shift” away from debates over historical responsibility that have often been used by governments to resist reparations claims.
“States parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for people of African descent, covering all aspects of remedies,” said the UN document, which may be cited in courtrooms.
At least 12.5 million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries in what CERD called the largest forced displacement in history.
Calls for reparations – ranging from official apologies to financial compensation – have gained momentum internationally, though opponents argue states and institutions should not be held responsible for historical crimes. The EU and Britain abstained from a UN resolution on slavery in March.
Some states have sought to dodge claims for justice in courtrooms by arguing that there were no international laws outlawing the slave trade at the time – the so-called intertemporality principle.
But the UN document argues that, regardless of whether slavery and the slave trade were illegal under the laws of the day, countries remain responsible under current international obligations to tackle their continuing effects.
“Irrespective of the legal characterisation of the original historical acts, states parties remain bound by their present obligations under the convention to address structural inequalities,” the UN document says.
Financial compensation alone is not sufficient, it adds, urging “transformative” measures including opening archives, revising public memorials and establishing independent truth commissions.
Pela Boker Wilson, a committee expert from Liberia who helped draft the document, said she expected states to move beyond broad expressions of regret and review policies and laws.
“We are calling on state parties to take concrete and meaningful action,” she told Reuters. “We want to affirm the dignity of those whose suffering was denied, whose suffering was minimised or forgotten.”

Republicans fear voters will punish them in November’s midterm elections after high fuel prices dramatically raised the cost of living
US President Donald Trump will meet oil refining executives on Tuesday as he tries to tame fuel prices sent spiralling by the Iran war ahead of midterm elections in November, the White House said.
The talks at the White House also come days after Trump announced a deal for a huge US stake in the oil reserves of Venezuela, whose leader Nicolas Maduro was toppled by US forces in January.
Republicans fear voters will punish them in November’s crucial US midterm elections after high fuel prices dramatically raised the cost of living for ordinary Americans.
“The president will meet with industry leaders to collaborate on the best ways to increase refining capacity, further unleash American energy dominance across the entire supply chain, and bring down prices for the American people,” White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement to Agence France-Presse on Monday.
The talks were “especially timely as we increase Venezuelan crude flow to US refineries”, a White House official said separately.
The White House did not release a list of companies attending Tuesday’s meeting but said it would include a “mix of small, medium, and large refiners and distributors”.

How to Raise Resilient Children
Introducing a new newsletter series on parenting with more happiness and less worry
Sign up for Raising Resilient Children, Russell Shaw’s eight-week guide to parenting with more happiness and less worry.
When I was 27, I became dean of students at a school in Northern California. I was responsible for 400 students across grades 6 through 12, immersing myself in the lives of other people’s children and learning so much along the way. But I didn’t have kids of my own.
And then I did. Driving him home from the hospital, I kept twisting around at red lights to check on the tiny person strapped into the car seat behind me. I couldn’t quite believe they were letting me take him home. There was no orientation, no manual, no one checking whether I actually knew what I was doing. Just me, my wife, and this small human we were now responsible for raising into an adult.
That’s the thing no one tells you when you’re 27 and confidently managing other people’s kids or newly a parent yourself: There isn’t a single right way to raise a child. Kids are different, circumstances are different, and anyone pitching a foolproof formula is making a fool’s promise. Still, after 25 years as a parent and more than 30 as a school administrator, I’ve come to believe that some approaches serve kids—and parents—better than others. In my eight-week newsletter series, I want to share some of what I’ve learned. I’m not offering a rulebook. Instead, I’m aiming for an invitation to think a little differently about the job.
Sign up now, and you’ll receive an email from me tomorrow at 6 a.m. ET, and then once a week for seven more weeks. Each week, I’ll discuss a different story I’ve written for The Atlantic. Topics will include motivation, friendship, failure, and AI. I’ll tell you a bit about what inspired the story, why it still feels true to me, and what it might mean for you. I’ll also include an original essay, written just for this course, and I’ll take some of your questions. I don’t have a tidy theory of parenting to sell you, and I won’t pretend that the next eight weeks will resolve the hardest questions that you might be carrying about your own kids. What I can offer is what I’ve noticed along the way: that even on the hardest days, there’s real joy in this work, if you know where to look for it.
